findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def` but its body contains no `await` — it calls `requests.get`, which is synchronous and blocks the calling thread. When awaited from an async request handler this freezes the entire event loop (and therefore every other in-flight request on that worker) for the full duration of the billing call, up to the 5-second timeout, and longer if connection setup stalls before the timeout applies.

The file already has the correct pattern immediately above: `fetch_plan` takes an `httpx.AsyncClient` and awaits `client.get(...)`. Mirror it — accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or construct one with `async with`) and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If a sync client genuinely must be used, wrap it in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor` so it does not occupy the loop thread.

findings.title: No test coverage for new fetch_plan_limits blocking-call behavior
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous `requests.get`, which blocks the event loop instead of yielding like fetch_plan's `await client.get`. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so nothing would catch either a regression in its JSON-parsing behavior or the blocking-call defect itself if it were later 'fixed' incorrectly (e.g., wrapped in a fake await that still blocks).

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is dropped into the URL path with an f-string and no `urllib.parse.quote` or format validation. If `tenant_id` originates from a request parameter, a value such as `..%2f..%2fadmin` or `x/../internal-op` lets the caller reach paths on `https://billing.internal/` other than `/limits/<id>` — a request-forgery-flavoured issue against an internal, likely unauthenticated service. `requests.get` also follows redirects by default, so a response from that host can pull the call onward to another internal address.

Suggested fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID/int) before use, or at minimum `quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`, and consider `allow_redirects=False`.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: `except:` catches `BaseException`, so Ctrl-C during a metrics push and `SystemExit` raised by a shutdown path are converted into a normal `return None`. That makes the process ignore interrupt/shutdown signals whenever they land inside `_client.send`, and it also hides genuine bugs such as `NameError` or `AttributeError` in the client. Narrow it to the failures you actually mean to tolerate (e.g. `except Exception:` at minimum, ideally the client's transport/timeout errors) and log the exception rather than discarding it.

findings.title: No test covers new exception-swallowing behavior in push_metrics
findings.body: The change makes push_metrics silently return None on any exception (including KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit via bare except) instead of propagating errors. No test file is present in this diff to verify that push_metrics returns None when _client.send raises, or that the exception is actually suppressed rather than propagated. If this behavior were wrong (e.g. exceptions still propagate, or the wrong value is returned on failure), nothing in the current change would catch it.

findings.title: Public function's exception handling is undocumented
findings.body: The `push_metrics` function is a public API (no leading underscore) that now silently catches and suppresses all exceptions, returning None on any error. This behavior is not documented, and callers have no way to know whether a None return means the payload was sent successfully but returned None, or whether it failed. The bare except also means the function will suppress KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, which is rarely intentional and breaks normal Python shutdown behavior. Either document the behavior in a docstring, or be more specific about which exceptions are caught.

findings.title: try_consume does check-then-act across an await without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, decides against `LIMIT` on line 16, then yields control at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18 before writing on line 19. Any other coroutine scheduled during that yield can perform the same check against the same stale `current`, so N concurrent callers can each pass the check and the tenant ends up well over `LIMIT`. The module already defines `_lock` and `consume` uses it (lines 9-11); `try_consume` should do the same, e.g. wrap lines 15-20 in `async with _lock:` so the read, the decision and the write are atomic with respect to other coroutines.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: unlocked check-then-act with lost update

findings.title: New racy try_consume() has no test covering concurrent calls
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters.get(tenant,0) without holding _lock, then awaits (asyncio.sleep(0)), then writes _counters[tenant] afterward. Two concurrent calls can both read the same 'current' value before either writes, letting the tenant exceed LIMIT. There is no test in this diff exercising concurrent/interleaved calls to try_consume, so this race would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: consume() contract is now ambiguous after try_consume() introduction
findings.body: The module now exports two rate-limit functions with different semantics: `consume()` enforces no limit (it only increments), while `try_consume()` checks against LIMIT before incrementing. A caller reading just the function names cannot tell which one to use or what the difference is. The `consume()` function needs a docstring clarifying that it does not enforce the rate limit and that `try_consume()` should be used for enforcement. Alternatively, `consume()` should be renamed to reflect that it only counts, not limits.

findings.title: try_consume() has no docstring documenting its contract
findings.body: The new public function `try_consume()` has no docstring explaining what it does, what the return value means, or what LIMIT is. While the code is fairly self-explanatory, a caller needs to know: (1) LIMIT is per-tenant and global, (2) it returns False if the operation would exceed the limit, True on success, and (3) the sleep() call on line 18 does not prevent the race condition noted elsewhere.

findings.title: Docstring describes outdated return type
findings.body:
The docstring states the function returns `(name, email)` as a tuple, but the implementation now returns a dictionary with keys `name`, `email`, and `tier`. This mismatch will mislead callers. The existing caller in `reports/weekly.py` unpacks the result as a tuple, which will now fail at runtime. Update the docstring to reflect the new return shape: `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old tuple return value

findings.title: Return shape change breaks existing tuple-unpacking caller
findings.body: `lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of a `(name, email)` tuple. The retrieved caller `reports/weekly.py:6` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`; unpacking a 3-key dict raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call, and even a 2-key dict would bind the *keys* rather than the values, silently producing `"name" <"email">`. Either update `render_row` (and any other callers) to `user = lookup_user(...); user["name"], user["email"]`, or keep the tuple contract and add `tier` as a third element / a separate accessor. Because this is a hard break of a published return shape, all callers must be migrated in the same change.

findings.title: Return-shape change from tuple to dict is untested
findings.body: lookup_user's return type changed from a (name, email) tuple to a dict with name/email/tier keys. The existing caller in reports/weekly.py still does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will now break (unpacking a dict yields its keys, not the expected values). There is no test exercising lookup_user or render_row that would catch this breaking change before it reaches production.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, swallowing insert failures
findings.body:
The `err` from `db.Exec` is scoped to the `if` statement on line 15, so it is only logged and never propagated. Lines 18-19 then declare a fresh `var err error` (zero value `nil`) and return it, meaning `WriteSettlement` unconditionally reports success whenever validation passes — even if the INSERT failed on a constraint violation, deadlock, or connection error. Callers that check `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil` will treat a lost settlement as committed.

Fix by propagating the error the way `WriteEntry` does on lines 7-8:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

findings.title: No test exercises WriteSettlement's error return path
findings.body: WriteSettlement always returns nil from the final `var err error; return err` regardless of whether the db.Exec on line 15 failed. There is no test in this diff that calls WriteSettlement with a failing db.Exec and asserts on the returned error. A test asserting err != nil on insert failure would immediately catch this dropped-error bug; without it, this silent-failure behavior ships uncaught.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` persists across calls
findings.body:
The default list for `attempted` is evaluated once at function-definition time, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, meaning the second call returns its own failures plus every failure from all prior calls — and the returned list is the live default, so a caller mutating it corrupts future calls. Use the idiom already present at line 2 of this file: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = list(attempted) if attempted is not None else []`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared default list leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Mutable default argument misleads callers about function behavior

findings.title: No test exercises send_with_retries across multiple calls
findings.body: send_with_retries uses a mutable default argument (attempted=[]) which persists across calls and accumulates failed recipients from previous invocations. There is no test in this diff verifying that calling send_with_retries twice returns independent results, so this bug would not be caught. A test that calls the function twice with different recipients and asserts the second call's returned list only contains recipients from that call would catch this.

findings.title: compute_rounding drops the exact-half case (>= 0.5 became > 0.5)
findings.body:
The rename of `calc_rounding` to `compute_rounding` also changed the comparison from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. For the exact boundary value `remainder_cents == 0.5` the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1, i.e. round-half-up became round-half-down. Exact halves are the common case in cent-level money arithmetic (any value ending in half a cent), so this will produce off-by-one-cent totals on real invoices and will not be caught by tests that only exercise 0.3/0.7-style inputs. Unless the change of rounding convention is intentional and documented, restore `>= 0.5`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rounding boundary silently flipped from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 inside a rename

findings.title: Boundary change in compute_rounding untested
findings.body: The comparison in the rounding function changed from `>= 0.5` to `> 0.5` during what was described as a pure rename. This changes behavior exactly at remainder_cents == 0.5 (previously rounds up, now does not). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch this regression if it is unintended.

findings.title: Module docstring calls functions 'calculators' but they are now 'compute' functions
findings.body: The module docstring describes the functions as 'Line-item calculators' but after the rename from calc_* to compute_*, this description is now misleading. The word 'calculators' suggests the old naming pattern, which no longer applies. Update the docstring to reflect the new naming: 'Line-item computer functions' or similar.

findings.title: Off-by-one slice drops the last record of every page
findings.body:
The slice end should be `start + PAGE_SIZE`, matching `page_of` on line 6. As written, each page returns only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items while `start` still advances by `PAGE_SIZE` per page, so the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned on any page — data is silently lost from the export rather than merely paginated oddly. Change line 12 to `return ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted slices one record short per page

findings.title: page_of_sorted drops last record per page, no test would catch it
findings.body: The new function slices `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, which returns one fewer record than PAGE_SIZE per page — silently dropping a record on every page. No test file is included in this diff, so this off-by-one bug (and any future regression of correct pagination logic) has nothing to catch it.

findings.title: AttributeError when purchase_order is None (the common case)
findings.body:
`invoice.purchase_order` is typed `str | None` and documented as set for only about one account in twenty. The removed guard was the only thing preventing `.upper()` from being called on `None`, so `header_lines` now raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for roughly 95% of invoices. Restore the conditional append, or guard the value inline (e.g. build the list then `if invoice.purchase_order is not None: lines.append(...)`).

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test would catch AttributeError when purchase_order is None

findings.title: Removed null guard contradicts documented optional field
findings.body: The function `header_lines()` now calls `.upper()` on `invoice.purchase_order` without checking for None (line 4). However, the `Invoice` model explicitly documents that `purchase_order` is optional: "only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty." This creates a contract violation — callers following the model's documentation will pass invoices with `purchase_order=None`, causing the function to crash. Either document the new precondition that `purchase_order` must be set before calling this function, or restore the null guard.

findings.title: File handle leaks when the header check fails
No test exercises read_validated's failure path
findings.body: read_validated(path, expected_header) is new behavior with a branch (header mismatch returns None without closing fh) that is not covered by any test in this diff. A test that calls it with a mismatched header and asserts the return value, and ideally checks the file handle is closed, would have caught the leak on line 14.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge; can double-charge customers
findings.body:
`billing.gateway.charge` documents itself as NOT idempotent — "each call creates a new charge" — and says the gateway supports an `Idempotency-Key` header to make retries safe. `charge_card` wraps it in `@retry(attempts=3)` without supplying such a key. Any failure mode where the request reaches the gateway but the response is lost (timeout, connection reset, 5xx after commit) will be retried and will create a second (and third) real charge against the customer's card. The adjacent `fetch_charge` is fine because GET is safe to repeat; the two are not equivalent.

Fix by generating a stable idempotency key per logical charge *outside* the retry loop and passing it to the gateway, so all attempts collapse to one charge; or drop the retry here and let the caller decide, reconciling with `get_charge` before re-attempting.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Retried non-idempotent call lacks safety documentation
findings.body: The `charge_card` function wraps `charge()` with `@retry`, but `charge()` is documented as NOT idempotent and requires an Idempotency-Key header to make retries safe. This new function's contract does not document: (1) that retries will occur, (2) that the underlying call is non-idempotent, or (3) how to ensure idempotent retry safety. A caller using this function could inadvertently create duplicate charges if the retry mechanism is triggered. The function needs a docstring explaining the retry behaviour and the idempotency requirement, or the retry decorator should not be applied without proper safeguards.

findings.title: No test catches retrying a non-idempotent charge call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge with @retry(attempts=3), but charge() is documented as NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge) and no Idempotency-Key is passed. There is no test verifying retry behavior for charge_card, so a scenario where a transient failure causes the gateway to actually create the charge before the client sees an error (leading to 3 duplicate charges on retry) would go undetected. Any test suite for this module would need to at least assert that charge_card either avoids retrying non-idempotent calls or passes an idempotency key.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`cutoff` is built from `datetime.now()` with no tzinfo, so it is naive. `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so line 10 fails for every invite — the function is unusable as written. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. Note that even with a naive comparison that happened to work, `datetime.now()` returns local wall time, which would silently skew the result by the UTC offset.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Expiry window control uses naive local time, not UTC

findings.title: Timezone-aware/naive datetime comparison violates documented contract
findings.body: The `expires_within()` function at line 8 creates a naive datetime on line 9 (`datetime.now()` without timezone) and subtracts it from `invite.expires_at`, which is documented as "always tz-aware" in models/invite.py. Python raises `TypeError` when comparing or performing arithmetic between timezone-aware and naive datetimes. This breaks the function regardless of whether the documentation or code is wrong—the documentation has made it explicit that `expires_at` is timezone-aware, so any operation assuming otherwise is now a breach of that contract.

findings.title: expires_within has no test, so its naive/aware datetime bug would go undetected
findings.body: The new function expires_within compares invite.expires_at (tz-aware, per models/invite.py) against datetime.now() (naive), which would raise a TypeError at runtime. No test file is included in this diff, so this defect would not be caught by CI before shipping.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding". `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it directly, so for any account that has not completed onboarding this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')` at runtime. The sibling function on line 4 handles exactly this case with `account.billingContact?.name ?? "No billing contact"`, which shows the absent case is reachable in practice.

Either mirror that pattern — e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? ""` — or change the return type to `string | undefined` and let callers decide. If `strictNullChecks` is enabled the compiler will already reject this, which suggests it is off and the bug will only surface in production.

findings.title: Public function does not document unsafe access to optional field
findings.body: The function `contactEmail` is public but lacks documentation explaining that it will throw a runtime error if `account.billingContact` is absent. The `Account` interface explicitly documents that `billingContact` is optional ("Absent until the customer completes onboarding"), but this function accesses `.email` without any null check, chaining, or guard. A caller reading the function signature alone cannot tell whether it is safe to call on any Account or only on certain states. This is a contract violation—a public function should document what states it accepts.

findings.title: No test covers contactEmail with missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail dereferences account.billingContact.email without a null check, even though Account.billingContact is optional (per types.ts). If an account without a billing contact is passed in, this throws a TypeError at runtime. There is no test in this diff exercising that path, so this defect would ship silently.

findings.title: Default retry count change breaks documented caller
findings.body: The function signature's default for `retries` has been reduced from 5 to 1. The docstring in sync/nightly.py explicitly documents that the partner sync relies on fetch()'s default retry count to survive a known flaky API that returns 503 roughly one in three calls. Callers acting on this documented behavior will now fail. Either restore the default to 5, update the caller to explicitly pass retries=5, or update the docstring in sync/nightly.py to reflect the new reality.

findings.title: Lowered retries default regresses the INC-4471 fix in nightly sync
findings.body:
`fetch()`'s default `retries` goes from 5 to 1. `sync_partner_catalogue()` calls `fetch("https://partner.example.com/catalogue")` with no `retries` argument and its docstring states explicitly that it depends on the default retry count to get past a partner API that returns 503 roughly one call in three, and that this was the fix for INC-4471. With 5 retries the chance of the nightly sync failing is under 1%; with 1 retry it is roughly 1 in 9 — a regression of a previously incident-generating failure mode, reintroduced silently because the caller passes no explicit value.

Either keep the default at 5, or make the change safe at the call site by passing `retries=5` explicitly in `sync_partner_catalogue()` (and auditing any other default-relying callers) in the same change.

findings.title: No test covers fetch()'s default retries relied on by sync_partner_catalogue
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() depends on fetch()'s default retry count to survive a documented flaky dependency (INC-4471), but there is no test asserting fetch's default retries value or exercising sync_partner_catalogue against a flaky/503-returning mock. Lowering retries from 5 to 1 would silently reintroduce INC-4471 with nothing failing to signal it.

findings.title: Index duplicates invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body:
`invoices_tenant_created_idx2` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same table, column list and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in `migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql` and applied 2025-11-02. Because the name differs, Postgres will happily build a second identical index rather than erroring, so the redundancy is silent: it costs disk, slows every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on `invoices`, and the planner will never prefer it over the existing one.

If the index was believed to be missing, drop this statement — 0007 already covers the tenant lookup. If a genuinely different access path is needed (e.g. a partial index, different column order, or INCLUDE columns), change the definition so it actually differs. Separately, building an index on `invoices` without `CONCURRENTLY` takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE-style write lock for the duration of the build, which is worth avoiding on a table large enough to warrant this index in the first place.

findings.title: Referer logged verbatim reintroduces auth token leak into logs
findings.body:
The previous code special-cased `Referer` and passed it through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before storing it in the `headers` dict that is dumped to the log on line 6. The new line copies the raw header value for every header, including `Referer`. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, and the browser echoes that URL in the `Referer` header of every subresource request — so any 5xx on such a request now writes a live auth token into the log. Anyone with read access to the logs (operators, log shippers, crash reports) obtains a valid credential. Restore the per-header scrub for `Referer` (and keep `extra_param_keys` flowing into it) rather than collapsing the branch.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token in Referer is logged verbatim after scrub removal

findings.title: No test guards against unscrubbed Referer header leaking tokens
findings.body: The change removes the _scrub_uri call for the Referer header, restoring the exact behavior the original fix addressed (tokens embedded in Referer URLs being logged verbatim). No test in this diff asserts that a token-bearing Referer is scrubbed before being logged, so this regression would not be caught by any existing suite as shown.

findings.title: `extra_param_keys` (and `_scrub_uri`) likely now unused/dead
findings.body: With the `Referer` branch removed, `extra_param_keys` no longer has a consumer in this function and `_scrub_uri` may have no remaining call site in this module. If the scrub is intentionally being dropped, the now-dead parameter and import should be removed too; if it is not intentional, that dead state is itself the signal that the removal was a mistake. I cannot see the enclosing function signature or module imports, so confirm before acting.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer scheme-checked, reopening javascript: XSS
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` matches neither arm of the condition, so it falls past this guard to whatever the function's trailing default is — evidently permissive, since that is why the explicit checks exist for `href`/`src`. An SVG element such as `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` in user-submitted markdown will therefore be rendered with an executable URL. The file header states this markdown includes end-user content and that `validateProp` is the only barrier before the DOM. Restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` unless xlink:href is now stripped upstream — and if it is, that stripping should be shown, because nothing in the retrieved context does it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, re-enabling SVG XSS

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref sanitisation, regression slipped through silently
findings.body: The removal of the `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` check reverts a prior XSS fix, but no test file is part of this diff. If there had been a regression test asserting that `xlinkhref` attributes with unsafe URI schemes are rejected by `validateProp`, this change would have failed CI. Since none exists (or none was updated to fail), this dangerous change merges silently. Add/restore a test asserting `validateProp('xlinkhref', 'javascript:...')` (or equivalent) returns false.

findings.title: Removed ValidateID lets query param reach buildPath unvalidated
findings.body:
`query.GetProjectQueryParam()` is user-controlled and, in the file-backed DAO, ends up as a path segment in `buildPath(project, kind)` via `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)`. `buildPath`'s doc comment states explicitly that it does no validation of its own and that callers are required to have validated the names before this point. This `list` handler was that caller. With the `common.ValidateID` check removed, a value such as `../../etc` or `..%2f..` survives to `filepath.Join`, which cleans the `..` segments and resolves outside `d.Folder`, allowing reads of arbitrary directories/documents outside the storage root. The remaining check on lines 4-6 only compares the query value against the path value; it does not constrain the character set, and it is skipped entirely when `parameters.Project` is empty. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` call (returning `HandleBadRequestError`) before the value is used or compared.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed ValidateID allows path traversal via project query parameter

findings.title: Removed path-traversal validation has no test guarding it
findings.body: The diff removes the common.ValidateID check on projectQueryParameter before it is used (per repository context) to build a filesystem path via buildPath. There is no test in this PR exercising the list() function with a malicious/invalid project query parameter (e.g. containing '../') to confirm it is rejected. If this validation is wrong or missing, nothing in the current test suite would fail, since no test file touches this behavior.

findings.title: Public API now violates documented precondition
findings.body: The `list` function removes validation of `projectQueryParameter` before it reaches filesystem operations. The `buildPath` function in `internal/api/database/file/file.go` explicitly documents: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." By removing the `ValidateID` check here, this function no longer meets that precondition. Callers who expect this function to validate its query parameter (a reasonable expectation given it previously did) will now pass unvalidated paths to filesystem operations.

findings.title: Part buffer pre-allocated from client-declared Content-Length
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` sizes the pool-backed buffer from a value the client controls (the `Content-Length` / part length of the upload request) *before* any of the body is read. A caller can send `PUT ...?partNumber=N` with `Content-Length: 10737418240` and then send no bytes (or trickle them), and the server commits the memory up front. Repeating this across a handful of connections drives the process into OOM; the previous code grew the RW a page at a time as `io.Copy` on line 8 actually consumed bytes, so the peak allocation was bounded by the bytes really delivered.

Fix: either restore the incremental growth, or clamp the hint — e.g. `Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartReserve))` with a small ceiling, and reject `contentLength` above the S3 part-size limit (5 GiB) before allocating. Any reservation must be a bounded optimisation, never an attacker-chosen allocation size.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Negative/unknown contentLength passed to Reserve unguarded

findings.title: Buffer sized from unvalidated client Content-Length before body is read
findings.body: `contentLength` on an S3 UploadPart request comes straight from the client's `Content-Length` header; nothing in this function bounds or cross-checks it. Reserving that many bytes up front means a request advertising a huge length commits the memory immediately, before `io.Copy` on line 8 has read a single byte, and a client can then send an empty or trivially small body (or several such requests concurrently) to exhaust the process heap at negligible cost. The previous code grew the pool-backed RW incrementally as bytes actually arrived, so peak memory tracked real data. Either drop the `Reserve` call and let the RW grow on demand, or clamp the reservation to a small maximum (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartBuffer)`) and reject the request once `n` exceeds the declared length.

findings.title: No test covers Reserve(contentLength) with an attacker-controlled length
findings.body: The change makes uploadPart eagerly reserve a buffer sized by the caller-supplied contentLength before any bytes are read, reversing the pool-backed incremental growth described in the removed comment. No test in this diff exercises a call with a large or mismatched contentLength (e.g. a declared length far exceeding the actual body size, or an excessively large declared length) to confirm memory allocation is bounded. If Reserve blindly allocates the declared amount, nothing here would fail even for pathological inputs.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The previous expression (`"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`) defaults to HTTPS and only downgrades when a caller explicitly opts in with `is_secure=False`. The new expression (`"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"`) defaults to HTTP whenever the meta key is missing, `None`, or any other falsy value — which is the common case, since most requests never set `is_secure` at all.

The scheme is interpolated straight into the request URL on line 6, so the AWS-signed request (Authorization header / query signature, and any object payload) is transmitted in cleartext. A network attacker on the path can read the signature and the object data, and can tamper with the response body that is then fed back into the spider. This is a transport-security control being switched off by default, not merely a degraded one.

Restore the fail-secure default: treat the absence of the key as HTTPS, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Default S3 scheme flips to plaintext http when is_secure is unset

findings.title: No test covers the default scheme when is_secure is absent
findings.body: The change flips the default behavior: previously, when request.meta has no 'is_secure' key, the scheme defaulted to 'https' (since the check was `is False`, and a missing key returns None, not False). Now, when 'is_secure' is absent, `request.meta.get('is_secure')` is falsy (None), so scheme defaults to 'http'. This is a behavior change with security implications (signed requests going over plaintext HTTP). No test file is present in this diff exercising download_request with is_secure unset, true, or false, so this regression would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: DELETE requests now authorize as "push", not "delete"
findings.body:
The previous switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `delete` action. The collapsed form only distinguishes GET/HEAD from everything else, so a DELETE request yields `action = "push"` and is authorized against the push grant. Per `pkg/api/config/config.go`, push and delete are intentionally separate actions — an account allowed to push new tags is explicitly not meant to be able to delete existing ones. Any credential holding push on a repository can now destroy tags/manifests in it. Restore an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` (or an equivalent `if m == http.MethodDelete` branch before the push fallback).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorised as "push": push token grants delete

findings.title: No test verifies DELETE requests require delete-action authorization
findings.body: The change collapses the switch so any non-GET/HEAD method (including DELETE) maps to "push". This means a token with only push permission could now perform deletes, which the repository's own docs explicitly warn against (config.go: "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones"). No test in this diff exercises a DELETE request and asserts the resulting action is "delete" (not "push"), so this regression would not be caught by any existing suite.

findings.title: DELETE method now maps to push, contradicting documented action contract
findings.body: The code now maps DELETE requests to the 'push' action (line 5-6), but pkg/api/config/config.go documents that 'delete' is a distinct action: 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' This means access control expectations are now inverted—callers relying on the documented three-action contract will be surprised that DELETE grants push access, not delete access.

findings.title: "delete" action is now unreachable, breaking delete-only grants
findings.body: After this change no code path can ever produce `action = "delete"`, so any configured grant of the `delete` action is dead configuration: an account granted delete but not push can no longer delete, while the check it was meant to gate is silently satisfied by push instead. Separately, methods the old code deliberately defaulted to `pull` (OPTIONS, TRACE, etc.) now require push, which will reject previously-allowed requests. Reinstating the explicit DELETE case and the `default: action = "pull"` fallback fixes both.

findings.title: get_* function mutates cache, violating naming convention
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh()` uses the `get_*` prefix, which conventionally indicates a read-only operation that returns a value without side effects. However, this function mutates the cache by writing to `_CACHE[tenant_id]` on line 10 and potentially clearing it on line 12. A caller expecting standard `get_*` semantics would be surprised by these mutations. Rename to `fetch_and_cache_tenant()` or similar to accurately convey that this is a fetch-and-store operation, not a lookup.

findings.title: Size cap clears the whole cache, discarding the entry just written
findings.body: When the cache crosses 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` drops every entry, including the `tenant` inserted on line 10 one statement earlier. The function still returns the fetched value, so the caller sees the right answer, but `get_tenant(tenant_id)` will return `None` immediately afterwards for the very tenant that was just refreshed \u2014 and for every other tenant too. In a workload that sits near the cap this degenerates into a full cold cache on roughly every insertion, so the hit rate collapses rather than settling at a bounded size. If bounded eviction is the intent, evict a single entry (or use `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache` semantics) instead of clearing, and perform the size check before inserting so the fresh entry survives.

findings.title: No test coverage for get_tenant_fresh's caching/eviction logic
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches a tenant, writes it into _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once size exceeds 1000. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. If the eviction threshold were wrong, or the cache write were omitted/broken, or _fetch's result were not properly cached, nothing would fail.

findings.title: A None result from _fetch is cached and is indistinguishable from a miss
findings.body: The return value of `_fetch` is stored unconditionally. If `_fetch` can return `None` for an unknown or deleted tenant, that `None` is written into `_CACHE`, and `get_tenant` (line 5) uses `_CACHE.get(tenant_id)`, which also returns `None` on a miss \u2014 so callers cannot distinguish "known absent" from "not cached", and the negative entry is never invalidated by a normal miss path. Consider only caching truthy results, or using a sentinel so misses and negative results are distinguishable. I have not been shown `_fetch`, so this depends on whether `None` is a reachable return value there.

findings.title: Caller-supplied tenant_id can flush the whole cache
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` inserts an entry for whatever `tenant_id` it is handed (line 10) and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries (lines 11-12). If this helper is reachable from a request path where `tenant_id` is attacker-influenced, ~1000 requests with distinct ids evict every legitimate entry, pushing all subsequent `get_tenant` calls back to `_fetch` — a cheap amplification lever against the backing store. Validating that `tenant_id` corresponds to a real, authorised tenant before inserting, and evicting LRU-style instead of `clear()`, removes both the poisoning surface and the thundering-herd effect. I could not see any caller, so whether `tenant_id` is attacker-controlled here is unverified.

findings.title: README documents renamed CLI flag with old name
findings.body: The README at line 7 documents the `--workers` flag, but the code has renamed it to `--concurrency` in cli.py line 6. Users following the README will use an argument that no longer exists, causing their command to fail. Update the README to reflect the new flag name.

findings.title: Flag rename changes argparse dest, breaking args.workers callers
findings.body: `p.add_argument("--workers", ...)` implicitly set `dest="workers"`; the replacement sets `dest="concurrency"`. Every consumer of the parsed namespace that reads `args.workers` will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime rather than fail at import/lint time, and any shell script or CI invocation passing `--workers N` will now exit 2 with "unrecognized arguments". If the rename is intended, either grep-and-update all `args.workers` readers in the same change, or keep compatibility by adding `p.add_argument("--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, help=argparse.SUPPRESS)` as a deprecated alias. I was not given the call sites, so I cannot confirm how many readers exist — that check is the thing to do before merging.

findings.title: Flag rename has no test verifying --concurrency parses correctly
findings.body: The --workers flag was renamed to --concurrency in cli.py but there is no test in this diff exercising the parser to confirm the new flag name is accepted (and the old one is gone). If this rename were reverted or typo'd, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Docstring does not match changed return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function "Return[s] the total number of API calls this month as an integer" but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping day to count. A caller reading the docstring will expect an integer and will fail when trying to use the result. Update the docstring to describe the new return contract: a dictionary with day as key and count as value.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict; docstring and callers unchanged
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a single integer via `_db.scalar(...)`. It now returns a `dict` mapping day -> count. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently misbehave or raise a TypeError. Either keep the scalar and add a separate `daily_usage` function, or update the docstring and audit/adjust every call site. At minimum the docstring on line 2 must stop claiming "the total number of API calls this month as an integer".

findings.title: Behavior change to monthly_usage has no accompanying test
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of a single integer total, a breaking change to its return contract. No test file is included in this diff to verify the new grouping/aggregation logic (e.g., that rows are correctly grouped by day and counts are correct). If this logic were wrong, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body:
`list_invoices` is a module-level function with no leading underscore, so it is part of the public surface of `api/listing.py`. Renaming the second parameter from `page_size` to `limit` is source-incompatible for any caller that passes it by keyword (`list_invoices(t, page_size=100)`), which will now fail with `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. Positional callers are unaffected, which is exactly why this breakage tends to slip past a quick grep.

No repository context was retrieved for this review, so the call sites could not be checked. Before merging, grep for `page_size=` across the codebase and any external consumers. If the name must change, either update all call sites in the same change or accept both temporarily (e.g. `def list_invoices(tenant_id, limit=50, cursor=None, page_size=None)` with a deprecation warning when `page_size` is supplied).

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter by old name
findings.body:
The parameter was renamed from `page_size` to `limit` in the function signature on line 1, but the docstring on line 6 still documents it as `page_size`. Update the docstring to match the new parameter name so callers see the correct name in help text and IDE tooltips.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the removed `page_size` parameter

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not a package-relative import
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is explicitly relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist on a normal install. Under Python 3 (or Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this raises `ImportError` at import time, so `import requests` fails entirely. It should be `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: `old_request` still calls the deleted `_send_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, but the retained `old_request` path still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or delete/redirect `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: New `request()` silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch, config, return_response
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies (plus three TODO attributes) before calling `self.send(prep)`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and then discarded. Existing callers that pass `timeout=5` now get a request with no timeout (indefinite hang), and callers passing `verify=False`/`cert=...` lose their TLS settings — a silent behaviour change rather than a visible error. Either thread these through to `send()` or raise `NotImplementedError` for the ones not yet wired up.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import ...` resolves off sys.path, not the package
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this file is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`), but this one is absolute. Under absolute-import semantics it will not find `requests/adapters.py`; it resolves against `sys.path`, whose first entry is the script/CWD directory for a directly-invoked program. That means any `adapters.py` an attacker (or an unrelated dependency) can place earlier on `sys.path` is imported and executed inside the library, and `HTTPAdapter()` on line 365 — the object that now performs every outbound request — comes from that module. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: `close()` became a no-op while each send builds a fresh adapter/pool
findings.body: `init_poolmanager` and the `self.poolmanager.clear()` in `close()` were removed, so `close()` (and therefore `__exit__` at line 129) no longer releases any pooled connections. At the same time `send()` constructs a brand-new `HTTPAdapter` — and thus a new connection pool — on every call, so nothing is reused and nothing is ever torn down. Sockets accumulate for the life of the process. The adapter should be created once per session (e.g. in `__init__`) and `close()` should close it.

findings.title: `verify`, `cert` and `timeout` accepted by request() but silently dropped
findings.body:
The new `request()` accepts `verify`, `cert`, `timeout` (and `prefetch`, `config`) but never assigns them to `req` or passes them to `self.send(prep)` — only method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies/redirects/proxies/hooks are carried over. A caller who explicitly passes `verify='/path/ca.pem'` or `verify=True` gets no error and no verification behaviour change: TLS peer validation falls back to whatever `HTTPAdapter.send()` defaults to, which is not visible here. Likewise a client certificate (`cert`) is dropped, and `timeout` is dropped so a hostile or slow server can hang the caller indefinitely. Either thread these through to the prepared request/adapter or remove them from the signature until they are wired up, so the silent no-op cannot be mistaken for enforcement.

Entry point: the public `Session.request()` arguments; sink: `adapter.send(request)` on line 366, which never sees them. I cannot see `adapters.py` or `Request.prepare()`, so the resulting default verification behaviour is unconfirmed.

findings.title: New adapter-based send() path and no-op close() are untested
findings.body: Session.send() now instantiates HTTPAdapter() and delegates to it instead of calling request.send() directly, and close() was changed to `pass`, dropping the PoolManager.clear() call. No test in this diff exercises Session.send(), Session.request(), or Session.close() to confirm the adapter actually returns a valid response or that resources are still released. If the adapter wiring is broken (e.g., import failure or wrong return value) or if removing the poolmanager cleanup leaks connections, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Deleted docstring for close() method now stale
findings.body: The `close()` method previously had a docstring explaining it disposed of internal state by closing the PoolManager and pooled connections. This docstring was removed when the method body was replaced with `pass`. If this is a temporary work-in-progress change, the old documentation should be restored or updated to reflect the new (empty) implementation. For a public method, callers expect either documentation or clear behavior.

findings.title: `Session.poolmanager` attribute removed without replacement
findings.body: Dropping the `self.init_poolmanager()` call from `__init__` means `session.poolmanager` no longer exists. `init_poolmanager()` was a public-looking hook and `poolmanager` was a documented attribute of the session; any user or internal code that overrides the hook or touches `session.poolmanager` now gets an `AttributeError`. If the pool now lives on the adapter, expose it there and keep a shim (or note the break) rather than removing it silently. The `PoolManager` import at line 19 is also now unused.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on parse failure, breaking callers
findings.body:
In the moved property, the `except Exception` branch sets `self._cookies = None` and the property then returns `None`. The original implementation in `web.py` kept `self._cookies` as a `SimpleCookie` (it called `self.clear_all_cookies()`, which does not rebind `_cookies`), so the property always returned a dict-like object.

The callers were not updated for the new `None` return shape:

- `web.py:321` — `if name in self.request.cookies:` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.
- `web.py:367` — `for name in self.request.cookies.iterkeys():` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'iterkeys'`.

Because `hasattr(self, "_cookies")` is true once it is set to `None`, the failure is sticky for the whole request. A client sending a malformed `Cookie` header (e.g. an illegal cookie name, which makes `SimpleCookie.load` raise `CookieError`) turns every cookie read — including secure-cookie and XSRF paths that go through `get_cookie` — into a 500.

Fix: on failure reset to an empty container rather than `None`, e.g. `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()`, so the documented "dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects" contract holds. Note this also silently drops the old side effect of instructing the browser to clear the bad cookies; if that behaviour matters it must be re-added on the `RequestHandler` side, since `HTTPRequest` cannot emit `Set-Cookie` headers.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing all callers

findings.title: Malformed-cookie fallback behavior change is untested
findings.body: The original RequestHandler.cookies property recovered from a bad Cookie header by calling self.clear_all_cookies() (leaving self._cookies as an empty SimpleCookie). The moved HTTPRequest.cookies property instead sets self._cookies = None on the same exception. This is a behavior change with a different failure mode for every caller that indexes into or iterates self.request.cookies (e.g. web.py's get_cookie and clear_all_cookies), since None does not support 'in' or iterkeys(). No test exercises the malformed-Cookie-header branch, so this regression would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Docstring does not mention None return value
findings.body: The `cookies` property docstring states it returns 'A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects,' but the implementation (line 523) sets `self._cookies = None` if cookie parsing fails. Callers cannot safely assume the return value is always dict-like without checking for None first. The docstring should document this possibility.

findings.title: Boundary never matched: split(";") leaves leading space in key
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` produces parameter segments that retain the leading space that virtually every client emits, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"` -> `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"]`. `field.partition("=")` then yields `k == " boundary"`, so `k == "boundary"` is false, the loop never breaks, and the `for ... else` branch logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" instead of parsing the body. `self._request.arguments` / files are left empty for all real-world multipart uploads — a regression from the previous `'boundary=' in content_type` substring test, which tolerated the whitespace.

Fix: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Content-Type parameters not stripped; boundary never matches

findings.title: New multipart boundary-parsing logic has no accompanying test
findings.body: The old boundary-extraction logic (`'boundary=' in content_type` + split) is replaced with a loop that splits on ';' and does an exact `k == "boundary"` match after partitioning on '='. This is fragile to whitespace around parameter names (e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=xxx` — a very common real-world header format — has `k == " boundary"` after split, which will never equal `"boundary"`), yet no test in the diff exercises this path with a realistic Content-Type header. Nothing here would fail if the new parsing silently stopped matching valid boundaries.

findings.title: Quoted boundary value passed through with quotes intact
findings.body: RFC 2046 permits (and some clients emit) a quoted boundary: `boundary="----abc"`. `v` here is the raw token, so the quotes are handed to `_parse_mime_body`, which will then look for `--\"----abc\"` and fail to split the parts. Since the code is already being rewritten to parse parameters properly, strip surrounding quotes: `v = v.strip('"')` (or use `email.utils`/`cgi.parse_header`). Note this was also true of the previous implementation, so it is not a regression — just an unfixed gap in the new parser.

findings.title: Error message format string missing argument
findings.body:
The error message raised at line 100 contains a format placeholder `%s` but is not formatted with the URL that failed to parse. When this exception is raised, it will display literally as "Failed to parse: %s" instead of showing the actual URL that caused the error. This makes debugging harder and the error message misleading about what actually failed. The exception should format the message with the URL: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`

_Also raised by the security agent:_ LocationParseError message has a %s placeholder with no argument

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ LocationParseError message has an unfilled %s placeholder

findings.title: get_host ignores query/fragment, can disagree with urlparse on the host
findings.body:
`get_host` splits on `://`, then `/`, then `@`, then `:`. It never accounts for `?` or `#`, which terminate the authority component just as `/` does. For `http://good.com?@evil.com` the `/` split does not fire, so the `@` split treats `good.com?` as userinfo and returns `evil.com` as the host; `urllib.parse.urlsplit` on the same string returns netloc `good.com`. Same for `http://good.com#@evil.com`.

The consequence is parser confusion: an application that allowlists a destination using the stdlib parser and then fetches the URL through urllib3 will validate one host and connect to another — the classic SSRF-allowlist bypass shape. Consider terminating the authority on the first of `/`, `?` or `#` (or delegating to `urlsplit`) before the `@` and `:` splits.

I cannot see the callers in this diff, so I cannot confirm that attacker-supplied URLs reach `get_host`; in urllib3 the entry point would be `PoolManager.urlopen`/`connection_from_url`, which is not in the retrieved context. Confidence is lowered accordingly, and note this code is lifted unchanged rather than written here.

findings.title: Invalid-port branch in get_host has no test coverage
findings.body: The branch that raises LocationParseError when the port isn't numeric (line 99-100) has no accompanying test in this diff. Nothing currently exercises this path, so if the error message or the raised exception type were wrong (as it in fact is here — the format string has a %s placeholder but no argument is interpolated), no test would fail. A test calling get_host with a malformed URL like 'google.com:abc' and asserting on the raised exception's message would catch this class of bug.

findings.title: `HTTPMove.location` changes from str to URL, breaking callers
findings.body:
`self.location` is now assigned the `URL(location)` object rather than the original string argument. The documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) states that `HTTPMove.location` is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**", and that application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`.

Two concrete failures for existing callers:
- `exc.location.startswith("/admin")` raises `AttributeError`, since `yarl.URL` has no `startswith`.
- `exc.location == "/login"` silently evaluates to `False` because a `URL` never compares equal to a `str` — a wrong result with no exception, which is the harder of the two to notice.

Additionally, `URL(location)` normalises/quotes its input, so even `str(self.location)` is not guaranteed to round-trip to the original argument.

Keep the public attribute as the value passed in, and use a local for header construction:

```python
self.location = location
self.headers['Location'] = str(URL(location))
```

If exposing a parsed URL is genuinely wanted, it belongs on a new attribute (e.g. `location_url`) with a documentation update, not by retyping an existing public one.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location attribute type change can silently void redirect allowlist checks

findings.title: Public attribute type contradicts documentation
findings.body: The `location` attribute is now assigned a `URL` object (line 8), but the documentation in `docs/web_reference.rst` explicitly states it should be "the string it was constructed with." Application code documented to use `str.startswith()` on this attribute will break. Either revert the assignment to `location = str(URL(location))` or update the documentation to describe the new URL object type and its interface.

findings.title: No test guards HTTPMove.location's documented string type
findings.body: This change makes `self.location` a `URL` instance rather than the original string, which contradicts the documented contract in docs/web_reference.rst stating location is 'the string it was constructed with' and used with `str.startswith`. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the existing suite, since none is shown) asserting `isinstance(exc.location, str)` or checking equality against the original string argument. If this change is wrong, nothing would fail — the regression would only surface when application code calls `.startswith()` on a URL object and raises AttributeError at runtime.

findings.title: `if` instead of `while` lets readany return b'' before EOF
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, which can happen with an empty buffer. With `while`, `readany` looped and waited again; with `if`, control falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)`, which returns `b''` when the buffer is still empty and `_eof` is False.

That breaks the `readany` contract that an empty bytes result means end-of-stream: callers that loop `while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break` will silently truncate a response. Restore the `while` loop so the condition is re-checked after each wake, as `_wait`'s docstring instructs.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single `if` ignores documented spurious wakeup; readany can return b"" early

findings.title: No test guards against spurious-wakeup regression in readany
findings.body: The change replaces `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` with a single `if`, meaning after a spurious wakeup (waiter resolved with no new data, per the docstring in _wait) readany() will return an empty read instead of re-waiting. This diff includes no test exercising a wakeup with an empty buffer and not-eof state, so this regression would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks `import requests` on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328), so on any Python 3 interpreter this line raises `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` at import time of `requests.sessions`, which is imported by the package root — i.e. `import requests` fails entirely. Even on Python 2 it is fragile: if a top-level module named `adapters` exists on `sys.path`, the wrong module is bound. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, matching line 6 in the same file.

findings.title: Non-relative `from adapters import` allows sys.path module shadowing
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` guaranteed the import resolved to the sibling module inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through `sys.path` instead (under Python 3 semantics; under Python 2 it falls back to the implicit relative lookup). That means any `adapters.py` reachable earlier on `sys.path` — the script directory / current working directory, a world-writable temp dir that got added to the path, or a `PYTHONPATH` entry an attacker can influence — is imported and executed in place of the library's own module, giving arbitrary code execution inside any process that imports `requests.sessions`. Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

No attacker-controlled *data* flow is introduced by this diff; the exposure is at import resolution, and it is only reachable by someone who can place a file on the interpreter's search path.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is explicitly documented and implemented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and line 4 would fail the same way. Any request carrying a malformed Cookie header that reaches a handler calling `get_cookie` (including framework internals such as XSRF/secure-cookie handling) turns into a 500 instead of falling back to `default`. Restore the `self.request.cookies is not None and ...` condition, or have the property return an empty dict instead of `None` — but the latter changes the documented contract for every other consumer.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header crashes any handler calling get_cookie

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie with malformed/None cookies
findings.body: The removed `is not None` guard protected against `self.request.cookies` being None when the Cookie header is present but unparseable (per httpserver.py docstring). This change reintroduces a TypeError in that case (`name in None`). No test in this diff or referenced elsewhere exercises get_cookie with request.cookies == None, so this regression would not be caught by the existing test suite.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() makes boundary lookup fail for normal Content-Type headers
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields segments that retain the leading space from the conventional header form `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz`. Without `.strip()`, the second segment partitions into `k = " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so `_parse_mime_body` is never invoked and the loop falls through silently — the request body is dropped with no error, and `request.arguments`/`request.files` come back empty. Only senders that emit the parameter with no whitespace after the semicolon would still work. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and note the value side may also carry trailing whitespace).

findings.title: Removing .strip() makes boundary parsing whitespace-sensitive
findings.body:
Entry point is the attacker-supplied `Content-Type` request header; sink is `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` on line 6. After splitting on `;`, RFC-conformant headers such as `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` yield the field `" boundary=abc"`, whose `partition("=")` key is `" boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails and the body is never parsed. Only the space-less variant `multipart/form-data;boundary=abc` still works.

Two consequences: (a) handlers see empty `arguments`/`files` for ordinary multipart uploads, so any logic that branches on the presence of a field (XSRF token lookup, required-parameter checks) now takes the "missing" path for well-formed requests; (b) the client controls which parser behaviour it gets purely by adding or omitting a space, so a front-end proxy or WAF that parses the boundary correctly and inspects the parts can disagree with what the application actually sees. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and ideally strip the value too).

findings.title: No test guards multipart boundary parsing whitespace handling
findings.body: The diff removes field.strip() before partitioning on '=', which will break parsing when a content-type header has a space after the semicolon (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz'), a very common real-world format. This is exactly the kind of regression the original .strip() fix was meant to prevent, per the PR description. No test file is part of this change, so nothing would fail if this regression ships.

findings.title: Format placeholder %s left without its argument in LocationParseError
findings.body: The `% url` interpolation was dropped but the `%s` placeholder remains, so the raised exception message is the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"`. Any caller logging or displaying this error loses the offending URL entirely, making malformed-URL failures undiagnosable. Restore the argument: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`.

findings.title: No test would catch broken format placeholder
findings.body: The change removes the `% url` argument from the format string, leaving a literal '%s' in the exception message (or raising a TypeError depending on Python version behavior with %-formatting and missing args). If there is no test asserting the exact content of the LocationParseError message raised when parsing an invalid port, this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: Format placeholder in error message left unreplaced
findings.body: The error message contains a format placeholder '%s' that is no longer populated with the `url` argument. When this exception is raised, the message will literally display 'Failed to parse: %s' to the user instead of showing the actual URL that failed to parse. This makes the error message less helpful for debugging. Either the placeholder should be removed entirely (if the URL is not needed in the message) or the format argument should be restored.

findings.title: Unquoted f-string interpolated into shell=True command
findings.body:
`cmd` is built by f-string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and then executed with `shell=True`. Anything in either argument is interpreted by the shell, so this is wrong for plain inputs as well as hostile ones:

- `name = "Q3 report"` produces `tar -czf /exports/Q3 report.tar.gz <dir>`, which tars the wrong files into `/exports/Q3`.
- `directory = "/data/*"` is glob-expanded by the shell, not by `tar`.
- `name = "x; rm -rf /exports"` runs an attacker-chosen command with the process's privileges.

Use the argument-list form with no shell, matching `list_exports` on line 5: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`. If `name` is caller-supplied, additionally validate it against an allowlist (e.g. `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) so it cannot contain `/` or `..` and escape `/exports`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Command injection: f-string interpolated into subprocess with shell=True

findings.title: create_archive has no test coverage
findings.body: The new create_archive function builds a shell command via string interpolation of `name` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test file in this diff exercising this function, so a change to its behavior (or a fix to the injection risk) would not be caught by any test. At minimum, a test verifying the command construction/behavior for both benign and malicious `name` inputs would be valuable, given the existing sibling function list_exports uses a safer subprocess pattern (list args, no shell=True) that presumably has some coverage precedent.

findings.title: Return shape differs from sibling helper (CompletedProcess vs stdout)
findings.body:
`list_exports` on line 5 returns `.stdout` (bytes), while `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess` object, and without `capture_output=True` that object's `stdout` is `None` while tar's output goes to the parent process's streams. Callers of this module will reasonably expect the same convention. Decide on one: either return `None`/a path from `create_archive`, or capture output and return `.stdout` as the neighbouring function does.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function lacks documentation of parameters

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, discarding the `ALLOWED` allowlist that the adjacent middleware (lines 6-7) enforces. Any route mounted with this middleware accepts cross-origin requests from an arbitrary attacker-controlled page and instructs the browser to attach the victim's cookies/Authorization credentials, letting the attacker read authenticated dashboard responses (and issue state-changing requests with the response readable).

Note the exact failure mode depends on the middleware implementation: the standard `cors` package emits the literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, which browsers refuse to honour for credentialed requests — so the intent here is almost certainly not achieved, and whichever way it resolves the configuration is wrong. If the wrapper instead reflects the request `Origin` (as several framework wrappers do), this is a fully exploitable cross-origin credential leak.

Fix: reuse `ALLOWED` (or a dashboard-specific allowlist) as the origin and keep `credentials: true`, or drop `credentials` if the dashboard endpoints are genuinely public and unauthenticated.

findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body: `dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"`, which makes the middleware emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch/CORS specification forbids that pairing: when a request is made with `credentials: 'include'` (cookies, `Authorization`, or TLS client certs), the browser treats a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` as a mismatch and blocks the response, so the dashboard's authenticated calls will fail even though the server responded 200. If the dashboard genuinely sends no credentials, drop `credentials: true`; if it does, reflect the concrete dashboard origin the way the existing config above does (`origin: ALLOWED`) — e.g. add the dashboard's origin to `ALLOWED` and reuse that middleware, or pass an origin callback/array so the response echoes a single specific origin.

findings.title: Public CORS export lacks documentation of browser-rejected configuration
findings.body: The `dashboardCors` export is a public API that combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`. This configuration is rejected by browsers — a browser will refuse to send credentials when the origin is a wildcard, and the preflight response becomes invalid. A caller using this export would reasonably expect it to work as written, but it will not. Add a comment explaining why this combination exists (e.g., if it is intentionally permissive for development, or if the wildcard is meant to be replaced), or document the actual behavior.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed as a literal with an `acme_live_` prefix, which is the production-key naming pattern for this kind of payments SDK, and it is assigned directly to `acmepay.api_key` in `client()`. The previous code read it from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so this change removes the only thing keeping the credential out of the repository.

Anyone with read access to the repo, to any clone, to CI logs, or to the git history after a later fix now holds a live payments credential. Treat the key as compromised: rotate it at the provider immediately, then restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch). Note that removing the line in a follow-up commit does not remove the key from history — rotation is the only remediation.

findings.title: Env-based key replaced by constant: all environments now use one live key
findings.body: `client()` previously read `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which let each deployment (local, CI, staging, production) supply its own key and failed loudly with `KeyError` when unconfigured. After this change the key is a fixed module constant whose value is prefixed `acme_live_`, so staging/CI/dev runs will silently authenticate against the live payments account and issue real charges instead of failing or using a test key. Keep the environment lookup (optionally falling back to a clearly non-live default, or raising a descriptive error) so the key remains per-environment configurable.

findings.title: tenant_of trusts an unverified token, diverging from claims_for
findings.body: `claims_for` (line 7) verifies the RS256 signature against `public_key()`, so the rest of the codebase can reasonably assume claims read out of this module are authentic. `tenant_of` returns `tenant_id` from a decode with `options={"verify_signature": False}`, which in PyJWT also disables the dependent checks (`verify_exp`, `verify_aud`, `verify_iss`) unless they are re-enabled explicitly. The result is that a caller using `tenant_of` for tenant scoping accepts an expired token, a token signed by any key, or a token whose payload was edited client-side \u2014 the tenant id is entirely attacker-chosen. If the goal is to avoid a key lookup on a hot path, cache the verified claims from `claims_for` (or cache `public_key()`), not the verification itself.

findings.title: tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]`. A JWT is a client-supplied bearer value; with verification off, its payload is just base64 that anyone can rewrite. An attacker can take (or fabricate) a token, change `tenant_id` to any other tenant, and every code path that scopes queries or authorisation on the return value of `tenant_of()` will operate against that tenant's data. This is cross-tenant access, not merely a weakened check.

The file already has the correct pattern one function above: `claims_for()` verifies with `public_key()` and `algorithms=["RS256"]`. Implement `tenant_of()` in terms of it:

```python
def tenant_of(token):
    return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]
```

If the motivation was avoiding the key lookup cost, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification. If there is a genuinely pre-authentication use (e.g. choosing which key/issuer to look up), rename it to something unmistakable like `unverified_tenant_hint()`, document that its result must never reach an authorisation or data-scoping decision, and re-verify before use.

findings.title: Public function with undocumented security contract
findings.body: The function `tenant_of()` decodes a JWT without signature verification. A caller reading only the function name and signature would reasonably assume the token is validated, but it is not. This is a public API function whose actual contract — that it trusts the caller to verify the token separately — cannot be worked out from its name. Document the security assumption explicitly in a docstring, or rename to make the contract obvious (e.g., `unverified_tenant_of()`).

findings.title: New tenant_of() function has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() disables signature verification and trusts tenant_id from an unverified token. If this were wrong (e.g. a tampered token forged tenant_id, or the key name changed causing a KeyError), nothing in the current change would catch it — there is no test file in this diff at all. At minimum a test should exercise tenant_of() with a crafted/unverified token to lock in the intended (if risky) behavior and catch accidental regressions.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without ownership check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (attacker-controlled route/query parameter) via `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12 and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and persists with `pm.save()` on lines 13-14, with no authorisation check between load and mutation. It calls `current_user(request)` on line 11 and then never uses the result — `require_owner` is imported/used by the read handler on line 6 but omitted here, which strongly suggests an oversight rather than intent.
