Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on payment methods belonging to other accounts. `api/auth.py` states explicitly that `current_user` is "Authentication only — never authorisation" and that "Every object mutation must call" `require_owner`.

Fix: insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` call on line 12, before any field assignment, mirroring line 6.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on a malformed request body

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ update_payment_method lacks ownership check

findings.title: No test covers update_payment_method, including missing authz check
findings.body: update_payment_method mutates a PaymentMethod loaded by id but never calls require_owner(user, pm), unlike the sibling read endpoint above it. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a test asserting that a non-owner cannot update another user's payment method (which would fail given the current code) is absent. Add a test that attempts an update as a non-owning user and asserts Forbidden is raised, plus a happy-path test asserting the saved fields change.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body: `request_reset` no longer carries the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator, and the `limits` import was dropped with it. The `email` parameter is caller-supplied and flows straight into `send_reset_email(email)` with no throttling in between, so an unauthenticated client can issue unbounded requests. Practical consequences: mail-bombing an arbitrary victim address, burning outbound mail quota / getting the sending domain reputation-flagged, and — if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown addresses — cheap bulk account enumeration. Reinstate the decorator, or move the limit to a middleware/gateway layer and note that in the code so the removal is auditable. A per-email limit in addition to a per-IP one is worth considering, since IP-based limits alone do not protect a single targeted victim address.

findings.title: request_reset now triggers unbounded reset emails per caller
findings.body: `@rate_limit("5/hour")` and its import were removed with nothing replacing them, so `request_reset` will call `send_reset_email(email)` once per inbound request with no ceiling. The function still returns `{"sent": True}` unconditionally, so a caller cannot distinguish a throttled request from a delivered one — there is no longer any mechanism, in-band or out, that bounds sends for a given email address. If the throttling genuinely moved (to middleware, a gateway, or inside `send_reset_email`), that should be stated, since nothing in this file or the diff shows it; otherwise restore the decorator or apply an equivalent per-email/per-IP limit before the send.

findings.title: No test guards rate limiting on request_reset
findings.body: The @rate_limit("5/hour") decorator was removed from request_reset with no test in this diff verifying that repeated calls are throttled. If this change is wrong (i.e., rate limiting should remain), nothing in the current test suite (none shown) would fail to catch it. Add a test that calls request_reset repeatedly and asserts requests beyond the limit are rejected.

findings.title: Password reset endpoint no longer rate-limited but may be documented as protected
findings.body: The `request_reset` function previously had a rate limit of 5 requests per hour, enforced by the `@rate_limit` decorator. This decorator has been removed, but if there is documentation (in a docstring, API schema, README, or security guide) that describes this endpoint as rate-limited or protected against brute-force attacks, that documentation is now stale and misleading. Review any public-facing documentation about the password reset endpoint to ensure it reflects that rate limiting has been removed.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing path traversal
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` builds its path with `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` and opens it directly. The sibling reader two lines above derives its path from `_confined(name)`, which is evidently the helper that normalises and pins a name inside the export root. Two concrete consequences for reachable inputs:

- `name="../../etc/passwd"` — `os.path.join` does no normalisation, so the traversal survives into `open()` and the first `limit` bytes of an arbitrary file are returned.
- `name="/etc/shadow"` — `os.path.join` discards the left operand entirely when the right operand is absolute, so `EXPORT_ROOT` is not even a prefix.

Fix by using the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` before the `open()`, so both entry points share one confinement rule.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function contract does not disclose path traversal risk
findings.body: The new `read_export_preview(name)` function accepts a `name` parameter and constructs a file path directly without confinement, unlike the existing `read_export(name)` function three lines above it which calls `_confined(name)`. A caller reading both function signatures would have no way to know that `read_export_preview()` is unsafe to call with untrusted input while `read_export()` is safe. Either: (1) apply `_confined(name)` here too, (2) add a docstring explicitly warning that `name` must be pre-validated by the caller, or (3) rename the function to make the risk clear (e.g., `read_export_preview_unchecked`).

findings.title: New unconfined path-join function has no test coverage
findings.body: read_export_preview builds a path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) without the _confined() normalization used by the neighboring handler, and no test exercises this function with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../../etc/passwd') or verifies it stays within EXPORT_ROOT. Nothing in the current diff would catch a regression or confirm the intended behavior here.

findings.title: bulk_export no longer enforces report ownership
findings.body:
`require_owner` was removed from both the import and the per-report loop, so `bulk_export` now serialises and returns every `Report` whose ID the caller supplies, with no tenant comparison anywhere in the function. `api/auth.py` documents that "every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this", and nothing else in the remaining body (`Report.get`, `to_dict`) performs a tenant check. Any authenticated user can enumerate `report_ids` and read other tenants' data.

If the loop was removed for performance, restore the check in a form that keeps the invariant — e.g. fetch with a tenant-scoped query (`Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) so the filter happens in one round trip rather than N calls to `require_owner`, or keep the loop and optimise the fetch instead.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR

findings.title: No test guards against cross-tenant data exposure in bulk_export
findings.body: The diff removes the require_owner authorization check from bulk_export, but no test file is included in this change. If a test existed asserting that bulk_export raises Forbidden for reports outside the user's tenant, it would now fail and catch this regression — but since none is shown in the diff, nothing would catch this behavior change. Add or verify a test that calls bulk_export with report_ids belonging to a different tenant and asserts Forbidden is raised.

findings.title: Unknown report IDs may now surface as AttributeError on None
findings.body: `Report.get(rid)` presumably returns `None` for an ID that does not exist. Previously the deleted loop touched `report.tenant_id` first, so a missing report failed inside the auth path; now the first dereference is `r.to_dict()` on line 7, which will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType'` and most likely surface as a 500 rather than a 404/403. Consider filtering out or explicitly rejecting missing IDs.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL string on line 9 and passes it to `execute(sql)` on line 10 with no `params` argument, so the driver never escapes them. Either value can terminate the quoted literal and append arbitrary SQL (e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` to dump the table, or `'; DROP ...` / stacked queries depending on the driver), giving read/write access to data the caller should not reach.

Fix by parameterising both values and building the LIKE wildcards in Python:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

This matches both `get_customer` on line 5 and the documented contract of `execute` ("`params` must carry every caller value").

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ search_customers interpolates inputs instead of parameterising

findings.title: search_customers has no test exercising its query construction
findings.body: The new function search_customers builds SQL via string interpolation rather than parameterization, unlike get_customer above it. No test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding repo, since none is shown) verifies the SQL string produced or the params passed to execute for this function. If the query construction were changed to be correct/parameterized or broken further, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary URL, skipping ALLOWED_HOSTS check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes its argument straight to `requests.get` with no scheme or host validation. The function directly above it, in the same module, parses the host and rejects anything not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before posting \u2014 so the control exists in this file and the new code does not use it.

As written, a customer registering a webhook target can make the server issue GETs to `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...` (cloud instance metadata), `http://localhost:*/` internal admin services, or RFC1918 addresses, and learn the result through the returned status code (a blind-but-oracle SSRF). `file://` is not handled by requests by default, but `requests` follows redirects by default, so even an allowlisted host could redirect into the internal network.

Fix: run the same `urlparse` + `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check used on line 8 before the request, restrict the scheme to `https` (or `http`/`https`), and pass `allow_redirects=False` so an allowlisted host cannot bounce the request inward.

Note: the caller that supplies `url` is not visible in this diff or in any retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the value is attacker-controlled end to end \u2014 but the PR description states the URL is caller-supplied, and a helper named `verify_endpoint` in a webhook-registration module is exercised at registration time by definition.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS guard the sibling function enforces
findings.body: The existing send path in this same module parses the URL's host and rejects anything not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing the request (lines 8-10). `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of caller-supplied URL and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no host or scheme check, so it is a server-side fetch of an arbitrary address — internal services, link-local metadata endpoints, or non-HTTP schemes. Apply the same host extraction and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check before the request, and since `requests` follows redirects by default, also pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop) so a permitted host cannot redirect the fetch to a disallowed one.

findings.title: New verify_endpoint SSRF-prone function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that fetches an arbitrary caller-supplied URL, unlike the sibling function above it which validates host against ALLOWED_HOSTS before requesting. There is no test exercising verify_endpoint at all, so if it were changed to add/remove validation, or if it silently omits the allowlist check present elsewhere in the file, nothing in the test suite would catch it. Add a test asserting that verify_endpoint rejects disallowed hosts the same way the existing post path does (or, if it's intentionally unrestricted, a test documenting that behavior explicitly).

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks documentation
findings.body: The `verify_endpoint` function is exported at module level and performs a server-side HTTP GET request to a caller-supplied URL. A docstring should document: what the function does, what the `url` parameter expects, what it returns, and what exceptions it may raise (e.g., network errors, timeouts, or invalid status codes). Without this, callers cannot determine the intended usage or error handling contract.

findings.title: Public access block disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guards (`block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to `false` for `acme-customer-invoices`. These settings are the last-resort control that prevents an accidental or malicious public ACL/bucket policy from exposing objects; with them off, any principal that can call `PutBucketPolicy`/`PutObjectAcl` (or any future Terraform change, or an object uploaded with `public-read`) makes customer invoices world-readable with no further safeguard. The bucket name strongly suggests PII/financial data.

Fix: either delete this `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` resource and rely on the account-level block, or set all four attributes to `true`. Only the `assets` bucket appears to be intentionally public; the invoices bucket appears to have had that block copied onto it by mistake.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Customer invoices bucket has all public access blocks disabled

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public access block allows public access to sensitive invoices bucket

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC hexdigest as `verify_stripe` but validates it with `expected == header`. Python's `==` on `str` short-circuits at the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading characters of the expected signature an attacker's guess matched, which permits byte-by-byte forgery of a valid signature by an attacker who can submit many webhook deliveries and measure response latency. The sibling function on line 7 already does the right thing. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`.

Secondary note while you are there: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` if `header` is `bytes` while `expected` is `str`, whereas `==` silently returns `False`. If any caller passes a bytes header, switching will surface that as an exception rather than a quiet verification failure — normalise the header type (e.g. `header or ""`, decoded) at the top of the function so both providers behave identically.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` (timing-unsafe)

findings.title: No test exercises verify_acmepay's comparison behavior
findings.body: verify_acmepay is new and untested. No test in this diff checks that it correctly accepts a valid signature and rejects an invalid one, so a regression (or the existing == vs compare_digest inconsistency) would go unnoticed by any test suite.

findings.title: Public webhook verifier lacks docstring
findings.body: `verify_acmepay` is a public function (follows the `verify_*` naming pattern of `verify_stripe`) that takes parameters whose roles are not obvious from context alone. A caller unfamiliar with ACME Pay's webhook format could incorrectly order the arguments or misunderstand what validation is happening. Add a docstring explaining the function's purpose, parameters, and return value.

findings.title: Exception message and traceback returned to the client
findings.body:
`handle(exc)` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()` into the 500 response. A traceback exposes absolute file paths, module and package layout, framework and library versions, function names and local call structure, and frequently the offending values themselves                                      — for example a `psycopg2` error leaks the SQL text and schema, a `KeyError` leaks internal key names, and a connection error leaks internal hostnames and ports. Any unauthenticated client that can trigger a fault (malformed input, oversized payload, unexpected type) gets a free map of the application, which materially accelerates follow-up attacks.

Keep the traceback on the server side only — it is already captured by `log.exception` on line 8. Return an opaque body plus a correlation id, e.g. `return {"error": "internal error", "request_id": rid}, 500`, and if detail is genuinely needed for debugging gate it behind an explicit non-production flag rather than emitting it by default.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response shape changed: message no longer stable, new key added

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and may return "NoneType: None"

findings.title: Public error handler lacks documentation of response contract
findings.body: The `handle()` function is a public error handler that now returns detailed exception messages and tracebacks to clients. This is a significant change to its contract — callers and API consumers need to know that internal error details are exposed. The function requires a docstring documenting what it returns and warning about information disclosure, or a comment explaining the deliberate choice to leak internals.

findings.title: No test guards response body against internal detail leakage
findings.body: The `handle` function now returns the raw exception string and full traceback in the client-facing response body. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) asserting what `handle(exc)` returns, so nothing would fail if this behavior is wrong or later needs to be reverted. A test asserting the response body does not contain internals (e.g., traceback text, exception message) would catch this regression and prevent recurrence.

findings.title: Password reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives the stored value with a single unsalted `hashlib.md5`, while `hash_password` on line 7 uses `bcrypt.hashpw` with a generated salt. MD5 is a fast, unsalted hash: an attacker who obtains the credential store can crack these at billions of guesses per second on commodity GPUs, and identical passwords across accounts produce identical digests, so rainbow tables apply directly. Any account whose password was last set through the reset flow is effectively stored in plaintext-equivalent form, and the mismatch also means a reset password will not verify against `bcrypt.checkpw`.

Use the same primitive as the main path: `return hash_password(raw)`, or delete this function and call `hash_password` at the reset call site. If the intent was to hash a reset *token* rather than a password, it still should not be MD5 — use `hashlib.sha256` and compare with `hmac.compare_digest`.

findings.title: Public password hashing function lacks security contract documentation
findings.body: The `hash_reset_password` function is public (module-level, no leading underscore) and performs password hashing using MD5. This creates a contract violation: a caller reading only the function signature and name would reasonably expect it to use the same secure hashing as `hash_password` (which uses bcrypt), but it uses a cryptographically weak algorithm instead. A docstring must explicitly document that this function uses MD5 and clarify its intended use case (e.g., if this is only for password reset tokens, that constraint belongs in the documentation so callers do not misuse it for storing actual password hashes).

findings.title: Reset path stores an MD5 digest incompatible with bcrypt hashes
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), but `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest for the same credential field. Any verification routine built around `bcrypt.checkpw` will either raise on the malformed salt or return False for every password set through the reset flow, silently locking users out (or, if verification branches on hash shape, permanently downgrading those accounts to an unsalted digest). The reset path should reuse `hash_password` so the stored format and the verification format stay identical; there is no reason for a second, weaker algorithm here.

findings.title: No test coverage for new password-reset hashing function
findings.body: hash_reset_password uses MD5 for password hashing, a weak/broken choice for password storage, but that's a security concern for another reviewer. From a test-coverage perspective, there is no test exercising this function at all, so any regression (e.g., switching algorithms, breaking hex output format, or changing behavior) would go undetected.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs fork-controlled code with repository secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` executes in the context of the base repository: the job receives repository secrets and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write scope, and it runs for pull requests from any fork without maintainer approval. This change then explicitly checks out the untrusted side (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`) and runs `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout with `NPM_TOKEN` in the environment.

Entry point: the head commit of any fork pull request — the attacker fully controls the contents of `scripts/measure.sh` (and anything it sources, plus any `package.json` lifecycle scripts or lockfile it pulls in). Sink: the `run:` step on line 13, which executes that attacker-authored file on a privileged runner. The attacker's script can simply `echo $NPM_TOKEN | base64` into the job log, or exfiltrate it over the network, on the very first PR they open. The publish token and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` should both be treated as compromised if this has already merged and run.

Fix by choosing one of:
- Revert to `on: pull_request`, which runs with a read-only token and no secrets for fork PRs. A size measurement does not need `pull_request_target`.
- If a privileged action (e.g. posting a comment) is genuinely required, split it: an unprivileged `pull_request` job builds and uploads the measurement as an artifact, and a separate `workflow_run` job with the secret consumes the artifact without ever executing fork code.

Do not keep `pull_request_target` + checkout of `head.sha` + execution of repo scripts in the same job under any configuration.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted context values; previously-working calls now raise
findings.body:
The old key was `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which accepted any *hashable* value — `datetime`, `Decimal`, enums, frozen dataclasses, arbitrary objects with `__hash__`. The new key path runs `json.dumps` over the whole context, which raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those. Any existing caller passing a non-JSON-serialisable-but-hashable value goes from a working memoised render to an uncaught exception, and the failure happens before `_render` is ever reached, so it is not recoverable by the caller in any obvious way.

If the digest form is wanted, pass a fallback (`json.dumps(..., default=repr)`) or keep the tuple key and hash `repr` of it — and make the narrowing explicit in the docstring either way.

findings.title: New name allowlist rejects inputs the old signature accepted
findings.body:
`create_archive` previously accepted any string for `name` and interpolated it into the command. It now raises `ValueError` for anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`. Common archive names that existing callers plausibly pass — timestamps with dots or colons (`2024.01.01`, `08:00`), dotted names (`backup.full`), names containing `.` or `/` from a config value, or names longer than 64 characters — will now raise instead of producing an archive. That turns a previously successful export into an unhandled exception at the call site.

Please confirm with the actual callers what name shapes are in use; if dots or longer names are legitimate, widen the pattern (e.g. allow `.` and raise the length cap) while still rejecting `/`, `..` and leading `-`. Also note that a non-`str` `name` now raises `TypeError` from `fullmatch` rather than the documented `ValueError`.

findings.title: Test depends on an undefined `spy` fixture and never asserts the argv
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` requests a `spy` fixture that is not defined in this diff and no `conftest.py` is added. If it does not already exist, the test errors at collection; if it does exist but does not patch `subprocess.run`, the test actually shells out and writes to `/exports`. Either way the assertion only checks `shell is False` — it does not check that `name` and `directory` arrive as separate argv elements, which is the property the fix exists to guarantee. Add the fixture (or a `monkeypatch` on `subprocess.run`) and assert on `args[0]` being the expected list.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Shell-safety test only checks a kwarg, not the actual argv

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated while `name` is allowlisted
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch` (line 9), but `directory` flows straight into the tar argv on line 12 with no check. Command injection is not possible (list argv, `shell=False`) and option injection is blocked by the `--` separator, so the residual risk is confined to path selection: if a caller passes an attacker-influenced path, tar will happily archive `/etc` or any other readable tree into a `/exports/*.tar.gz` that the requester can presumably retrieve — an arbitrary-file-read primitive rather than code execution.

If `directory` is ever caller-supplied, resolve it (`os.path.realpath`) and assert it stays under an expected export root before invoking tar. If it is always an internal constant, a one-line comment saying so would close the question for the next reader.

findings.title: directory is now a single literal argv element, losing splitting and globbing
findings.body: Under the old `shell=True` string, `directory` was word-split and glob-expanded by the shell, so a caller passing `"/srv/data /srv/logs"` archived two trees and `"/srv/data/*"` expanded to its entries. With the list argv, the same value is passed to `tar` as one literal path and the command fails with `check=True` raising `CalledProcessError`. If any caller relies on multiple paths or a glob, this is a silent behaviour change that only shows up at runtime. Consider accepting a sequence of directories and splatting it into the argv, or document that exactly one literal path is supported.

findings.title: No test for the `--` guard against directory-as-flag injection
findings.body: The fix adds `"--"` before `directory` specifically to stop a `directory` value starting with `-` (e.g. `-C/etc`) from being parsed by tar as an option. Nothing in tests/test_archive.py calls create_archive with such a directory and checks the resulting argv still contains `--` before it, or that tar behaves safely. If the `--` were accidentally dropped in a future edit, no test here would catch it.

findings.title: Test has no assertion; cannot fail
findings.body:
test_renders_empty_invoice calls render() but never asserts anything about the result. It would pass even if render() raised no exception but returned garbage, wrong formatting, or None for an empty invoice. Add an assertion on the actual output, e.g. checking for a total of 0.00 or an appropriate empty-state string.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing about the result

findings.title: Test asserts on mock call_count, not actual output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only checks that it was called twice. It never verifies what render() actually produces, so it would pass even if the line items were formatted incorrectly, rendered in the wrong order, or omitted from the final output entirely. Assert on the actual rendered string/content instead of the mock's call count.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_line_items verifies the mock, not the rendered output

findings.title: Test for rounding fix deleted instead of updated
findings.body:
The PR's stated purpose is fixing the rounding behavior, but the test that exercises that exact behavior (`test_rounds_half_to_even`, asserting `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.34")`) is deleted rather than updated to reflect the corrected expected value. If the fix regresses in the future, nothing in this file will catch it — the remaining test (`test_rounds_up_above_half`) covers a different input/case. The deleted test should be restored with an assertion matching the corrected rounding output.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Tie-breaking test deleted instead of updated; behaviour now unverified

findings.title: Patch targets definition module, so real deliver() still runs
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` as a module-level name in `notify.sender` at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only; `send_with_retry` still resolves the original function object through `notify.sender.deliver`. The test therefore exercises the real transport three times (possible network I/O, slowness, or non-deterministic results) and asserts nothing about the retry-exhaustion path. If the real `deliver` ever returns truthy the test fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test; if it returns falsy the test passes without the mock contributing anything.

Use the same target as the passing test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the call count is 3, which is the behaviour this test is evidently trying to pin down and which the current form cannot check.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; retry-failure path untested

findings.title: csv_rows joins fields without applying csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line with a bare `",".join(...)` over the stringified cell values, so a cell containing a comma or a double quote silently shifts every subsequent column on that row (and mismatches the header produced by `csv_header`). The escaping helper the module needs is defined immediately below at line 10 but is never called — as written, `csv_escape` is dead code. Apply it per cell, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note that `csv_escape` also does not handle embedded newlines, which likewise require quoting in RFC 4180 CSV.

findings.title: New exporter functions ship with no tests
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape (reports/csv_export.py), dump_streaming, dump_pretty (reports/json_export.py), and margins_for, usable_width (reports/pdf_export.py) are all new public functions with non-trivial logic (chunking, escaping, arithmetic on margins) but no accompanying tests. A regression in any of them—e.g. an off-by-one in csv_escape's quote handling, a wrong chunk boundary in dump_streaming, or an incorrect margin calculation—would pass unnoticed. The repo already tests the analogous csv_header function, so the same standard should apply here.

findings.title: csv_rows does not use csv_escape, allowing delimiter injection
findings.body:
`csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,` with no quoting, while the `csv_escape` helper added immediately below (lines 10-14) is never called by it. A single field value containing a comma or a double quote therefore splits into extra fields, letting whoever controls a row value shift or spoof columns for any consumer that parses the output (spreadsheet, downstream importer, log pipeline).

Fix: pipe each field through `csv_escape` (e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`), or use the stdlib `csv` module, which handles quoting, embedded newlines and `\r` correctly — note that `csv_escape` as written also does not quote values containing newlines, which break the line-per-row assumption. Separately, if this CSV is opened in a spreadsheet, values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` are still formula-injection candidates and neither helper neutralises them.

findings.title: Date comparison against a second now() read fails at UTC midnight
findings.body:
`token.issued_at` is captured inside `issue_token()` on line 10, and line 11 takes a *second* wall-clock reading with `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. If the two reads land on opposite sides of a UTC midnight (issue at 23:59:59.999, assert at 00:00:00.001), `.date()` differs and the test fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test. Freeze the clock (e.g. inject/patch the time source as the sibling test on lines 4-6 does by passing explicit `issued`/`now` values), or capture `before = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` up front and assert `before <= token.issued_at <= datetime.now(timezone.utc)` instead of comparing calendar dates.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Time-dependent test flakes at midnight UTC boundary

findings.title: is_expired called without the now= argument the sibling test supplies
findings.body: The existing test on line 6 always passes `now=` explicitly, while line 12 relies on an implicit default. If `is_expired` has no default for `now`, this raises `TypeError`; if it does default to the live clock, the assertion becomes time-dependent in the same way as line 11. Pass an explicit `now=` here for determinism and to match the established call style.

findings.title: No test for CouponExpired branch
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated in this PR (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon with expires_at=tomorrow(), which never exercises this branch. If the condition were inverted, wrong, or removed entirely, no test would fail. Add a test that passes an expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

findings.title: apply_coupon now requires expires_at on every coupon
findings.body: Line 9 unconditionally dereferences `coupon.expires_at`. The test in the same PR had to be edited from `Coupon(amount=10)` to `Coupon(amount=10, expires_at=tomorrow())`, which is direct evidence that coupons could previously be constructed without this attribute. Any other construction site, fixture, or persisted coupon row that does not populate `expires_at` will now raise `AttributeError` (or `TypeError: '<' not supported between NoneType and datetime` if the field defaults to `None`) instead of applying the discount. Either give `expires_at` a safe default and guard with `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < ...`, or confirm every caller supplies it.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async handler stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but its body contains no `await`; the HTTP call is made with the synchronous `requests` library. When awaited from an event loop, `requests.get` blocks the entire loop thread until the response arrives or the 5s timeout fires, stalling every other concurrent task — including the `httpx` call in `fetch_plan` right above it. Use the existing `httpx.AsyncClient` (mirroring `fetch_plan`'s signature, which takes the client as a parameter) and `await client.get(...)`, or if the sync client must be kept, dispatch it via `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor`. Dropping the `requests` import on line 2 as well would keep the module on a single HTTP stack.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Async function uses blocking HTTP call

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits or its blocking-call behavior
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that internally uses the synchronous `requests.get` call instead of an async client. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so if it blocks the event loop or returns unexpected data, nothing would fail. Add a test that calls fetch_plan_limits (e.g., under an event loop with concurrency) to catch blocking behavior, and/or a test asserting on the parsed JSON return value.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL by f-string interpolation of `tenant_id` directly into the path of `https://billing.internal/limits/...`. If `tenant_id` is ever attacker-influenced (e.g. taken from a request path/body/JWT claim upstream), a value such as `../admin/tenants` or one containing `?`/`#`/`%2F` lets the caller steer the request at a different endpoint on the internal billing host \u2014 a service that is presumably reachable only from this process and may trust it implicitly. `requests.get` also follows redirects by default, so a response from that host can pull the client onward to another target.

Suggested fixes: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before use, or pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`; consider `allow_redirects=False` for an internal RPC-style call.

Note the pre-existing `client.get(f"/plans/{tenant_id}")` on line 6 has the same shape; a shared validation helper would cover both.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: `except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, not just `Exception`. That means a Ctrl-C arriving while `_client.send` is blocked on the network, a `SystemExit` raised during interpreter shutdown, or a `GeneratorExit` will all be converted into a normal `return None`, so the process keeps running instead of terminating. Narrow this to the failures you actually intend to make non-fatal, e.g. `except Exception:` at minimum, ideally the client's own transport/timeout exception types.

findings.title: No test covers the new exception-swallowing behavior
findings.body: push_metrics now catches all exceptions (including KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit) and returns None instead of propagating. There is no test in this diff verifying that a failing _client.send still returns None rather than raising, nor one verifying the success path still returns the client's result. If this bare except were removed or changed to re-raise, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Public function lacks contract documentation for error handling
findings.body: The `push_metrics` function is a public API with changed behavior: it now catches all exceptions (including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit) and returns None on failure, but this is not documented. A caller cannot determine from the signature what happens on error—they will not know whether None is a valid payload response or an error condition. Add a docstring documenting the return contract and that exceptions are suppressed.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, then writes back `current + cost` on line 19 — all without holding `_lock`, which `consume` (line 9) does take. Two coroutines can both read the same `current`, both pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and both commit, so the effective total can reach nearly `2 * LIMIT` (or N*cost over LIMIT for N concurrent callers). Worse, the write is an absolute assignment from a stale read rather than a read-modify-write, so any increment applied by `consume` or another `try_consume` between lines 15 and 19 is silently discarded and the counter drifts permanently low, further weakening the limit. Wrap the whole read/check/write sequence in `async with _lock:` and compute the new value from a fresh read inside the lock (`_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`), or drop the intermediate `await` entirely so the sequence is atomic under the single-threaded event loop.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: unlocked check-then-act across an await

findings.title: Public function contract undocumented for check-then-act race
findings.body: `try_consume` is a public async function that performs a check-then-act on shared state across an await (lines 15–19). The function reads `_counters[tenant]` on line 15, then yields control on line 18, then writes to `_counters[tenant]` on line 19. If another task mutates `_counters[tenant]` between the read and write, the function will silently accept a request that exceeds the limit. A caller needs to know this is possible and accept the trade-off, but there is no docstring explaining the race condition, when it occurs, or what the caller should do about it. This makes the function's contract unknowable from its name and signature alone.

findings.title: No test exercises try_consume's race condition or limit logic
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters, awaits, then writes without holding _lock, unlike consume which uses async with _lock. There is no test in this diff verifying that concurrent calls to try_consume can overshoot LIMIT, nor even a basic test that try_consume returns False when the limit is exceeded or True/updates state when under it. Since no test file is included at all, any regression here (including the race itself) would go undetected.

findings.title: Docstring describes old return type; function now returns dict
findings.body:
The docstring states 'Return (name, email) for a user.' but the function now returns a dict with keys 'name', 'email', and 'tier'. This is stale documentation that will mislead callers who expect a tuple and may break existing code like the caller in reports/weekly.py that unpacks the result. Update the docstring to describe the new dict return type.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the removed (name, email) tuple return

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body:
`lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of `(name, email)`. The existing caller `render_row` in `reports/weekly.py` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a dict iterates its keys, so with three keys this raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` at runtime for every call \u2014 and even with two keys it would bind the strings "name"/"email" rather than the values, which is silently wrong.

Either update all callers in the same change (`u = lookup_user(id); u["name"], u["email"]`), or preserve backwards compatibility by returning a `NamedTuple`/dataclass that still unpacks as `(name, email)`, or add the tier via a separate function.

findings.title: Return-shape change to lookup_user is untested and breaks a known caller
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple, but reports/weekly.py:6 still does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will now raise a ValueError (dict unpacking yields keys, not the tuple shape expected) or otherwise break at runtime. There is no test exercising lookup_user's return value or render_row's use of it, so this contract break would not be caught by any existing or new test in this diff.

findings.title: Insert error is swallowed; WriteSettlement always returns nil
findings.body:
The `err` bound by `if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil` is scoped to the if-statement. Inside that scope the failure is only logged; control then falls through to `var err error` / `return err`, which declares a brand-new nil error and returns it. WriteSettlement therefore reports success on every path where the INSERT fails — the settlement row is silently lost and any caller that treats a nil return as "persisted" (e.g. committing a transaction, acking a message, marking the settlement complete upstream) will proceed on false information.

Fix by propagating the error, matching the style of `Write` above (line 7-8):

    if _, err := db.Exec("INSERT INTO settlements ...", s.ID, s.Cents); err != nil {
        log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
        return err
    }
    return nil

The trailing `var err error; return err` should be deleted outright — it is a constant nil and can never carry a failure.

findings.title: WriteSettlement has no test covering the insert-failure path
findings.body: WriteSettlement's error handling is subtle (the insert error is logged but never propagated because a fresh `var err error` shadows it). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing exercises the case where db.Exec fails at line 15 — a test that injects a failing db/mock would catch that the function still returns nil, but currently nothing would fail if this behaviour is wrong.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that does not pass `attempted` explicitly shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the failures from the first call as well, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will get wrong results from the second invocation onward.

Fix with the same idiom already used two lines above: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = list(attempted or [])` (or `if attempted is None: attempted = []`) as the first statement.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared default list leaks recipients across unrelated calls

findings.title: send_with_retries has no test coverage at all
findings.body: The new function send_with_retries introduces stateful behavior (appending to a list across calls due to the mutable default) and retry logic, but no test file is included in this diff. Nothing would catch a regression in the retry logic, nor the mutable-default bug where repeated calls without an explicit `attempted` argument accumulate state across invocations. Add a test that calls send_with_retries twice with no `attempted` argument and asserts the second call's result does not include recipients from the first call.

findings.title: compute_rounding drops the exact-half case (>= 0.5 became > 0.5)
findings.body: Every other function in this diff is a pure rename with an unchanged body. `compute_rounding` also changed its comparison: the old code rounded up when `remainder_cents >= 0.5`, the new code only when `remainder_cents > 0.5`. For a remainder of exactly 0.5 — the single most common remainder in half-cent money splits — the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1, so totals will be one cent low on those lines. If this flip was intentional (switching from half-up to truncate-at-half), it does not belong in a rename commit and needs a test plus a note about the reconciliation impact; otherwise restore `>=`.

findings.title: Boundary change in rounding comparison lacks a test at 0.5
findings.body: The comparison changed from `>= 0.5` to `> 0.5` while renaming calc_rounding to compute_rounding. This changes behavior exactly at remainder_cents == 0.5 (previously rounds up to 1, now rounds to 0). No test file is present in this diff, so nothing would catch this regression; any existing test suite (not shown) would need a case with remainder_cents == 0.5 to detect it.

findings.title: Module docstring uses 'calculators' but functions renamed to compute_*
findings.body: The module docstring refers to these as 'Line-item calculators', but all exported functions have been renamed from calc_* to compute_*. While the term 'calculator' is still semantically accurate, the docstring should align with the new naming convention to avoid confusion about whether the code matches its documentation. Update to 'Line-item computers' or similar.

findings.title: Off-by-one slice drops the last record of every page
findings.body:
The slice end is `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, so each page yields only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records. Because `start` still advances by the full `PAGE_SIZE` per page (`start = page * PAGE_SIZE`), the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — it is silently dropped from the export rather than merely deferred. The sibling function `page_of` on line 6 uses the correct bound. Change line 12 to `return ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function `page_of_sorted` lacks documentation of its contract

findings.title: New pagination function lacks any test to catch off-by-one
findings.body: page_of_sorted slices ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1], which drops the last record of every page (off-by-one). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this logic is wrong. Add a test that asserts page_of_sorted returns exactly PAGE_SIZE records per page (except possibly the last page) and that concatenating pages reproduces the full sorted input without gaps.

findings.title: Removed None guard: header_lines crashes when purchase_order is None
findings.body:
`invoice.purchase_order` is declared as `str | None` in `models/invoice.py` and documented as only set for customers on invoicing terms ("roughly one account in twenty"). The new unconditional `f"PO {invoice.purchase_order.upper()}"` calls `.upper()` on `None` for every other invoice, raising `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` — i.e. rendering fails for the majority of invoices. Restore the conditional append (or use a fallback such as `if invoice.purchase_order:`) before building the list.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Unguarded attribute access crashes rendering for optional purchase_order

findings.title: No test guards against missing purchase_order regression
findings.body: header_lines now unconditionally calls invoice.purchase_order.upper(), which will throw AttributeError whenever purchase_order is None — the documented common case (roughly 19 of 20 accounts per models/invoice.py). This diff includes no test exercising header_lines with purchase_order=None, so nothing in the change set would fail even though the removed guard was load-bearing.

findings.title: File handle leaks when the header does not match
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` on line 10 is not wrapped in a context manager, and the early `return None` on line 14 bypasses `fh.close()` on line 16. Every call with a mismatched header leaks an open file descriptor; on CPython it is reclaimed non-deterministically by refcounting, and on PyPy/other implementations or when the handle is captured in a traceback it can persist indefinitely — an importer that validates many files can exhaust the descriptor limit. The same leak occurs on any exception from `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` (e.g. a decoding error).

Use the same pattern as `read_rows` on lines 5–6:

```python
def read_validated(path, expected_header):
    with open(path) as fh:
        reader = csv.reader(fh)
        header = next(reader)
        if header != expected_header:
            return None
        return list(reader)
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ File descriptor leaked on header-mismatch path (exhaustion vector)

findings.title: No test covers read_validated, including its leak-on-failure path
findings.body: read_validated is new behavior with no accompanying test in this diff. In particular, the early `return None` at line 14 skips `fh.close()` at line 16, leaking the file handle whenever the header doesn't match. There is no test exercising the mismatched-header branch (or the success branch) that would catch this leak or verify correct return values.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge_card`, which calls `billing.gateway.charge`. The gateway's own docstring states "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and that the caller must pass an Idempotency-Key header to make retries safe. No such key is threaded through here. Any failure mode where the POST reaches the gateway but the response is lost (timeout, connection reset, 5xx after commit) will be retried and will create a second and third real charge against the customer's card.

Fix by generating a stable idempotency key per logical charge attempt (e.g. a caller-supplied `idempotency_key` parameter, or a UUID created once outside the retried function) and passing it to `charge`, so all three attempts collapse to one charge server-side. Until the key is plumbed through, the retry decorator should be removed from this function. Note the sibling `fetch_charge` on line 5-7 is correctly retried because `get_charge` is a documented-safe GET; that contrast is what makes this one stand out.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Retry wrapper on non-idempotent API lacks safety documentation
findings.body: The new `charge_card` function applies `@retry(attempts=3)` to `charge()`, which is documented in gateway.py as NOT idempotent and explicitly requires an Idempotency-Key header to make retries safe. The wrapper function has no docstring documenting this contract or the risk of duplicate charges on retry. A caller using this function naively will create multiple charges on transient failures, contrary to the intent of adding retries.

findings.title: No test covers retry behavior on non-idempotent charge_card
findings.body: charge_card wraps the non-idempotent gateway.charge call with @retry(attempts=3). Nothing in this diff (or apparently the existing suite, since none is shown) verifies that retries either pass an idempotency key or otherwise avoid creating duplicate charges on retry. A test simulating a transient failure followed by a successful retry would currently pass even though it results in two real charges — the exact defect this change risks introducing.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` returns a naive local-time datetime, while `invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does; that also fixes the secondary bug of comparing UTC timestamps against local wall-clock time.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Naive datetime comparison with timezone-aware field

findings.title: New expires_within function has no test coverage
findings.body: expires_within is new behavior added in this diff, and no test exercises it. It also uses datetime.now() (naive) instead of datetime.now(timezone.utc), which per models/invite.py's documented invariant (expires_at is always tz-aware) will raise 'TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes' at line 10 the first time it's called. A basic test calling expires_within with a real Invite would have caught this immediately.

findings.title: expires_within returns True for already-expired invites
findings.body: Once the tz bug is fixed, an invite that expired in the past yields a negative `delta`, so `delta.total_seconds() < hours * 3600` is True. If callers use this to decide "expiring soon, send a reminder", already-dead invites will be included. Consider `0 <= delta.total_seconds() < hours * 3600`, or document that expired invites count as within the window.

findings.title: contactEmail throws when billingContact is absent
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` accesses `.email` on it directly, so any account that has not finished onboarding will produce `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')` at runtime. Note that the sibling function `bannerFor` on line 4 already guards the exact same field with `?.` plus a fallback, which confirms the absent case is reachable in practice.

Suggested fix: mirror the existing pattern, e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";` — or change the return type to `string | undefined` and let callers decide the fallback. If the repo compiles with `strictNullChecks`, the current form will also fail type checking.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function lacks contract documentation for optional field

findings.title: contactEmail has no test covering missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail dereferences account.billingContact.email without optional chaining, even though Account.billingContact is documented as optional. No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing exercising contactEmail with an account lacking billingContact — the exact case that would throw a TypeError at runtime. A test calling contactEmail with an account where billingContact is undefined would fail today and catch this regression.

findings.title: Default retry parameter change breaks documented caller dependency
findings.body: The `fetch()` function's default `retries` parameter has been lowered from 5 to 1. However, `sync/nightly.py` contains a docstring that explicitly documents reliance on fetch()'s default retry count to survive a known flaky dependency (INC-4471). The documented contract between this function and its callers is now broken. Either restore the default to 5, or update the docstring in sync/nightly.py and add explicit `retries=5` to that call site.

findings.title: Lowering retries default regresses INC-4471 in nightly partner sync
findings.body:
`fetch()`'s `retries` default drops from 5 to 1. `sync_partner_catalogue()` calls `fetch("https://partner.example.com/catalogue")` with no `retries` argument and its docstring states explicitly that it relies on the default retry count because the partner API 503s roughly one call in three, and that this was the fix for INC-4471. With a ~1/3 per-call failure rate, going from 5 attempts-worth of retries to 1 raises the nightly failure probability from well under 1% to roughly 1-in-9 runs, reintroducing the incident.

Either keep the default at 5, or pass `retries=5` explicitly at the call site in `sync/nightly.py` (and update its docstring so the dependency is no longer implicit) as part of this change. A grep for other no-argument `fetch()` callers is worth doing before merging, since any of them silently inherit the new value too.

findings.title: No test covers fetch()'s default retry count relied on by callers
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() depends on fetch()'s default retries value (previously 5) to survive the partner API's ~33% 503 rate, per the INC-4471 comment. There is no test asserting fetch's default retries or exercising sync_partner_catalogue against a flaky/503-returning dependency, so lowering the default from 5 to 1 has nothing that would fail to signal the regression. Add a test that pins fetch's default retry count (or a test for sync_partner_catalogue that simulates transient 503s) so this class of change is caught.

findings.title: New index duplicates invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_created_idx2` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — identical table, identical column list, identical sort direction to `invoices_tenant_created_idx` already created in `migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql` (applied 2025-11-02). Because the name differs, the statement will succeed rather than error, so this will silently land a second copy of the same B-tree: extra storage, extra write amplification on every INSERT/UPDATE of `invoices`, and extra work for the planner, with zero additional query coverage. Drop this statement; the existing index already serves any `WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC` lookup the reporting feature needs. If the intent was a different shape (e.g. a partial index, a different leading column, or an INCLUDE clause), the definition here does not express it and should be corrected.

findings.title: Referer logged unscrubbed leaks auth token into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the Referer through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging; line 5 now copies `request.headers[header]` verbatim for every header including Referer. `token_authenticated_url` builds notebook URLs as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, and browsers send that full URL in the Referer header on every subresource request, so any 5xx on a subresource writes a live auth token into the log stream. Logs are typically retained, shipped to aggregators, and readable by operators who are not entitled to the token, so this is a credential disclosure, not just noisy output. Restore the per-header scrub for Referer (keeping the `extra_param_keys` argument in play), or strip the query string entirely before logging.

Secondary consequence of the same edit: `extra_param_keys` is now unused inside this loop, so callers that still pass it get silently no scrubbing rather than an error \u2014 a contract that existing callers assume is now a no-op.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token in Referer is written verbatim to the request log

findings.title: Referer header logging behavior changed but not documented
findings.body: The code now logs Referer headers verbatim (line 5), but the surrounding context from identity.py confirms that Referer headers contain auth tokens: 'Notebook URLs are handed out in this form, which means the browser sends the token back in the Referer header on every subresource request.' This means the logging code will now write sensitive tokens to logs without warning. Either add a comment explaining why tokens are now being logged, or restore the scrubbing and document that it happens.

findings.title: Removal of Referer scrubbing has no visible test guarding it
findings.body: The diff removes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, meaning tokens embedded in Referer URLs (per token_authenticated_url) will now be logged verbatim. This is a reintroduction of a previously fixed vulnerability. No test file is part of this change, so if a regression test previously existed asserting that Referer values are scrubbed before logging, it should have failed and blocked this change — but none is shown, and no new test was added to catch this regression going forward.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer URL-validated, reopening javascript: injection
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the schemes listed in `unsafeLinkPrefix` (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` falls out of that branch and reaches whatever the function's default return is, so a value like `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` in author markdown is emitted unchecked. Per the header comment in this same file, the markdown is end-user-submitted and `validateProp` is the only guard before the DOM, so this is directly reachable, not defence-in-depth. `xlink:href` is an SVG alias for `href` and is honoured by browsers on `<a>` inside SVG, so it must be validated identically. Restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in the condition.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer URL-validated, re-enabling SVG XSS

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref sanitisation removal
findings.body: The change removes 'xlinkhref' from the attributes routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed, reverting a prior XSS fix. No test in this diff exercises validateProp with attribute 'xlinkhref' and a javascript:/data:text/html value, so this regression would pass CI silently. Add a test asserting that an xlinkhref attribute with an unsafe URI scheme is rejected by validateProp.

findings.title: Comment claims validateProp is the only XSS protection, but xlink:href is no longer caught
findings.body: The block comment (lines 1-3) states that `validateProp` is 'the only thing standing between that markdown and the DOM', implying comprehensive XSS prevention. However, the change on line 6 removes the check for 'xlinkhref', which means SVG xlink:href attributes can now reach the DOM unsanitized. This makes the documentation actively misleading about what protection this function provides. Either the comment needs to be updated to clarify the limitations, or the xlinkhref check should be restored.

findings.title: Unvalidated project query param reaches filesystem path construction
findings.body:
`query.GetProjectQueryParam()` is now passed downstream with no identifier check. The file DAO's `buildPath` documents that it "does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point" and passes the value straight to `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)`. `filepath.Join` cleans `..` segments, so a value like `../../etc` resolves to a path outside the storage root, allowing reads of documents outside the intended project directory. Additionally, the remaining equality check on line 4 only rejects a mismatch when a path project is also present — a request with only the query parameter set bypasses every check. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` call and the corresponding `HandleBadRequestError` before the value is used.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: project query param no longer validated before filesystem use

findings.title: No test guards against removal of project ID validation
findings.body: The diff deletes the common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) check and its bad-request error return. If this change is wrong (i.e., it reintroduces a path-traversal-capable value flowing to buildPath), nothing in the visible test suite would fail: there is no test exercising list() with a malicious or malformed projectQueryParameter (e.g. containing '../') that asserts a 400 error is returned. Add a regression test that calls list() with an invalid/traversal project query parameter and asserts HandleBadRequestError is returned, so future removal or regression of this check is caught.

findings.title: Buffer sized from client-declared contentLength before body is read
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory based on a value the client asserts in the request, before a single byte of the body has been consumed. A request that declares a huge `Content-Length` (or many concurrent requests each declaring a moderately large one) causes the server to allocate that much backing store regardless of whether the client ever sends the data — the connection can be opened, the header sent, and then stalled. The prior code deliberately grew the RW incrementally as `io.Copy` on line 8 consumed the body, so allocation tracked bytes actually received.

Either restore the incremental growth, or clamp the reservation to a configured maximum part size (and reject `contentLength` above that limit outright) so the declared value can never drive an unbounded allocation.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Buffer reserved from client-declared Content-Length before reading body

findings.title: No test verifies buffer sizing against a large/mismatched contentLength
findings.body: The change adds `.Reserve(contentLength)`, allocating memory based on a client-declared length before the body is read. This is exactly the kind of change that needs a test asserting that (a) a large declared contentLength with a small/absent body doesn't cause unbounded allocation, or (b) the reserved capacity matches actual bytes copied. No test file appears in this diff, so nothing would fail if this allocation strategy were wrong (e.g. if contentLength were attacker-controlled and much larger than the real body).

findings.title: S3 scheme now defaults to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
Previously the scheme was `https` unless the caller explicitly opted out with `request.meta["is_secure"] is False`. After this change the scheme is `https` only when `request.meta.get("is_secure")` is truthy, so every request that does not set the key at all — the common case — is downgraded to `http://`. The resulting URL on line 6 is what the S3 download handler fetches, and S3 requests carry AWS authentication material (an `Authorization` signature header, or presigned query parameters in `p.query`, which is concatenated into `path` on line 5). Sending these over cleartext exposes the signature and the fetched object body to any network observer, and allows an on-path attacker to tamper with the response.

Restore the secure default: `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, so that plaintext requires an explicit opt-out rather than being the fallback.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Default flipped to plaintext HTTP when `is_secure` meta is absent

findings.title: No test covers the scheme-selection default behavior change
findings.body: The diff changes the default scheme when `is_secure` is absent from request.meta: previously it defaulted to "https" (only "http" when explicitly `is_secure is False`), now it defaults to "http" unless `is_secure` is truthy. No test in this change exercises the case where `is_secure` is unset/None, which is exactly the case whose behavior flipped. Without such a test, this regression (or any future reintroduction of it) would not be caught.

findings.title: DELETE now resolves to "push", so push tokens can delete tags
findings.body:
The previous switch had an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"`. The new predicate is `m != http.MethodGet && m != http.MethodHead`, which is true for DELETE, so `requestedAccess` is built with `Action: "push"`. Any credential holding push on a repository will now pass authorisation for DELETE requests, and the "delete" action becomes unreachable — no request can ever produce it, so any policy granting or denying delete is dead configuration.

Restore an explicit DELETE arm: keep pull for GET/HEAD, delete for DELETE, push for the write verbs.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorized as "push", removing the delete permission check

findings.title: Fail-open default: unknown methods now require push instead of pull
findings.body:
The old `default:` arm assigned "pull", the least-privileged action, for any method not explicitly listed (OPTIONS, TRACE, and anything a proxy or client sends). The new form inverts that default: everything other than GET/HEAD is treated as "push". For OPTIONS in particular this means a read-only credential can no longer complete a preflight/capability request that previously succeeded, and a push credential is granted access to method surfaces that were never intended to be write-scoped.

Keep an explicit allowlist of write methods (POST/PATCH/PUT) and fall back to "pull" for anything unrecognised.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE-to-action mapping regression
findings.body: The diff collapses the method-to-action switch so that DELETE now maps to 'push' instead of 'delete', which the PR title itself flags as an inversion of a prior fix. No test file is part of this change, so nothing would fail if this mapping is wrong (e.g. a DELETE request being authorized against a push token instead of a delete token). A test asserting requestedAccess.Action == "delete" for http.MethodDelete would have caught this immediately.

findings.title: Attacker-chosen tenant_id can flush the whole cache, amplifying backend load
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` writes `_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` for whatever `tenant_id` it is handed, including ids that do not exist (the result of `_fetch` is stored unconditionally, so `None`/miss results are cached too). Once the dict crosses 1000 entries the whole cache is discarded with `_CACHE.clear()`, not just the oldest entry. If any request path lets a caller influence `tenant_id`, iterating 1001 junk ids repeatedly evicts every legitimate tenant and forces `_fetch` for all of them — a cheap request-amplification / cache-stampede against whatever `_fetch` talks to.

Mitigations: only insert after confirming the tenant exists and the caller is authorised for it, and evict a bounded number of entries (e.g. `functools.lru_cache` or an LRU/TTL structure) instead of clearing everything.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Overflow clear discards the entry just written by this call

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unsynchronised check-then-act on module-level shared cache

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ A missing tenant may be cached as None and returned as a hit

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh has misleading name for mutating operation
findings.body: The function name `get_tenant_fresh()` follows the `get_*` naming convention, which in most codebases implies a read-only lookup operation. However, this function mutates the cache by storing a value (line 10) and conditionally clearing it (lines 11-12). Callers expecting a side-effect-free getter will be surprised. Consider renaming to `fetch_tenant_fresh()` or `refresh_tenant()` to accurately reflect that this operation has side effects.

findings.title: No test for get_tenant_fresh's cache mutation/eviction behavior
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches a tenant, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by a test in the diff, so a regression (e.g. wrong eviction threshold, failing to update the cache, or clearing on every call) would go unnoticed.

findings.title: README documents renamed CLI flag with old name
findings.body: The README still documents `--workers` as a CLI flag, but the code has been renamed to `--concurrency`. A user following the README will pass an unrecognized flag and the tool will fail. Update line 7 to document the new flag name.

findings.title: Renaming --workers breaks existing callers and argparse attribute
findings.body: `p.add_argument("--workers", ...)` became `p.add_argument("--concurrency", ...)`. This changes two contracts at once: (1) the parsed namespace attribute is now `args.concurrency`, so any code still reading `args.workers` will raise `AttributeError` at runtime rather than failing at import; (2) any existing invocation — scripts, CI jobs, systemd units, Dockerfiles — passing `--workers N` will now exit with argparse's "unrecognized arguments" error (exit code 2). Nothing in this diff updates a call site, and the README one hunk below still documents `--workers`, which is a concrete signal that at least one consumer of the old name was not swept. If the rename is intentional, either grep and update every `args.workers` reader, or keep backward compatibility with `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", type=int, default=4, dest="concurrency")` so old invocations keep working during a deprecation window.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed return type
findings.body: The docstring on line 2 states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to call counts. A caller reading the docstring will attempt to use the return value as an integer (e.g., arithmetic operations, comparisons) and will break. Update the docstring to reflect the new return type and structure.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict without renaming the function
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently misbehave or raise `TypeError`. Either keep the scalar contract and add a separate `daily_usage` function, or update every caller in the same change and rename the function to reflect the new shape. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", which is now false and will mislead callers reading it.

findings.title: No test covers the new day-by-day return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict mapping day -> count instead of a single integer total, but no test file is included in this diff. If the grouping query or dict construction were wrong (e.g., wrong key names, wrong aggregation, or a regression back to returning a scalar), nothing would fail. Add a test asserting the returned dict's structure and values for a known set of rows.

findings.title: Function name no longer matches behavior
findings.body: The function is named `monthly_usage()` but now returns usage broken down by day rather than aggregated monthly totals. Consider renaming to `daily_usage()` or `usage_by_day()` to match the new behavior, or clarify in the docstring that it returns daily breakdowns within the month.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter by old name
findings.body: The docstring on line 6 describes the parameter as `page_size`, but the function signature on line 1 has renamed it to `limit`. A caller reading this docstring would use the wrong parameter name. Update line 6 to say `limit: how many invoices to return.`

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body:
`page_size` is a positional-or-keyword parameter in a module that looks like a public API surface (`api/listing.py`). Any existing caller written as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at call time, not at import time, so it will not be caught by a syntax or import check. Positional callers are unaffected.

Either grep for `page_size=` at every call site and update them in this same change, or keep backwards compatibility temporarily, e.g. accept `page_size=None` as a deprecated alias that is folded into `limit` and warns. If the function is internal-only and all call sites are positional, this is fine 
tbut that should be confirmed before merging.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail at import time
findings.body: Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist on `sys.path` for an installed package. This raises `ImportError` on `import requests` under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import` in effect). It should be `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves off sys.path
findings.body:
Every other intra-package import in this file is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`), but this one is absolute.
